\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving_system&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Emergency heating of the bell")\]

There is a need for emergency heating of divers trapped in a closed diving bell. The breathing gas may be helium based, at a high pressure, and the ambient water temperature may be quite low, down to 2 °C, with a typical temperature in the North Sea of about 5 °C. The bell itself is usually made of steel, a good thermal conductor, and the quality of bell insulation is variable, so the internal atmosphere tends to match the water temperature fairly soon after the primary heating fails. Divers trapped in bells for long periods have been subjected to various degrees of hypothermia when the primary heating systems failed. There have been [deaths attributed to this cause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildrake_diving_accident "Wildrake diving accident").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-IMCA_D059-33)

Passive systems were the first to be developed to a stage where they were considered functionally sufficient, and are relatively simple, economical and immediately available, and are used as standard equipment when applicable. Personal insulation for the diver, in the form of an insulated bag, combined with a breathing gas [heat exchanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_exchanger "Heat exchanger") to conserve the heat of exhaled gas, and heat liberated by a personal [carbon dioxide scrubber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide_scrubber "Carbon dioxide scrubber") kept within the insulation layer round the diver is usually sufficient to keep the divers in thermal balance while waiting for rescue. The scrubber has an orinasal mask, and the bag is secured to the inside of the bell by a harness, to prevent the diver from collapsing if rendered unconscious, and potentially blocking access to the bell by rescuers.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-IMCA_D059-33)[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-hatch-34)

### Communication systems

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving_system&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Communication systems")\]

Helium and high pressure both cause [hyperbaric distortion of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_communications#Hyperbaric_speech_distortion "Diver communications"). The process of talking underwater is influenced by the internal geometry of the life support equipment and constraints on the communications systems as well as the physical and physiological influences of the environment on the processes of speaking and vocal sound production.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Hollien_and_Rothman_2013-35): 6, 16  The use of breathing gases under pressure or containing helium causes problems in intelligibility of diver speech due to distortion caused by the different speed of sound in the gas and the different density of the gas compared to air at surface pressure. These parameters induce changes in the vocal tract [formants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formant "Formant"), which affect the [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre"), and a slight change of [pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_/(music/) "Pitch (music)"). Several studies indicate that the loss in intelligibility is mainly due to the change in the formants.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Daymi_et_al_2005-36)

The difference in density of the breathing gas causes a non-linear shift of low-pitch vocal resonance, due to resonance shifts in the vocal cavities, giving a nasal effect, and a linear shift of vocal resonances which is a function of the velocity of sound in the gas, known as the Donald Duck effect. Another effect of higher density is the relative increase in intensity of voiced sounds relative to unvoiced sounds. The contrast between closed and open voiced sounds and the contrast between voiced consonants and adjacent vowels decrease with increased pressure.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Fant_and_Lindqvist_1968-37) Change of the speed of sound is relatively large in relation to depth increase at shallower depths, but this effect reduces as the pressure increases, and at greater depths a change in depth makes a smaller difference.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Daymi_et_al_2005-36) [Helium speech unscramblers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helium_speech_unscrambler "Helium speech unscrambler") are a partial technical solution. They improve intelligibility of transmitted speech to surface personnel.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Fant_and_Lindqvist_1968-37)

The communications system may have four component systems.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-usn_ch15-2)

*   The hardwired intercom system, an amplified voice system with speech unscrambler to reduce the pitch of the speech of the occupants of the pressurized system. This system will provide communications between the main control console and the bell and accommodation chambers. This two-way system is the primary communications mode.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-usn_ch15-2)
*   Wireless [through-water communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Through-water_communications "Through-water communications") between bell and main control console is a backup system in case of failure of the hardwired system with the bell.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-usn_ch15-2)
*   Closed circuit video from cameras on the bell and diver helmets allow visual monitoring of the dive and the divers by the supervisor.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-usn_ch15-2)
*   A [sound powered phone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_acoustic_communication#Applications "Underwater acoustic communication") system may be provided as a backup voice communication system between bell and control console.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-usn_ch15-2)

The [sanitation system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanitation_system "Sanitation system") includes hot and cold water supply for washbasins and showers, drainage, and [marine toilets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_toilet "Marine toilet") with holding tank and discharge system.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-usn_ch15-2) Clean hot and cold fresh water is supplied either from a holding tank/accumulator at higher pressure than the habitat pressure or directly from a booster pump. The water is fed into the chamber where it is used through a hull penetration with a [quarter-turn shut off valve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarter-turn_valve "Quarter-turn valve") on the outside and a [non-return valve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-return_valve "Non-return valve") on the inside.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-JP_Mag-17)

The usual site for the sanitation system is in the transfer chamber,[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-JP_Mag-17) but there are systems where each living chamber has an attached sanitation chamber.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-JFD_Mod-13)

Toilets have a [valve interlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Valve_interlock&action=edit&redlink=1 "Valve interlock (page does not exist)") system to ensure that the discharge cannot be operated while in use. After use a LST will open the external drain valve. The internal drain valve is opened to depressurise the holding tank then closed and the toilet drain valve opened while the contents are drained into the holding tank, then closed. The holding tank interior drain valve is opened again to discharge the contents to the exterior drain pipe. then closed again and finally the external valve is closed.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-JP_Mag-17)

It is common for the control room of a modular system to be installed in an ISO intermodal container for convenience of transport. There are three main control panels, for life support, dive control and gas management.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-PDC-38)

#### Gas management panel

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving_system&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Gas management panel")\]

The gas management panel includes pressure regulation of gases from high pressure storage, and distribution to the consumers. Gases will include air, oxygen and heliox mixes[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-PDC-38)

#### Saturation life support panel

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving_system&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Saturation life support panel")\]

The chamber control panel will typically include pressure gauges for each compartment, including trunking, blowdown and exhaust valves, oxygen monitoring and other gas analysis equipment, make-up system for oxygen replenishment, valves for supplying therapeutic breathing mixture, closed circuit television monitoring displays, and monitoring systems with alarms for temperature and pressure in the system chambers. Pressures of compartments are usually expresses as metres of feet of seawater.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-PDC-38)

The dive control panel will include depth gauges for bell internal and external pressure, diver and bellman depth, and trunking pressure for transfer to the accommodation chambers. There will also be breathing gas pressure gauges and control valves for each diver, and blowdown and exhaust valves for the bell interior, diver communications systems with speech unscramblers, a through-water emergency communications system to the bell, controls, monitors and recording equipment for helmet and bell mounted video cameras, oxygen analysers for diver breathing gas, oxygen and carbon dioxide analysers for bell and reclaim gas, alarms for reclaim gas flow, dynamic positioning and hot water supply.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-PDC-38)

### Fire suppression system

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving_system&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Fire suppression system")\]

Firefighting systems include hand held fire extinguishers to automatic [deluge sprinkler systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deluge_sprinkler_system "Deluge sprinkler system"). Special fire extinguishers which do not use toxic materials and which will discharge adequately under pressure must be used. In the event of a fire, toxic gases may be released by burning materials, and the occupants will have to use the [built-in breathing systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Built-in_breathing_system "Built-in breathing system") (BIBS) until the chamber gas has been flushed sufficiently. As far as possible, the contents of a saturation system, including firefighting materials, should minimise the production of highly toxic combustion products. When a system with oxygen partial pressure 0.48 bar is pressurized to more than about 70 msw (231 fsw), the oxygen fraction is too low to support combustion (less than 6%), and the fire risk is low. During the early stages of compression and towards the end of decompression the oxygen levels will support combustion, and greater care must be taken.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-usn_ch15-2) The saturation system support team will be provided with firefighting breathing apparatus allowing them to work in smoke and toxic fumes.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)

### Hyperbaric rescue and escape systems

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving_system&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Hyperbaric rescue and escape systems")\]

[![Image 11: End view of a small hyperbaric chamber with open pressure door supported by a steel tubular frame, with two tubular ring floats at the top](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Hyperbaric_escape_module_20151203_133659.jpg/250px-Hyperbaric_escape_module_20151203_133659.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hyperbaric_escape_module_20151203_133659.jpg)

Hyperbaric escape module

[![Image 12: A small steel container housing the controls for the launch system for a hyperbaric escape capsule.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Hyperbaric_escape_module_launch_control_room_20151203_134118.jpg/250px-Hyperbaric_escape_module_launch_control_room_20151203_134118.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hyperbaric_escape_module_launch_control_room_20151203_134118.jpg)

Hyperbaric escape module launch control room

[![Image 13: A-frame gantry over the side of a ship with a hyperbaric rescue chamber suspended over the water.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/THOR_Thrust_Maritime.jpg/250px-THOR_Thrust_Maritime.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:THOR_Thrust_Maritime.jpg)

Hyperbaric rescue chamber recovery drill

A saturated diver who needs to be [evacuated in an emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_evacuation "Emergency evacuation") should preferably be transported without a significant change in their environmental pressure. Hyperbaric evacuation requires pressurised transportation equipment, and could be required in a range of situations:[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-P_D_Handbook_2-40)

*   The support vessel at risk of capsize or sinking.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-P_D_Handbook_2-40)
*   Unacceptable fire or explosion hazard.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-P_D_Handbook_2-40)
*   Failure of the hyperbaric life support system.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-P_D_Handbook_2-40)
*   A medical problem which cannot be dealt with on site.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-P_D_Handbook_2-40)
*   A "lost" bell (a bell which has been broken free of lifting cables and umbilical; the actual position of the bell is usually still known with considerable accuracy).[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-P_D_Handbook_2-40)

A [hyperbaric lifeboat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbaric_lifeboat "Hyperbaric lifeboat") or [rescue chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbaric_rescue_chamber "Hyperbaric rescue chamber") may be provided for emergency evacuation of saturation divers from a saturation system.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-MGD-6) This would be used if the platform is at immediate risk due to fire or sinking, and allows the divers under saturation to get clear of the immediate danger. A hyperbaric lifeboat is self-contained and can be operated by a surface pressure crew while the chamber occupants are under pressure. It must be self-sufficient for several days at sea, in case of a delay in rescue due to sea conditions. It is possible to start decompression after launching if the occupants are medically stable, but seasickness and dehydration may delay the decompression until the module has been recovered.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-IMCA_D052-41): Ch. 2

The rescue chamber or hyperbaric lifeboat will generally be recovered for completion of decompression due to the limited onboard life support and facilities. The recovery plan will include a standby vessel to perform the recovery.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-THOR-42)

The [International Maritime Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Maritime_Organization "International Maritime Organization") (IMO) and [International Marine Contractors Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Marine_Contractors_Association "International Marine Contractors Association") IMCA recognise that though the number of hyperbaric evacuations which have been successfully carried out is small, and the likelihood of an incident needing hyperbaric evacuation is extremely low, the risk is sufficient to justify requiring the equipment to be available. The original meaning for the term _hyperbaric evacuation system_ covered the system that actually transported the divers away from the working hyperbaric system such as a hyperbaric rescue chamber, a self-propelled hyperbaric lifeboat, or [hyperbaric rescue vessel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbaric_rescue_vessel "Hyperbaric rescue vessel"), all of which float and carry short term life-support systems of varied endurance, but it has more recently come to include all of the equipment that would support a hyperbaric evacuation, such as a life support package that can be connected to a recovered hyperbaric rescue unit, to provide interim life support until decompression facilities are available, and the [hyperbaric reception facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbaric_reception_facility "Hyperbaric reception facility") where divers can be decompressed and treated in relative comfort. The four main classes of problem that must be managed during a hyperbaric evacuation are thermal balance, motion sickness, dealing with metabolic waste products, and severely cramped and confined conditions.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-IMCA_D052-41): Ch. 2 [\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-IMO08E-43)

Bell to bell transfer may be used to rescue divers from a lost or entrapped bell. This will generally occur at or near the bottom, and the divers transfer between bells at ambient water pressure.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-P_D_Handbook_2-40) It is possible in some circumstances to use a bell as a rescue chamber to transport divers from one saturation system to another. This may require temporary modifications to the bell, and is only possible if the mating flanges of the systems are compatible.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-P_D_Handbook_2-40)

Personnel requirements
----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving_system&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Personnel requirements")\]

The operation of a saturation system is the work of a team of life support technicians, who are part of the [diving team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_team "Diving team") associated with the diving operation. There is also work for [diving systems technicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_systems_technician "Diving systems technician") to install and maintain the equipment.

### Life support system operation

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving_system&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Life support system operation")\]

A person who operates a saturation diving system is called a [life support technician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_support_technician "Life support technician") (LST).[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-IMCA_D014-5): 23  The life support system is operated by the [life-support technicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life-support_technician "Life-support technician") under the [life-support supervisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life-support_supervisor "Life-support supervisor"), who are part of the [saturation diving team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_team "Saturation diving team"). There will be at least two life support technicians working shifts, as one must be on duty at all times while there are divers under pressure.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Annexure_B-44)

The pressure, oxygen and carbon dioxide content of the breathing gas, and temperature and humidity of the environment are monitored and controlled. Sewage disposal from the habitat, and locking food, stores and equipment into and out of the chambers are also controlled from outside by life support personnel. The LST is also responsible for communication with the divers in saturation, managing transfer of personnel into and out of the accommodation chambers, maintaining the hyperbaric rescue craft and [hyperbaric evacuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbaric_evacuation_and_rescue "Hyperbaric evacuation and rescue") of the divers in an emergency.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-LST-45)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-ADAS_LST-46)

Most saturation diving is done offshore, in the vicinity of drilling and production platforms, or for salvage work, and requires precise positioning of the bell during the dive. In deep water this is usually done from a specialised [diving support vessel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_support_vessel "Diving support vessel"), or a suitable [vessel of opportunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vessel_of_opportunity "Vessel of opportunity") on which a saturation system has been temporarily installed. Positioning can either be by a substantial [anchor pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchor_pattern "Anchor pattern"), which may interfere with other anchoring spreads already established, and which presents its own set of hazards, or by dynamic positioning, which must be sufficiently reliable and fail-safe for the expected conditions.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-SMP-47)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Rana-25) [Heave compensation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heave_compensation "Heave compensation") gear may be used to limit vertical movement when the bell is in the water and clear of the bell cursor, particularly at working depth when the diver may be locked out and the bell is open to ambient pressure.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-IMCA_D022_2016-18)

Underwater habitats
-------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving_system&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Underwater habitats")\]

[![Image 14: A structure of several dome-ended yellow steel cylinders standing on two full-length skids on a concrete slab.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/UWL_Helgoland_im_Nautineum_D%C3%A4nholm%2C_Stralsund%2C_Ansicht_%282008-05-10%29.JPG/250px-UWL_Helgoland_im_Nautineum_D%C3%A4nholm%2C_Stralsund%2C_Ansicht_%282008-05-10%29.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UWL_Helgoland_im_Nautineum_D%C3%A4nholm,_Stralsund,_Ansicht_/(2008-05-10/).JPG)

The German saturation habitat _Helgoland_

[Scientific saturation diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_saturation_diving "Scientific saturation diving") is usually conducted by researchers and technicians known as [aquanauts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquanaut "Aquanaut") living in an [underwater habitat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_habitat "Underwater habitat"), a structure designed for people to live in for extended periods, where they can carry out almost all basic human functions: working, resting, eating, attending to personal hygiene, and sleeping, all while remaining under pressure beneath the surface.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Living1-48)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Schiffspotter-49)

An underwater habitat has to meet the needs of human [physiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology") and provide suitable [environmental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_environment "Natural environment") conditions, and the one which is most critical is [breathing gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas") of suitable quality. Others concern the [physical environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_environment "Physical environment") ([pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure "Pressure"), [temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperature "Temperature"), [light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light "Light"), [humidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humidity "Humidity")), the [chemical environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_chemistry "Environmental chemistry") (drinking water, food, [waste products](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_waste "Human waste"), [toxins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toxin "Toxin")) and the [biological environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecology "Ecology") (hazardous sea creatures, [microorganisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microorganism "Microorganism"), [marine fungi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_fungi "Marine fungi")). Much of the science covering underwater habitats and their technology designed to meet human requirements is shared with [diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving "Underwater diving"), [diving bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell "Diving bell"), surface saturation systems, [submersible vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submersible "Submersible"), [submarines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine "Submarine"), and [spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft "Spacecraft").[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-LivingWorking-50)

Numerous ambient pressure underwater habitats have been designed, built and used around the world since the early 1960s, either by private individuals, research institutions, or by government agencies. They have been used almost exclusively for [research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research "Research") and [exploration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploration "Exploration"). Research has been devoted particularly to the physiological processes and limits of breathing gases under pressure, for [aquanaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquanaut "Aquanaut") and [astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut") training, as well as for research on marine ecosystems. Access to and from the exterior is generally vertically through a hole in the bottom of the structure called a [moon pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon_pool "Moon pool") or wet porch. The habitat may include a decompression chamber, or personnel transfer to the surface may be via a closed diving bell.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Lombardi-51)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Aquarius-52)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-LivingWorking-50)

Systems hazards and risk
------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving_system&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Systems hazards and risk")\]

Risk analysis and management is necessary for acceptably safe saturation diving, and reasonable confidence that the goals of the operation can be achieved and schedules maintained.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39) There are various possible responses to identified risks:

*   A high risk system may be replaced.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Possible failure of a system may be accepted, leaving the residual risk. In some cases this is the only option where there is no suitable response plan in place, and the reserve capacity is acceptable.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Action may be taken to reduce the risk of failure of the sytstem to an acceptable level. [\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Liability for the risk may be transferred to another party, who is then responsible for precautionary measures. [\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Monitoring systems may be established which will give sufficient warning of system status that corrective action can be taken in time to avoid failure or allow safe failure. [\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)

Some hazards of saturation systems which can result in unacceptable consequences, and are therefore considered high risk if not corrected within a short time:

*   Loss of control of oxygen content of the hyperbaric chamber atmosphere or diver breathing gas. These problems can lead to oxygen toxicity or hypoxia, but due to the large volumes of gas in the chambers, will develop slowly, and provided that the monitoring equipment is functional can be manually corrected without great difficulty. Chamber BIBS can be used to provide appropriate breathing gas in an emergency.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Loss of control of the carbon dioxide content of chamber atmosphere or diver breathing gas. In this type of failure there is a upper tolerable short term limit for carbon dioxide content which is significantly higher than the normal chamber level. It too will take some time to develop a high level, and there are redundant scrubbers which can be used when necessary.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Contamination of chamber atmosphere or breating gas.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Loss of control of the temperature of the dry hyperbaric environment or of the diver in the water.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Loss of control over chamber humidity.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Loss of control over chamber pressure is considered the hazard with the greatest risk to saturation divers.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Fire in or around the hyperbaric habitat and support services. After loss of pressure, fire is considered the highest risk hazard to saturation divers. Several hazards which exist independently of fire hazard also exist as complications of fire hazars, such as contamination of chamber gas, loss of control of chamber temperature, and loss of control over chamber pressure. A range of increased fire risk is recognised for oxygen fraction of the chamber atmosphere greater than 6%, which corresponds to pressures less than 70 msw for the usual oxygen partial pressures of living spaces. An upper limit of 23% is imposed when decompession is approaching normal atmospheric pressure.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Circumstances requiring [emergency decompression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_decompression_from_saturation "Emergency decompression from saturation") or [hyperbaric evacuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbaric_evacuation "Hyperbaric evacuation").[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Loss of adequate reserve of breathing gas.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Loss of required quality of breathing gas[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Loss of correct distribution of pressure within the saturarion spaces.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)
*   Failure to maintain the planned decompression profile.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)

The ideal of quantitative risk assessment requires availability of statistics on the probability of occurrence of specific events. Accumulation of such data requires experience with the system, or sufficiently similar systems, components, and service conditions that an analysis can be meaningful. There may be complex interactions of relevant factors, and these may not always be recognised, and some hazards also may not be recognised.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)

Qualitative risk assessment generally falls short when a comparison of risk in different scenarios is desired. Risk assessment also does not always suggest appropriate responses to failure, and tends to have a subjective component due to the varied experience of assessors.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Wo%C5%BAniak_and_Tala%C5%9Bka_2025-39)

Standards and classification
----------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving_system&action=edit&section=34 "Edit section: Standards and classification")\]

Design, manufacture, testing and maintenance may be required to comply with national occupational safety and health regulations for inshore work and IMCA requirements or the equivalent for offshore work.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-IMO08E-43) Saturation systems are generally designed, manufactured, and classified to the standards of a recognised [classification society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_society "Classification society") like [Lloyd's Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd%27s_Register "Lloyd's Register"), [Bureau Veritas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_Veritas "Bureau Veritas"), [American Bureau of Shipping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bureau_of_Shipping "American Bureau of Shipping") or [Det Norske Veritas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Det_Norske_Veritas "Det Norske Veritas") for quality assurance.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-SMP-47)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-JFD_Mod-13)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Rana-25) Relevant standards and guidance include:[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Sat_manual_1-53)

*   IMCA D 024: DESIGN for saturation (bell) diving systems provides guidance on the inspection, testing, and certification of saturation diving systems.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-IMCA_D024-4)[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Sat_manual_1-53)
*   IMCA D 052: Guidance on Hyperbaric Evacuation Systems.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-IMCA_D052-41)[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Sat_manual_1-53)
*   IMCA D 053: DESIGN for the Hyperbaric Reception Facility (HRF) forming part of a Hyperbaric Evacuation System (HES).[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#cite_note-Sat_manual_1-53)

Regulatory and advisory bodies, registration authorities:

*   [International Marine Contractors Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Marine_Contractors_Association "International Marine Contractors Association") (IMCA) – International trade association for the marine contracting industry
*   [United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_Experimental_Diving_Unit "United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit") (NEDU) – US military research and development unit

Manufacturers of saturation diving equipment:

*   [James Fisher & Sons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fisher_%26_Sons "James Fisher & Sons") – British shipowner and provider of marine engineering services
*   [Kirby Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirby_Morgan "Kirby Morgan") – Brand of underwater diving equipment
*   [Diving helmet#Manufacturers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_helmet#Manufacturers "Diving helmet")

Alternative technology:

*   [Surface oriented diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_oriented_diving "Surface oriented diving") – Underwater diving in which the diver starts and finishes at surface pressure
    *   [Bell bounce diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_bounce_diving "Bell bounce diving") – Surface oriented diving using a closed bell
    *   [Transfer under pressure diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transfer_under_pressure_diving "Transfer under pressure diving") (TUP diving) – Surface oriented diving from a closed bell and a chamber for decompression
*   [Atmospheric diving suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit "Atmospheric diving suit") – Articulated pressure-resistant anthropomorphic housing for an underwater diver
*   [Lock-out submersible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lock-out_submersible "Lock-out submersible") – Submersible with an airlock and diving chamber from which divers can be deployed
*   [Remotely operated underwater vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remotely_operated_underwater_vehicle "Remotely operated underwater vehicle") – A tethered underwater mobile device operated by a remote crew

5.content:
[![Image 1: A diver wearing lightweight helmet and hot-water suit working on a piece of corroded and encrusted wreckage with a club hammer](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/US_Navy_010703-N-5329L-005_Diver_working_on_USS_Monitor_salvage.jpg/250px-US_Navy_010703-N-5329L-005_Diver_working_on_USS_Monitor_salvage.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Navy_010703-N-5329L-005_Diver_working_on_USS_Monitor_salvage.jpg)

Saturation diver working on the [USS _Monitor_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Monitor "USS Monitor") wreck at 70 m (230 ft) depth

[![Image 2: A diver in lightweight helmet and hot-water suit sits on a spreader bar while making adjustments. The emergency gas supply cylinder and excursion umbilical are clearly visible.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/US_Navy_020723-N-7479T-002_Navy_diver_conducts_deep_sea_salvage_operations.jpg/250px-US_Navy_020723-N-7479T-002_Navy_diver_conducts_deep_sea_salvage_operations.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Navy_020723-N-7479T-002_Navy_diver_conducts_deep_sea_salvage_operations.jpg)

Saturation diver conducting deep-sea salvage operations

**Saturation diving** is an [ambient pressure diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_pressure_diving "Ambient pressure diving") technique which allows a diver to remain at working depth for extended periods during which the [body tissues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_tissue "Body tissue") become [saturated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solubility "Solubility") with [metabolically inert gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolically_inert_gas "Metabolically inert gas") from the [breathing gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas") mixture. Once saturated, the time required for [decompression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_/(diving/) "Decompression (diving)") to surface pressure will not increase with longer exposure. The diver undergoes a single decompression to surface pressure at the end of the exposure of several days to weeks duration. The ratio of productive working time at depth to unproductive decompression time is thereby increased, and the health risk to the diver incurred by decompression is minimised. Unlike other ambient pressure diving, the saturation diver is only exposed to external ambient pressure while at diving depth.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-usn_ch15-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-NUI-2)

The extreme exposures common in saturation diving make the physiological effects of ambient pressure diving more pronounced, and they tend to have more significant effects on the divers' safety, health, and general well-being. Several short and long term physiological effects of ambient pressure diving must be managed, including [decompression stress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_stress "Decompression stress"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-beyerstein2006-3) [high pressure nervous syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_pressure_nervous_syndrome "High pressure nervous syndrome") (HPNS),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-NUI-2) [compression arthralgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compression_arthralgia "Compression arthralgia"),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Scubadoc-4) [dysbaric osteonecrosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysbaric_osteonecrosis "Dysbaric osteonecrosis"), [oxygen toxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity "Oxygen toxicity"),[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Imbert_et_al_2024-5) [inert gas narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inert_gas_narcosis "Inert gas narcosis"),[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-usn-6) high [work of breathing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_of_breathing "Work of breathing"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Mitchell_2024-7) and disruption of thermal balance.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Neves_and_Thomas-8)

Most saturation diving procedures are common to all surface-supplied diving, but there are some which are specific to the use of a closed bell, the restrictions of excursion limits, and the use of saturation decompression. Surface saturation systems transport the divers to the worksite in a closed bell, use [surface-supplied diving equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving_equipment "Surface-supplied diving equipment"), and are usually installed on an [offshore platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offshore_platform "Offshore platform") or [dynamically positioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamically_positioned "Dynamically positioned") [diving support vessel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_support_vessel "Diving support vessel"). Divers operating from [underwater habitats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_habitats "Underwater habitats") may use surface-supplied equipment from the habitat or [scuba equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_equipment "Scuba equipment"), and access the water through a [wet porch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wet_porch "Wet porch"), but will usually have to surface in a closed bell, unless the habitat includes a [decompression chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_chamber "Decompression chamber").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Living1-9) The life support systems provide breathing gas, climate control, and sanitation for the personnel under pressure, in the accommodation and in the bell and the water. There are also communications, fire suppression and other emergency services.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Crawford_2016-10) Bell services are provided via the [bell umbilical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_umbilical "Bell umbilical") and distributed to divers through [excursion umbilicals](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Excursion_umbilicals&action=edit&redlink=1 "Excursion umbilicals (page does not exist)").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-usn_ch15-1)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Crawford_2016-10) Life support systems for emergency evacuation are independent of the accommodation system as they must travel with the evacuation module.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-IMCA_D052-11)

Saturation diving is a specialized [mode of diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mode_of_underwater_diving "Mode of underwater diving");[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Class_1_diver_training_standard-12) of the 3,300 commercial divers employed in the United States in 2015,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-bls-13) 336 were saturation divers.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Fed_reg_2015-14) Special training and certification is required, as the activity is inherently hazardous, and a set of standard operating procedures, emergency procedures, and a range of specialised equipment is used to control the risk, that require consistently correct performance by all the members of an extended diving team.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-usn-6)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-PDC-15) The combination of relatively large skilled personnel requirements, complex engineering, and bulky, heavy equipment required to support a saturation diving project make it an expensive diving mode, but it allows direct human intervention at places that would not otherwise be practical, and where it is applied, it is generally more economically viable than other options, if such exist.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-economics-16)

On December 22, 1938, [Edgar End](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edgar_End&action=edit&redlink=1 "Edgar End (page does not exist)") and [Max Nohl](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Max_Nohl&action=edit&redlink=1 "Max Nohl (page does not exist)") made the first intentional saturation dive by spending 27 hours breathing air at 101 [feet sea water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feet_sea_water "Feet sea water") (fsw) (30.8 [metres sea water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metres_sea_water "Metres sea water") (msw) in the County Emergency Hospital recompression facility in [Milwaukee, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee,_Wisconsin "Milwaukee, Wisconsin"). Their decompression lasted five hours leaving Nohl with a mild case of decompression sickness that resolved with [recompression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Therapeutic_recompression "Therapeutic recompression").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Bove2ndEd-17)

[Albert R. Behnke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_R._Behnke "Albert R. Behnke") proposed the idea of exposing humans to increased ambient pressures long enough for the blood and tissues to become [saturated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solubility "Solubility") with inert gases in 1942.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-LivingWorking-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Behnke1942-19) In 1957, [George F. Bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_F._Bond "George F. Bond") began the [Genesis project](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Genesis_project&action=edit&redlink=1 "Genesis project (page does not exist)") at the [Naval Submarine Medical Research Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Submarine_Medical_Research_Laboratory "Naval Submarine Medical Research Laboratory") proving that humans could in fact withstand prolonged exposure to different [breathing gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas") and increased environmental pressures.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-LivingWorking-18)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-FaceplateMurray-20) Once saturation is achieved, the amount of time needed for [decompression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_stop "Decompression stop") depends on the depth and gases breathed, and does not increase with further exposure. This was the beginning of saturation diving and the US Navy's [Man-in-the-Sea Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man-in-the-Sea_Program&action=edit&redlink=1 "Man-in-the-Sea Program (page does not exist)").[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Pressure1983-21) The first commercial saturation dives were performed in 1965 by [Westinghouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westinghouse_Electric_/(1886/) "Westinghouse Electric (1886)") to replace faulty [trash racks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trash_rack "Trash rack") at 200 feet (61 m) on the [Smith Mountain Dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith_Mountain_Dam "Smith Mountain Dam").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Bove2ndEd-17) In the same year, the [Conshelf III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conshelf_III "Conshelf III") experiment was carried out by [Jacques Cousteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Cousteau "Jacques Cousteau") and a group of divers for three weeks at the depth of 100 m.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-legacy-22)

[Peter B. Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_B._Bennett "Peter B. Bennett") is credited with the invention of [trimix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimix_/(breathing_gas/) "Trimix (breathing gas)") breathing gas as a method to eliminate [high pressure nervous syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_pressure_nervous_syndrome "High pressure nervous syndrome"). In 1981, at the [Duke University Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_University_Medical_Center "Duke University Medical Center"), Bennett conducted an experiment called _Atlantis III_, which involved subjecting volunteers to a pressure of 2250 fsw (686 msw), and slowly decompressing them to atmospheric pressure over a period of over 31 days, setting an early world record for depth-equivalent pressure in the process. A later experiment, _Atlantis IV_, encountered problems as one of the volunteers experienced [euphoric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphoria "Euphoria") [hallucinations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallucination "Hallucination") and [hypomania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypomania "Hypomania").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Atlantis2007-23)

Early experiments in saturation diving were often done in underwater habitats, usually serviced by surface vessels, but in relatively exposed waters the advantage of being able to abandon the site in bad conditions encouraged the use of saturation facilities on board the support vessel, where logistics are simplified.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Imbert_et_al_2024-5)

The history of commercial saturation diving is closely linked to [offshore oil and gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offshore_oil_and_gas "Offshore oil and gas") extraction. In the early 1960s exploration of the North Sea started on the premise that the Dutch gas fields might extend under the sea. This was borne out when the [Gulf Tide](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gulf_Tide&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gulf Tide (page does not exist)") drill rig hit the [Ekofisk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekofisk "Ekofisk") reservoir in 1969, and in 1971 [Shell oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_oil "Shell oil") found the [Brent oilfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brent_oilfield "Brent oilfield") between Norway and [Shetland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shetland "Shetland"). From this time to the 1990s the industry developed the procedures and equipment for saturation diving from pioneering and experimental, with a somewhat dubious safety record, to a mature industry with greatly improved occupational health and safety.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Balestra_and_Germonpre_2017-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Gyerde_and_Ryggvik_2014-25)

The first US Navy saturation procedures were published in the US Navy Diving Manual revision 2 of 1979. They allowed an [upward excursion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upward_excursion "Upward excursion") to start decompression, used a constant decompression rate deeper than 60 msw and varied rates from 60 msw to surface. Decompression was interrupted for a night stop and an afternoon stop, and partial pressure of oxygen was constant deeper than the fire risk zone, after which oxygen fraction was limited.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Imbert_et_al_2024-5)

When the North Sea drilling started, there was little diving support infrastructure in Europe, and the high wages attracted divers from the Gulf of Mexico oilfields, who introduced the fibre reinforced resin [lightweight demand helmets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightweight_demand_helmet "Lightweight demand helmet") from [Kirby Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirby_Morgan "Kirby Morgan"), [hot water suits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_water_suit "Hot water suit") from [Diving Unlimited International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_Unlimited_International "Diving Unlimited International"), and the [U.S. Navy Diving Manual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Navy_Diving_Manual "U.S. Navy Diving Manual"), at the time the leading set of offshore diving procedures. Research and development money was available, and new technical developments were supported by the [European Economic Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Economic_Community "European Economic Community"). A major challenge was developing saturation diving practices suitable to the common North Sea depth range of 100 to 180 m.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Balestra_and_Germonpre_2017-24)

During the early drilling stages most of the diving work was for relatively short periods and was generally suitable for [bell bounce diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_bounce_diving "Bell bounce diving"), but the development of oilfield seabed infrastructure required much longer diver interventions, and saturation diving procedures were developed to suit. By 1982, a large amount of shallow maintenance work was becoming necessary, which brought in more air diving to service the rigs. By 2017 about 80% of North Sea diving was heliox saturation diving and the other 20% shallow air diving.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Balestra_and_Germonpre_2017-24)

Excursion dives without decompression stops can be done both upward and downward from saturation storage pressure within limits, allowing the divers a range of working depths, and if work is required beyond excursion range, the divers can be compressed or decompressed in storage to suit the changed depth range. Further work was done by the [United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_Experimental_Diving_Unit "United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit") on excursion dives from February 1974 to June 1976, and the results published in the 1984 U.S. Navy Diving Manual.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Balestra_and_Germonpre_2017-24) These tables used a partial pressure of oxygen of 0.35 to 0.4 bar during decompression, with quite slow decompression rates, which varied with the depth, getting slower as the depth decreased, with a 6-hour stop from midnight and a two-hour stop from 14:00 and a gas fraction limit for oxygen of 22% for the last part of the ascent to reduce fire risk. The tables allowed decompression to start directly after return from a dive provided there had not been an upward excursion, as this was found to increase the risk of bubble development.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Balestra_and_Germonpre_2017-24)

At the same time, the commercial diving contractor [Compagnie maritime d'expertises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compagnie_maritime_d%27expertises "Compagnie maritime d'expertises") (COMEX) had been developing slightly different decompression procedures, in which the oxygen partial pressures were higher, between 0.6 and 0.8 bar, and the ascent rates were faster to take advantage of the high PO2. Continuous decompression without night stops was used, and excursions were allowed. Over time these were revised to use lower PO2 and slower ascent rates, particularly at the shallower depths. Competing tables were thought to be used to gain competitive advantage, so in 1988 the [Norwegian Petroleum Directorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Petroleum_Directorate "Norwegian Petroleum Directorate") organised a conference on saturation decompression safety under [Val Hempleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Hempleman "Val Hempleman"),[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Balestra_and_Germonpre_2017-24) and in 1990 a conference to harmonise the saturation tables to be used in the Norwegial sector of the North Sea used input from five contractors. In 1999 the [NORSOK U100 standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NORSOK_U100_standard&action=edit&redlink=1 "NORSOK U100 standard (page does not exist)") was published, which was a compromise using aspects of several of the tables, and has proven in use to be sufficiently conservative with a good safety record.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Balestra_and_Germonpre_2017-24)

In the 1980s the Royal Navy were using an oxygen partial pressure of 0.42 bar for decompression from saturation, which is slightly higher than the 0.40 bar of the US Navy table. This reduced the time for decompression by a small percentage.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Leitch_1985-26)

The 1981 salvage of the gold on [HMS Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Edinburgh "HMS Edinburgh") at 256 m was the first commercial use of helium reclaim systems,and set a new depth record for sustained commercial saturation diving.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-JFD_Edinburgh-27)

Saturation decompression in the Brazil oilfields took a slightly different route, and was originally based on company tables, until Brazil produced their own legislation in 1988, similar to that of the UK's [Health and Safety Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_and_Safety_Executive "Health and Safety Executive"). In 2004 revised legislation was closer to the COMEX procedures.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Balestra_and_Germonpre_2017-24)

There have been no major research projects since the Norwegian deep diving contracts, and since then commercial procedures have evolved through cumulative empirical adjustments based on the experience of freelance personnel moving between companies, changes due to mergers and takeovers between contractors, and guidance by regulations, industry standards and client requirements.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Imbert_et_al_2024-5) By 2017 the system had settled into a chamber PO2 of 0.5 bar while deeper than 15 msw, and limited to 22 to 23% at the end of decompression to limit fire risk.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Balestra_and_Germonpre_2017-24)

### Extreme depth effects

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Extreme depth effects")\]

A breathing gas mixture of oxygen, helium and hydrogen ([hydreliox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydreliox "Hydreliox")) was developed for use at extreme diving pressures to reduce the effects of high pressure nervous syndrome. Between 1978 and 1984, a group of divers at Duke University in North Carolina conducted the _Atlantis_ series of onshore [hyperbaric chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_chamber#Hyperbaric_chamber "Diving chamber") deep experimental dives.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Atlantis2007-23) In 1981, during an extreme depth test dive to 686 metres (2251 ft) they breathed a conventional heliox mixture with difficulty and experienced tremors and memory lapses.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Atlantis2007-23)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-NS1992-28)

A ([hydreliox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydreliox "Hydreliox")) gas mixture was used during a similar experimental chamber dive by three divers for the French [Comex S.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compagnie_maritime_d%27expertises "Compagnie maritime d'expertises") [offshore diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_diving#Commercial_diving "Commercial diving") contractor in 1992. On 18 November 1992, Comex stopped the dive at a pressure of 675 [meters of sea water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre_sea_water "Metre sea water") (msw) (2215 fsw) because the divers were suffering from insomnia and fatigue. All three divers were willing to continue, but the research leader decided to decompress the chamber to 650 msw (2133 fsw). On 20 November, Comex diver Theo Mavrostomos was allowed to continue but spent only two hours at 701 msw (2300 fsw), although the intention had been to spend four and a half days at this depth and perform planned tasks.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-NS1992-28)

It has heavy lifting gear on the quarterdeck and a helipad over the forecastle.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Iremis_da_Vinci_at_the_Albert_Dock_Basin%2C_Port_of_Leith.jpg/250px-Iremis_da_Vinci_at_the_Albert_Dock_Basin%2C_Port_of_Leith.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iremis_da_Vinci_at_the_Albert_Dock_Basin,_Port_of_Leith.jpg)
