A **saturation diving system** is the combined and installed equipment required to support a saturation diving operation. It may be an underwater habitat, or more commonly for commercial diving operations, a hyperbaric habitat complex, known in the industry as a saturation spread, assembled on a surface platform, supported by a range of surface support equipment, some of which is common to other surface-supplied diving activities, and some of which is used mostly or only for saturation diving. Much of the equipment can be classed as [life-support equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life-support_equipment "Life-support equipment"), and some of it is required for emergency and rescue functions.

The basic components include living space accommodations for the divers when they are not diving, with sanitation facilities and a means of providing supplies to the occupants. There area also facilities for compression and decompression, treatment of dysbaric maladies, transfer under pressure between accommodation and transportation modules for transport between the accommodation and workplace, and for emergency evacuation. Units are interconnected by trunking and can be isolated by airlock doors.

Auxiliary and support equipment includes:

*   The hyperbaric life support systems
*   Breathing gas supply, distribution and recycling equipment: scrubbers, filters, boosters, compressors, mixing, monitoring, and storage facilities[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Crawford_2016-10) The divers use [surface-supplied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving "Surface-supplied diving") umbilical diving equipment, usually utilizing deep diving [breathing gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas"), such as helium and oxygen mixtures, stored in large capacity, high pressure [gas storage cylinders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas_storage_cylinder "Gas storage cylinder").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-beyerstein2006-3)
*   [Built-in breathing systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Built-in_breathing_system "Built-in breathing system")
*   Chamber climate control system – control of temperature and humidity, and filtration of gas[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Crawford_2016-10)
*   Instrumentation, control, monitoring and communications equipment[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Crawford_2016-10)
*   [Fire suppression systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#Fire_suppression_system "Saturation diving system")[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Crawford_2016-10)
*   [Sanitation systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving_system#Sanitation_system "Saturation diving system")[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Crawford_2016-10)
*   [Bell launch and recovery system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_and_recovery_system_/(diving/) "Launch and recovery system (diving)")
*   Control rooms for diving operations and saturation system life support
*   [Hyperbaric evacuation and rescue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbaric_evacuation_and_rescue "Hyperbaric evacuation and rescue") systems[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-IMCA_D052-11)

The diving depth record for offshore diving was achieved in 1988 by a team of [professional divers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_diver "Professional diver") (Th. Arnold, S. Icart, J.G. Marcel Auda, R. Peilho, P. Raude, L. Schneider) of the Comex S.A. [industrial deep-sea diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_diving#Commercial_diving "Commercial diving") company performing pipe line connection exercises at a depth of 534 [meters of sea water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meters_of_sea_water "Meters of sea water") (msw) (1752 fsw) in the [Mediterranean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea") during a record scientific dive.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Ciesielski_and_Imbert_1989-79)[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Hydra_8-80)[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-NS1992-2-81)

In the real working conditions of the offshore oil industry, in Campos Basin, Brazil, Brazilian saturation divers from the DSV _Stena Marianos_ (later _Mermaid Commander_ (2006)) performed a manifold installation for [Petrobras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrobras "Petrobras") at 316 metres (1,037 ft) depth in February 1990. When a lift bag attachment failed, the equipment was carried by the bottom currents to 328 metres (1,076 ft) depth, and the Brazilian diver Adelson D'Araujo Santos Jr. made the recovery and installation.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-ScubaRec-82)

In 1992, Greek diver Theodoros Mavrostomos of the Comex S.A. achieved a simulated 701 m (2,300 ft) of seawater depth in an on shore [hyperbaric chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_chamber#Hyperbaric_chamber "Diving chamber"). He took 43 days to complete the record experimental dive, where a hydrogen–helium–oxygen gas mixture was used as [breathing gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas").[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-NS1992-28)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-pmid7742710-83)[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-comex_hx-84)[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Comex_HEC-85)[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-ClickDive-86)[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Diving_heritage_2022-87)

The complexity, medical problems and accompanying high costs of professional diving to such extreme depths and the development of deep water [atmospheric diving suits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit "Atmospheric diving suit") and [ROVs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remotely_operated_underwater_vehicle "Remotely operated underwater vehicle") in offshore oilfield drilling and production have effectively eliminated the need for ambient pressure manned intervention at extreme depths for some applications.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-ROV-88)

The primary purpose of saturation diving is to extend the useful working time for dives without increasing the exposure to risk of decompression sickness There is also a secondary benefit that the reduced compression rates that are possible can reduce or avoid HPNS and compression arthralgia, making deeper dives practicable. There is a trade-off against other risks associated with living under high-pressure saturation conditions, and the financial cost is high due to the complex infrastructure and expensive equipment and consumables required. The risk of decompression sickness is reduced at the cost of increased risk due to being committed to the saturation environment for the duration of the decompression schedule associated with the storage depth. Hyperbaric evacuation from saturation is possible, but not universally available, and is logistically complicated. Having an evacuation system on standby is expensive.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-IMCA_D052-11)

Some notable saturation diving incidents include:

*   [_Byford Dolphin_ diving bell accident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byford_Dolphin_diving_bell_accident "Byford Dolphin diving bell accident") – Explosive decompression of an occupied saturation chamber
*   [_Drill Master_ diving accident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drill_Master_diving_accident "Drill Master diving accident") – Fatal diving bell accident off Norway in 1974
*   [_Star Canopus_ diving accident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Canopus_diving_accident "Star Canopus diving accident") – Fatal offshore diving bell accident in 1978
*   [_Stena Seaspread_ diving accident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stena_Seaspread_diving_accident "Stena Seaspread diving accident") – Saturation diving bell incident with successful rescue in the North Sea in 1981
*   [_Venture One_ diving accident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_One_diving_accident "Venture One diving accident") – Saturation diving fatality in the North Sea in 1977
*   [_Waage Drill II_ diving accident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waage_Drill_II_diving_accident "Waage Drill II diving accident") – Fatal saturation diving accident in the North Sea in 1975
*   [_Wildrake_ diving accident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildrake_diving_accident "Wildrake diving accident") – Fatal offshore diving accident in Scotland, 1979
*   _Bibby Topaz_ diving accident, documented by the 2019 film [_Last Breath_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Breath_/(2019_film/) "Last Breath (2019 film)")

### Incidence of decompression sickness

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Incidence of decompression sickness")\]

It is difficult to assess decompression risk in recent saturation decompressions as the data is generally not available, however it is known to be very uncommon since 2000, with some operators not having any cases in a 10-year period, while in the early days it was in the order of 1%. Saturation decompression is most likely to produce joint pain symptoms in the late stages of decompression. Venous gas bubbles are generally detected without symptomatic DCS, but this has also become rare.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Imbert_et_al_2024-5)

### Oxygen content of breathing gases

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving&action=edit&section=34 "Edit section: Oxygen content of breathing gases")\]

In nominal conditions, the human body functions normally with an oxygen partial pressure of about 0.21 bar. In saturation conditions a partial pressure of approximately double this value is chosen for the accommodations as it gives a large margin in case of accidental pressure loss – pressure in the chamber could drop by 50% and still support consciousness, allowing the divers to respond effectively to the emergency. This has actually happened, and the divers were able to close off necessary internal valves and pressure was duly restored. This partial pressure is approaching the upper limits of long term tolerability, so higher partial pressures can only be used for shorter exposures where there is a more urgent need. This is typically the case when the divers are in the water, particularly if there is an in-water depth excursion from storage depth, and during final decompression, where the efficacy of decompression is strongly dependent on the [oxygen window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_window "Oxygen window").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Imbert_et_al_2024-5) In an emergency decompression the partial pressure may be increased to a level where temporary lung injury may occur as this is likely to be less severe than decompression sickness.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Imbert_et_al_2022-76)

The closed, warm, humid, and hyperoxic internal environment of a saturation facility is conducive to microbial growth and associated infections, particularly of the external ear canal and minor soft tissue injuries. Potential sources include contaminated water supplies, food and equipment. Gram negative bacteria are a common problem. Good personal hygiene, adequate cleaning and disinfection of the chamber, and maintaining a relatively low humidity can reduce these risks. Routine microbial analysis can ensure that cleaning and disinfection is effective.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-DMAC26-65)

### Minimum gas requirements

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: Minimum gas requirements")\]

A saturation diving operation must be able to recover from any reasonably foreseeable contingency with minimum risk to the health of the divers, and one possible contingency is a substantial loss of gas from the accommodations. Sufficient backup gas must be provided to recompress and carry out a controlled decompression. Even with exhaled gas reclaim, there is unavoidable loss of diver and bell gas and the quantity of planned backup and bailout gas is also based on working depth and number of planned dives. Therapeutic gas supplies are also required in case of need, and their quantity is also based on the number of divers and maximum operational depth.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-IMCA_D_050-89)

### Training and registration

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saturation_diving&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: Training and registration")\]

Training of saturation divers generally takes place at commercial diving schools registered to train saturation divers, and having the required infrastructure and equipment.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-CoP_Training-90) Diver training standards for saturation divers are published by a small number of organisations, and there is some international recognition of equivalence. The prerequisites for starting training are generally that the diver is already qualified as a bell diver and has a specified number of dives and hours of experience since qualifying.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-PDC-15)

Training of saturation divers generally starts with a competent and at least moderately experienced surface oriented bell diver and concentrates on the additional knowledge and skills required for saturation diving. There is a large additional technical component related to the specialised equipment. For the South African Department of Labour Class I Diver, the additional knowledge and skills include:[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Class_1_diver_training_standard-12)

*   A basic knowledge of the history of mixed gas and saturation diving,[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Class_1_diver_training_standard-12)
*   An understanding of modular and diving support vessel based saturation diving systems, saturation life-support systems including environmental control, diver heating systems, sump drains and hyperbaric toilet discharges[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Class_1_diver_training_standard-12)
*   An understanding and practical operating skills for closed diving bells, their standard and emergency equipment, handling systems, bell and excursion umbilicals and personal diving equipment, and their testing and maintenance requirements,[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Class_1_diver_training_standard-12)
*   An understanding and practical operating skills for transfer under pressure and closed bell diving from 4-point moored and dynamically positioned vessels.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Class_1_diver_training_standard-12)
*   An understanding of gas supplies and saturation consumables, including minimum gas requirements, gas transfer pumps, gas blending, and gas reclaim systems,
*   An understanding and practical experience in committing divers to saturation, and pressurisation.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Class_1_diver_training_standard-12)
*   An understanding of split level saturation diving.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Class_1_diver_training_standard-12)
*   Knowledge of the minimum personnel requirements for saturation diving operations and the responsibilities of the diving team members, including the superintendent, supervisor, life support supervisor, life support technician, support and systems technicians, gas man, and the bellman and diver, and experience and skills as diver and bellman.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Class_1_diver_training_standard-12)
*   Knowledge of saturation decompression procedures, emergency saturation decompression and hyperbaric evacuation and practical experience of standard procedures and simulated emergency procedures.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Class_1_diver_training_standard-12)
*   Certification as a level 2 first aider, with additional knowledge of saturation hygiene, saturation first aid requirements and the deep diving compression disorders, high pressure nervous syndrome and compression arthralgia.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Class_1_diver_training_standard-12)

The living and working conditions of the saturation diver are unusual. There are shifting demands and large contrasts. The diver is required to be adaptable to the variations in work and coworkers, and to do so for several weeks at a time. The future of the occupation is uncertain and linked to the oil and gas industry. The work environment and living conditions on contract tend to be monotonous, but they are interspersed with periods of leisure. There is a conflict between family commitments and extended work periods in relative isolation, but in the continuous close proximity with a small group of co-workers. The job is prestigious, the pay is good, and there are fairly long periods of leisure between jobs. The occupation needs mental endurance, flexibility, and willingness to adapt and learn. Maintaining personal routines may help in maintaining mental health. The quality of the team can have a large effect on the members. The ability to get along well with each other and mutual trust are important to cooperation and efficiency in a group who depend on each other for safety and sometimes for survival. A sense of humour is an advantage, though there is a tendency for this to be relatively dark, possibly due to the high risk environment.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Romsbotn_et_al_2022-91)

Offshore saturation diving was developed as a tool for a job. The procedures and equipment evolved to meet the demand for the specific work, and in the development years of offshore petroleum extraction, money was available for research and development. As oilfield diving operations became deeper, the ratio of productive time on the job compared to decompression reduced for surface oriented diving, and the possibility of improving the cost benefit balance by reducing overall unproductive and relatively high risk decompression time became more financially attractive.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Gyerde_and_Ryggvik_2014-25) Saturation diving incurs significant costs and provides significant benefits.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-economics-16) The use of observation and work class [ROVs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remotely_operated_underwater_vehicle "Remotely operated underwater vehicle") has been integrated with saturation diving, which has improved efficiency and safety.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Offshore_Energy-92)[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-IMCA_D014-68)

The initial investment includes the purchase and installation of specialized equipment and the infrastructure required to support the system. Operational expenses of running the system are also large, and include skilled personnel in an intermittently competitive and volatile economic environment heavily dependent on current oil price. Regular maintenance and occasionally repair, replacement, and upgrading, is essential to ensure that the equipment remains safe and efficient and sufficiently flexible to adapt to changing needs and standards. The cost of the appropriate gas mixtures for breathing and pressurization is high, and availability of helium is variable.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-economics-16)

The large capital outlay required to set up a saturation system made it desirable to utilise the hardware as much as possible, which encouraged the use of specialist contractors.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Gyerde_and_Ryggvik_2014-25)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-HSE-29) The often fatal or crippling consequences of human error or equipment failure made health and safety concerns important. The offshore location of much of the work made industry self-regulation possible and desirable, but occasionally government intervention was necessary to prevent excessive cutting of corners for profit forcing competitors to follow the lead of the least ethical practices.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-economics-16)

Although the costs are high there are several compelling benefits that can justify the investment for some types of operations.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-economics-16) A big advantage is increased operational efficiency. Productive working time is greatly enhanced when the decompression time is moved to the end of the job, allowing workers to spend more time on the task, particularly on complex projects, where knowledge and experience on the particular task is retained within the working group.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-economics-16)

The controlled saturation living environment, although stressful and relatively uncomfortable, is less stressful and uncomfortable than the surface oriented alternative, and the safety advantage of a single slow decompression minimises health related hazards and risks.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-economics-16)

Saturation diving also allows work at depths that would not be possible by surface oriented diving due to health limits on the speed of compression to those depths.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-economics-16)

Of the 3,300 commercial divers employed in the United States in 2015,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-bls-13) 336 were saturation divers.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Fed_reg_2015-14) Special training and certification is required, as the activity is inherently hazardous, and a set of standard operating procedures, emergency procedures, and a range of specialised equipment is used to control the risk, that require consistently correct performance by all the members of an extended diving team.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-usn-6)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-PDC-15) The combination of relatively large skilled personnel requirements, complex engineering, and bulky, heavy equipment required to support a saturation diving project make it an expensive diving mode, but it allows direct human intervention at places that would not otherwise be practical, and where it is applied, it is generally more economically viable than other options, if such exist.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-economics-16)

In 2019, [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") released _[Last Breath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Breath_/(2019_film/) "Last Breath (2019 film)")_, a documentary which tells the story of Chris Lemons, a saturation diver who survived 38 minutes without a surface-supplied breathing gas supply after the vessel's [dynamic positioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_positioning "Dynamic positioning") system failed during a storm, setting off a [red alert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_positioning#Dynamic_positioning_alarm_and_runout_response_for_bell_divers "Dynamic positioning"). The two working divers started returning to the [bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell#Closed_bell "Diving bell"), but the ship drifted from the work site, dragging the bell with it, and his umbilical was snagged and severed under the load. He was able to return to the workplace using his bailout set, so was easily found by an [ROV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remotely_operated_underwater_vehicle "Remotely operated underwater vehicle") from the ship, but his [bailout gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailout_gas "Bailout gas") was insufficient for the time it took to get the ship back on position for a rescue attempt from the bell. Although presumed dead by support crew aboard the vessel, he was recovered by the second diver and successfully resuscitated in the bell. It has been hypothesised that his survival may have been a result of [hypothermia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothermia "Hypothermia"), high partial pressure of oxygen in the bailout gas, or a combination. The ROV video footage shows him twitching while unconscious, which is consistent with an [oxygen toxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity "Oxygen toxicity") blackout.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-Independent-93)[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#cite_note-inews-94)

[![Image 1: Two divers wearing lightweight demand helmets stand back-to-back on an underwater platform holding on to the railings. The photo also shows the support vessel above the surface in the background.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Diving_stage.jpg/250px-Diving_stage.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Diving_stage.jpg)

Surface-supplied divers riding a stage to the underwater workplace

**Underwater diving**, as a human activity, is the practice of descending below the water's surface to interact with the environment. It is also often referred to as [diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_/(disambiguation/) "Diving (disambiguation)"), an ambiguous term with several possible meanings, depending on context. Immersion in water and exposure to high [ambient pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_pressure "Ambient pressure") have [physiological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology") effects that limit the depths and duration possible in [ambient pressure diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_pressure_diving "Ambient pressure diving"). Humans are not physiologically and anatomically well-adapted to the environmental conditions of diving, and various equipment has been developed to extend the depth and duration of human dives, and allow different types of work to be done.

In ambient pressure diving, the diver is directly exposed to the pressure of the surrounding water. The ambient pressure diver may dive on breath-hold ([freediving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freediving "Freediving")) or use breathing apparatus for [scuba diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_diving "Scuba diving") or [surface-supplied diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving "Surface-supplied diving"), and the [saturation diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving "Saturation diving") technique reduces the risk of [decompression sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_sickness "Decompression sickness") (DCS) after long-duration deep dives. [Atmospheric diving suits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit "Atmospheric diving suit") (ADS) may be used to isolate the diver from high ambient pressure. Crewed [submersibles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submersible "Submersible") can extend depth range to [full ocean depth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_ocean_depth "Full ocean depth"), and remotely controlled or robotic machines can reduce risk to humans.

The environment exposes the diver to a wide range of hazards, and though the risks are largely controlled by appropriate [diving skills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_skills "Scuba skills"), [training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_training "Diver training"), types of [equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_equipment "Diving equipment") and [breathing gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas") used depending on the mode, depth and purpose of diving, it remains a relatively dangerous activity. Professional diving is usually regulated by occupational health and safety legislation, while recreational diving may be entirely unregulated. Diving activities are restricted to maximum depths of about 40 metres (130 ft) for recreational scuba diving, 530 metres (1,740 ft) for commercial saturation diving, and 610 metres (2,000 ft) wearing atmospheric suits. Diving is also restricted to conditions which are not excessively hazardous, though the level of risk acceptable can vary, and fatal incidents may occur.

[Recreational diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_diving "Recreational diving") (sometimes called sport diving or subaquatics) is a popular leisure activity. [Technical diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_diving "Technical diving") is a form of recreational diving under more challenging conditions. [Professional diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_diving "Professional diving") (commercial diving, diving for research purposes, or for financial gain) involves working underwater. [Public safety diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_safety_diving "Public safety diving") is the underwater work done by law enforcement, fire rescue, and [underwater search and recovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_search_and_recovery "Underwater search and recovery") dive teams. [Military diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_diving "Military diving") includes combat diving, [clearance diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clearance_diving "Clearance diving") and [ships husbandry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ships_husbandry "Ships husbandry"). _Deep sea diving_ is underwater diving, usually with surface-supplied equipment, and often refers to the use of [standard diving dress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_diving_dress "Standard diving dress") with the traditional copper helmet. _Hard hat_ diving is any form of diving with a [helmet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_helmet "Diving helmet"), including the standard copper helmet, and other forms of [free-flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_helmet#Free-flow_helmets "Diving helmet") and [lightweight demand helmets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_helmet#Lightweight_demand_helmets "Diving helmet"). The history of breath-hold diving goes back at least to classical times, and there is evidence of prehistoric [hunting and gathering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter-gatherer "Hunter-gatherer") of seafoods that may have involved underwater swimming. Technical advances allowing the provision of breathing gas to a diver underwater at ambient pressure are recent, and self-contained breathing systems developed at an accelerated rate following the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War").

Physiological effects of ambient pressure diving
------------------------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Underwater_diving&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Physiological effects of ambient pressure diving")\]

Immersion in water and exposure to cold water and high pressure have physiological effects on the diver which limit the depths and duration possible in ambient pressure diving. Breath-hold endurance is a severe limitation, and breathing at high ambient pressure adds further complications, both directly and indirectly. Technological solutions have been developed which can greatly extend depth and duration of human ambient pressure dives, and allow useful work to be done underwater.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ECHM-EDTM_2011-1)

As of 2009, there was no clear evidence that diving causes long term neurological dysfunction except by acute damage.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Lang_and_Brubakk_2009-2)

Immersion of the human body in water affects the [circulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circulatory_system "Circulatory system"), [renal system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renal_system "Renal system"), [fluid balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_balance "Fluid balance"), and breathing, because the external [hydrostatic pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrostatic_pressure "Hydrostatic pressure") of the water provides support against the internal hydrostatic pressure of the blood. This causes a [blood shift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_shift_/(diving/) "Blood shift (diving)") from the [extravascular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravascular "Extravascular") tissues of the limbs into the chest cavity,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Pendergast_and_Lundgren_2009-3) and fluid losses known as [immersion diuresis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immersion_diuresis "Immersion diuresis") compensate for the blood shift in hydrated subjects soon after immersion.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Kollias_et_al_1976-4)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Pendergast_and_Lundgren_2009-3) Hydrostatic pressure on the body from head-out immersion causes negative pressure breathing which contributes to the blood shift.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Kollias_et_al_1976-4)

The blood shift causes an increased respiratory and cardiac workload. Stroke volume is not greatly affected by immersion or variation in ambient pressure, but [slowed heartbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradycardia "Bradycardia") reduces the overall cardiac output, particularly because of the diving reflex in [breath-hold diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breath-hold_diving "Breath-hold diving").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Pendergast_and_Lundgren_2009-3) Lung volume decreases in the upright position, owing to cranial displacement of the abdomen from hydrostatic pressure, and resistance to air flow in the airways increases because of the decrease in lung volume.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Kollias_et_al_1976-4) There appears to be a connection between [pulmonary edema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulmonary_edema "Pulmonary edema") and increased pulmonary blood flow and pressure, which results in capillary engorgement. This may occur during higher intensity exercise while immersed or submerged.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Pendergast_and_Lundgren_2009-3)

The [diving reflex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_reflex "Diving reflex") is a response to immersion that overrides the basic homeostatic [reflexes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflex "Reflex").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Physiology_and_Pathophysiology-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Panneton_2013-6) It optimises [respiration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiration_/(physiology/) "Respiration (physiology)") by preferentially distributing oxygen stores to the heart and brain, which allows extended periods underwater. It is exhibited strongly in [aquatic mammals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquatic_mammal "Aquatic mammal") ([seals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinniped "Pinniped"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Zapol_et_al_1989-7) [otters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otter "Otter"), [dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolphin "Dolphin") and [muskrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muskrat "Muskrat")),[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-McCulloch_2012-8) and also exists in other mammals, including [humans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human "Human"). [Diving birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bird "Diving bird"), such as [penguins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin "Penguin"), have a similar diving reflex.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Physiology_and_Pathophysiology-5) The diving reflex is triggered by chilling the face and holding the breath.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Physiology_and_Pathophysiology-5)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Speck_and_Bruce_1978-9) The cardiovascular system constricts peripheral blood vessels, slows the pulse rate, redirects blood to the vital organs to conserve oxygen, releases red blood cells stored in the [spleen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spleen "Spleen"), and, in humans, causes heart rhythm irregularities.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Physiology_and_Pathophysiology-5) Aquatic mammals have evolved [physiological adaptations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology_of_underwater_diving "Physiology of underwater diving") to conserve oxygen during submersion, but apnea, slowed pulse rate, and vasoconstriction are shared with terrestrial mammals.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Panneton_2013-6)

[Cold shock response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_shock_response "Cold shock response") is the [physiological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiological "Physiological") response of organisms to sudden cold, especially cold water, and is a common cause of death from immersion in very cold water,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-coldii-10) such as by falling through thin ice. The immediate shock of the cold causes involuntary inhalation, which if underwater can result in drowning. The cold water can also cause heart attack due to vasoconstriction;[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-phases-11) the heart has to work harder to pump the same volume of blood throughout the body, and for people with heart disease, this additional workload can cause the heart to go into arrest. A person who survives the initial minute after falling into cold water can survive for at least thirty minutes provided they do not drown. The ability to stay afloat declines substantially after about ten minutes as the chilled muscles lose strength and co-ordination.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-coldii-10)

[Hypothermia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothermia "Hypothermia") is reduced core body temperature that occurs when a body loses more heat than it generates.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-NEJM2012-12) It is a major limitation to swimming or diving in cold water.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-sterba-13) The reduction in finger dexterity due to pain or numbness decreases general safety and work capacity, which in turn increases the risk of other injuries.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-sterba-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-cheung-14) [Non-freezing cold injury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-freezing_cold_injury "Non-freezing cold injury") can affect the extremities in cold water diving, and [frostbite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frostbite "Frostbite") can occur when air temperatures are low enough to cause tissue freezing. Body heat is lost much more quickly in water than in air, so water temperatures that would be tolerable as outdoor air temperatures can lead to hypothermia, which may lead to death from other causes in inadequately protected divers.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-sterba-13)

[Thermoregulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermoregulation "Thermoregulation") of divers is complicated by breathing gases at raised ambient pressure and by gas mixtures necessary for limiting inert gas narcosis, work of breathing, and for accelerating decompression.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Neves_and_Thomas-15)

### Breath-hold limitations

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Underwater_diving&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Breath-hold limitations")\]

Breath-hold diving by an air-breathing animal is limited to the physiological capacity to perform the dive on the oxygen available until it returns to a source of fresh breathing gas, usually the air at the surface. As this internal oxygen supply reduces, the animal experiences an increasing urge to breathe caused by [buildup of carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercapnia "Hypercapnia") and [lactate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lactic_acid "Lactic acid") in the blood,[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Berta_et_al_2015-16) followed by loss of consciousness due to [cerebral hypoxia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerebral_hypoxia "Cerebral hypoxia"). If this occurs underwater, it will drown.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Campbell_1996-17)

[Blackouts in freediving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freediving_blackout "Freediving blackout") can occur when the breath is held long enough for metabolic activity to reduce the oxygen partial pressure sufficiently to cause loss of consciousness. This is accelerated by exertion, which uses oxygen faster, and can be exacerbated by hyperventilation directly before the dive, which reduces the carbon dioxide level in the blood. Lower carbon dioxide levels increase the oxygen-haemoglobin affinity, reducing availability of oxygen to brain tissue towards the end of the dive ([Bohr effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohr_effect "Bohr effect")); they also suppress the urge to breathe, making it easier to hold the breath to the point of blackout. This can happen at any depth.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Pollock_2014-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Johnson_2015-19)

[Ascent-induced hypoxia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypoxia_of_ascent "Hypoxia of ascent") is caused by a drop in oxygen partial pressure as ambient pressure is reduced. The partial pressure of oxygen at depth may be sufficient to maintain consciousness at that depth and not at the reduced pressures nearer the surface.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Campbell_1996-17)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Johnson_2015-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-CNS_clinic-20)

### Ambient pressure changes

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Underwater_diving&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Ambient pressure changes")\]

[![Image 2: Eye and surrounding skin of young male showing petechial and subconjunctival haemmorhages](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Mask_Squeeze.jpg/250px-Mask_Squeeze.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mask_Squeeze.jpg)

Mild barotrauma to a diver caused by mask squeeze

[Barotrauma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barotrauma "Barotrauma"), a type of [dysbarism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysbarism "Dysbarism"), is physical damage to body tissues caused by a difference in [pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure "Pressure") between a gas space inside, or in contact with the body, and the surrounding gas or fluid.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Brubakk-21) It typically occurs when the organism is exposed to a large change in ambient pressure, such as when a diver ascends or descends. When diving, the pressure differences which cause the barotrauma are changes in hydrostatic pressure.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''2006-22)

The initial damage is usually due to over-stretching the tissues in tension or shear, either directly by expansion of the gas in the closed space, or by pressure difference hydrostatically transmitted through the tissue.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Brubakk-21)

Barotrauma generally manifests as sinus or middle ear effects, decompression sickness, lung over-expansion injuries, and injuries resulting from external squeezes.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Brubakk-21) Barotraumas of descent are caused by preventing the free change of volume of the gas in a closed space in contact with the diver, resulting in a pressure difference between the tissues and the gas space, and the unbalanced force due to this pressure difference causes deformation of the tissues resulting in cell rupture.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Brubakk-21) Barotraumas of ascent are also caused when the free change of volume of the gas in a closed space in contact with the diver is prevented. In this case the pressure difference causes a resultant tension in the surrounding tissues which exceeds their tensile strength. Besides tissue rupture, the overpressure may cause ingress of gases into the adjoining tissues and further afield by bubble transport through the circulatory system. This can cause blockage of circulation at distant sites, or interfere with the normal function of an organ by its presence.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Brubakk-21)

### Breathing under pressure

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Underwater_diving&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Breathing under pressure")\]

Provision of breathing gas at ambient pressure can greatly prolong the duration of a dive, but there are other problems that may result from this technological solution. Absorption of metabolically inert gases is increased as a function of time and pressure, and these may both produce undesirable effects immediately, as a consequence of their presence in the tissues in the dissolved state, such as [nitrogen narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_narcosis "Nitrogen narcosis") and [high pressure nervous syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_pressure_nervous_syndrome "High pressure nervous syndrome"),[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrubakk2003305-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrubakk2003%22The_High_Pressure_Nervous_Syndrome%22,_pp323-57-24) or cause problems when coming out of solution within the tissues during [decompression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_/(diving/) "Decompression (diving)").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''2006vol._1,_ch._3,_sec._9.3-25)

Other problems arise when the concentration of metabolically active gases is increased. These range from the [toxic effects of oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity "Oxygen toxicity") at high partial pressure,[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''200644vol._1,_ch._3-26) through [buildup of carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercarbia "Hypercarbia") due to excessive work of breathing, increased [dead space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_space_/(physiology/) "Dead space (physiology)"),[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Lanphier_1956b-27) or inefficient removal, to the exacerbation of the toxic effects of contaminants in the breathing gas due to the increased concentration at high pressures.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''NOAA_Diving_Manual''2001Chapter_5_Table_5.2_Air_Purity_Standards-28) Hydrostatic pressure differences between the interior of the lung and the breathing gas delivery, increased breathing gas density due to ambient pressure, and increased flow resistance due to higher breathing rates may all cause increased [work of breathing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_of_breathing "Work of breathing"), fatigue of the respiratory muscles, and a physiological limit to effective ventilation.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Pendergast_and_Lundgren_2009-3)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Mitchell_et_al_2007-29) Studies of the effects of single dives have shown that hyperoxia and decompression stress can affect lung function directly following a dive, and hyperoxia can have a persistent residual effect on lung function for several years. Other studies indicate that a reduction in the conductance of small airways is related to accumulated diving exposure.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Thorsen_2009-30)

[![Image 3: View of a rectangular grating through a flat-glazed diving half-mask, showing magnification and a detail of slight pincushion distortion and chromatic aberration in the through-water view.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/FlatMask_above-below.jpg/250px-FlatMask_above-below.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FlatMask_above-below.jpg)

Views through a flat mask, above and below water

[Underwater vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_vision "Underwater vision") is affected by the clarity and the [refractive index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractive_index "Refractive index") of the medium. Visibility underwater is reduced because light passing through water attenuates rapidly with distance, leading to lower levels of natural illumination. Underwater objects are also blurred by scattering of light between the object and the viewer, resulting in lower contrast. These effects vary with the wavelength of the light, and the colour and [turbidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turbidity "Turbidity") of the water. The human eye is optimised for air vision, and when it is immersed in direct contact with water, [visual acuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_acuity "Visual acuity") is adversely affected by the difference in refractive index between water and air. Provision of an airspace between the cornea and the water can compensate, but causes scale and distance distortion. Artificial illumination can improve visibility at short range.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Luria_and_Kinney_1970-31) Stereoscopic acuity, the ability to judge relative distances of different objects, is considerably reduced underwater, and this is affected by the field of vision. A narrow field of vision caused by a small viewport in a helmet results in greatly reduced stereoacuity,[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Luria_and_Kinney_1970-31) and an apparent movement of a stationary object when the head is moved.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Ferris_1972-32) These effects lead to poorer hand-eye coordination.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Luria_and_Kinney_1970-31)

Water has different [acoustic properties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_acoustics "Underwater acoustics") from those of air. Sound from an underwater source can propagate relatively freely through body tissues where there is contact with the water as the acoustic properties are similar. When the head is exposed to the water, some sound is transmitted by the eardrum and middle ear, but a significant part reaches the cochlea independently, by bone conduction.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Anthony_et_al_2009-33)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Shupak_et_al_2005-34) Some sound localisation is possible, though difficult.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Anthony_et_al_2009-33) Human hearing underwater, in cases where the diver's ear is wet, is less sensitive than in air.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Anthony_et_al_2009-33) Frequency sensitivity underwater also differs from that in air, with a consistently higher threshold of hearing underwater; sensitivity to higher frequency sounds is reduced the most.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Anthony_et_al_2009-33) The type of headgear affects noise sensitivity and noise hazard depending on whether transmission is wet or dry.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Anthony_et_al_2009-33) Human hearing underwater is less sensitive with wet ears than in air, and a neoprene hood causes substantial attenuation. When wearing a helmet, hearing sensitivity is similar to that in surface air, as it is not greatly affected by the breathing gas or chamber atmosphere composition or pressure.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Anthony_et_al_2009-33) Because sound travels faster in heliox than in air, voice [formants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formant "Formant") are raised, making divers' speech high-pitched and distorted, and hard to understand for people not used to it.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Ackerman_and_Maitland_1975-35) The increased density of breathing gases under pressure has a similar and additive effect.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Rothman_et_al_1980-36)

Tactile sensory perception in divers may be impaired by the environmental protection suit and low temperatures. The combination of instability, equipment, neutral buoyancy and resistance to movement by the inertial and viscous effects of the water encumbers the diver. Cold causes losses in sensory and motor function and distracts from and disrupts cognitive activity. The ability to exert large and precise force is reduced.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Shilling_et_al_2013-37)

[Balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense_of_balance "Sense of balance") and equilibrium depend on [vestibular function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestibular_function "Vestibular function") and secondary input from visual, organic, cutaneous, kinesthetic and sometimes auditory senses which are processed by the central nervous system to provide the sense of balance. Underwater, some of these inputs may be absent or diminished, making the remaining cues more important. Conflicting input may result in vertigo, disorientation and [motion sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_sickness "Motion sickness"). The vestibular sense is essential in these conditions for rapid, intricate and accurate movement.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Shilling_et_al_2013-37) [Proprioceptive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proprioception "Proprioception") perception makes the diver aware of personal position and movement, in association with the vestibular and visual input, and allows the diver to function effectively in maintaining physical equilibrium and balance in the water.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Shilling_et_al_2013-37) In the water at neutral buoyancy, the proprioceptive cues of position are reduced or absent. This effect may be exacerbated by the diver's suit and other equipment.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Shilling_et_al_2013-37)

Taste and smell are not very important to the diver in the water but more important to the saturation diver while in accommodation chambers. There is evidence of a slight decrease in threshold for taste and smell after extended periods under pressure.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Shilling_et_al_2013-37)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Luciana_Civico_risalita_record_ARA_meno_80_stringe_pinza_scafandro_Verardi.jpg/250px-Luciana_Civico_risalita_record_ARA_meno_80_stringe_pinza_scafandro_Verardi.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Luciana_Civico_risalita_record_ARA_meno_80_stringe_pinza_scafandro_Verardi.jpg)

Two very different modes of diving: Ambient pressure open circuit scuba diving (left) and atmospheric pressure diving in a pressure resistant suit (right)

A mode of diving, or diving mode, is a particular way to dive underwater that requires [specific equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_equipment "Diving equipment"), procedures and techniques, and may expose the diver to a [particular range of hazards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazards_of_the_mode_of_diving "Hazards of the mode of diving").[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Hong_Kong-38)

There are several modes of diving; these are distinguished by the type of [breathing apparatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_apparatus "Breathing apparatus"), diving equipment, procedures and techniques involved, and whether the diver is exposed to ambient pressure.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Hong_Kong-38) [Ambient pressure diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_pressure_diving "Ambient pressure diving") includes [freediving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freediving "Freediving") and [compressed-gas diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compressed-gas_diving "Compressed-gas diving"),[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Mitchell_et_al_2012-39)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Loudoun-40) which may also be classed as [air diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_diving "Air diving"), [oxygen diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_diving "Oxygen diving"), and [mixed gas diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_gas_diving "Mixed gas diving") by the breathing gas used, and as [open circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_circuit_diving "Open circuit diving"), [semi-closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-closed_circuit_diving "Semi-closed circuit diving"), or [closed circuit diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_circuit_diving "Closed circuit diving") depending on the type of breathing apparatus used. There is also [atmospheric pressure diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure_diving "Atmospheric pressure diving"), which involves encapsulation in an [atmospheric pressure diving suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure_diving_suit "Atmospheric pressure diving suit") or [submersible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submersible "Submersible"),[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Thornton_2000-41) and [unmanned diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unmanned_diving "Unmanned diving"), where there are no human divers involved. The [diving equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_equipment "Diving equipment"), [support equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_support_equipment "Diving support equipment") and [procedures used](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_procedures "Diving procedures") largely depend on the mode of diving.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Hong_Kong-38)

In certain circumstances, some modes of diving may be impracticable, unsafe, not permitted by the governing organisation, or illegal.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-IMCA_D014-42)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Diving_at_Work_Regulations_1997-43) All modes of diving carry a certain amount of risk; this is mitigated with [planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dive_planning "Dive planning"), [training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_training "Diver training"), and the appropriate equipment.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Hong_Kong-38)

[![Image 5: A croup of three divers dressed in wetsuits standing on a rocky shore with the sea in the background. On the ground are inflated truck inner tube floats with nets to support their catch](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Divers_%282901939922%29.jpg/250px-Divers_%282901939922%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Divers_/(2901939922/).jpg)

Recreational breath-hold divers in basic equipment with floats and catch bags suitable for collecting lobster or shellfish

The ability to dive and swim underwater while holding one's breath is considered a useful emergency skill, an important part of water sport and Navy safety training, and an enjoyable leisure activity.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-BSAC_Sport_Diving-44) Underwater diving without breathing apparatus can be categorised as underwater swimming, [snorkelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snorkeling "Snorkeling") and freediving. These categories overlap considerably. Several competitive [underwater sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_sports "Underwater sports") are practised without breathing apparatus.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Aquathon-45)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Apnoea-46)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Hockey-47)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Rugby-48)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Spearfishing-49)

Freediving precludes the use of external breathing devices, and relies on the ability of divers to hold their breath until resurfacing. The technique ranges from simple breath-hold diving to competitive [apnea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apnea "Apnea") dives. Fins and a diving mask are often used in free diving to improve vision and provide more efficient propulsion. A short breathing tube called a snorkel allows the diver to breathe at the surface while the face is immersed. [Snorkelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snorkelling "Snorkelling") on the surface with no intention of diving is a popular water sport and recreational activity.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-BSAC_Sport_Diving-44)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-NPAL-50)

[![Image 6: Two divers swim over a rocky reef in clear water. They are trimmed level and show good technique](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/DIR_Divers_Sandra_edwards_2010.JPG/330px-DIR_Divers_Sandra_edwards_2010.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DIR_Divers_Sandra_edwards_2010.JPG)

Recreational scuba divers on open circuit

[![Image 7: A diver appears to work on a large spherical mine, with another diver observing from a distance in the background](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/US_Navy_explosive_ordnance_disposal_%28EOD%29_divers.jpg/250px-US_Navy_explosive_ordnance_disposal_%28EOD%29_divers.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Navy_explosive_ordnance_disposal_/(EOD/)_divers.jpg)

Scuba diving is diving with a [self-contained underwater breathing apparatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_set "Scuba set"), which is completely independent of surface supply. Scuba gives the diver mobility and horizontal range far beyond the reach of an umbilical hose attached to surface-supplied diving equipment (SSDE).[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''2006Chapter_1_Section_3_Scuba_Diving-51) Scuba divers engaged in armed forces covert operations may be referred to as [frogmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frogmen "Frogmen"), combat divers or attack swimmers.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Welham_1999-52)

Open circuit scuba systems discharge the breathing gas into the environment as it is exhaled, and consist of one or more [diving cylinders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_cylinder "Diving cylinder") containing breathing gas at high pressure which is supplied to the diver through a [diving regulator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_regulator "Diving regulator"). They may include additional cylinders for decompression gas or emergency breathing gas.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''NOAA_Diving_Manual''2001Chapter_5_Section_4_Emergency_Air_Supply-53)

Closed-circuit or semi-closed circuit [rebreather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebreather_diving "Rebreather diving") scuba systems allow recycling of exhaled gases. The volume of gas used is reduced compared to that of open circuit, so a smaller cylinder or cylinders may be used for an equivalent dive duration. They greatly extend the time spent underwater as compared to open circuit for the same gas consumption. Rebreathers produce fewer bubbles and less noise than scuba which makes them attractive to covert military divers to avoid detection, scientific divers to avoid disturbing marine animals, and media divers to avoid bubble interference.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''2006Chapter_17_Section_1_Introduction-54)

A scuba diver moves underwater primarily by using [fins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimfin "Swimfin") attached to the feet;[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''NOAA_Diving_Manual''2001Chapter_1_Section_4_Scuba_Diving-55) external propulsion can be provided by a [diver propulsion vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_propulsion_vehicle "Diver propulsion vehicle"), or a [towboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Towboard "Towboard") pulled from the surface. Other equipment includes a [diving mask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_mask "Diving mask") to improve [underwater vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_vision "Underwater vision"), a protective [diving suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_suit "Diving suit"), [equipment to control buoyancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buoyancy_compensator_/(diving/) "Buoyancy compensator (diving)"), and equipment related to the specific circumstances and purpose of the dive.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''NOAA_Diving_Manual''2001Chapter_5_Diver_and_Diving_Support_Equipment-56) Scuba divers are trained in the [procedures and skills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_skills "Scuba skills") appropriate to their level of certification by instructors affiliated to the [diver certification organisations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diver_certification_organizations "List of diver certification organizations") which issue these [diver certifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_certification "Diver certification"). These include standard operating procedures for using the equipment and dealing with the general [hazards of the underwater environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diving_hazards_and_precautions "List of diving hazards and precautions"), and emergency procedures for self-help and assistance of a similarly equipped diver experiencing problems. A minimum level of [fitness and health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitness_to_dive "Fitness to dive") is required by most training organisations, and a higher level of fitness may be needed for some applications.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''NOAA_Diving_Manual''2001Chapter_7_Diver_and_Support_Personnel_Training-57)

### Surface-supplied diving

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Underwater_diving&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Surface-supplied diving")\]

The view is from the deck from which the diver has jumped, and shows the back of the diver as the fins first contact the water](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/U.S._Navy_Diver_enters_the_water_during_a_training_evolution_at_the_Naval_Diving_and_Salvage_Training_Center_140218-N-IC111-156.jpg/250px-U.S._Navy_Diver_enters_the_water_during_a_training_evolution_at_the_Naval_Diving_and_Salvage_Training_Center_140218-N-IC111-156.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:U.S._Navy_Diver_enters_the_water_during_a_training_evolution_at_the_Naval_Diving_and_Salvage_Training_Center_140218-N-IC111-156.jpg)
