[![Image 9: Night view of a white spherical pressure chamber in a blue pipe frame supporting several blue bulk gas storage clinders, suspended over the water by cables. The bell umbilical is visible at the top and a ballast weight can be seen below at the water surface](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/US_Navy_010707-N-3093M-003_Diver_Transfer_Capsule.jpg/250px-US_Navy_010707-N-3093M-003_Diver_Transfer_Capsule.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Navy_010707-N-3093M-003_Diver_Transfer_Capsule.jpg)

Closed diving bell, also known as a diver transfer capsule

An alternative to self-contained breathing systems is to supply breathing gases from the surface through a hose. When combined with a communication cable, a [pneumofathometer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumofathometer "Pneumofathometer") hose and a safety line it is called the [diver's umbilical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umbilical_cable "Umbilical cable"), which may include a hot water hose for heating, video cable and breathing gas [reclaim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving#Gas_reclaim_systems "Saturation diving") line. The diver wears a full-face mask or helmet, and gas may be supplied on demand or as a continuous free flow. More basic equipment that uses only an air hose is called an [airline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#Air_line "Surface-supplied diving") or hookah system.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-CoP_Inshore-58)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''NOAA_Diving_Manual''2001Chapter_5_Diver_and_Diving_Support_Equipment-56)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Eleftheriou_2013-59) This allows the diver to breathe using an air supply hose from a high pressure cylinder or [diving air compressor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_air_compressor "Diving air compressor") at the surface. Breathing gas is supplied through a mouth-held demand valve or light full-face mask. Airline diving is used for work such as hull cleaning and archaeological surveys, for shellfish harvesting, and as [snuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snuba "Snuba"), a shallow water activity typically practised by tourists and those who are not scuba-certified.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Eleftheriou_2013-59)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Huffington_2014-60)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-snuba-61)

[Saturation diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving "Saturation diving") lets professional divers live and work under pressure for days or weeks at a time. After working in the water, the divers rest and live in a dry pressurised [underwater habitat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_habitat "Underwater habitat") on the bottom or a saturation life support system of pressure chambers on the deck of a [diving support vessel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_support_vessel "Diving support vessel"), [oil platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_platform "Oil platform") or other floating platform at a similar pressure to the work depth. They are transferred between the surface accommodation and the underwater workplace in a pressurised [closed diving bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_diving_bell "Closed diving bell"). Decompression at the end of the dive may take many days, but since it is done only once for a long period of exposure, rather than after each of many shorter exposures, the overall risk of decompression injury to the diver and the total time spent decompressing are reduced. This type of diving allows greater work efficiency and safety.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''2006Chapter_15_Saturation_Diving-62)

Commercial divers refer to diving operations where the diver starts and finishes the diving operation at atmospheric pressure as [surface oriented](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving "Surface-supplied diving"), or bounce diving.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Rekdal_2004-63) The diver may be deployed from the shore or a diving support vessel and may be transported on a [diving stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_stage "Diving stage") or in a [diving bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell "Diving bell"). Surface-supplied divers almost always wear [diving helmets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_helmet "Diving helmet") or [full-face diving masks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full-face_diving_mask "Full-face diving mask"). The bottom gas can be air, [nitrox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrox "Nitrox"), [heliox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliox "Heliox") or [trimix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimix_/(breathing_gas/) "Trimix (breathing gas)"); the decompression gases may be similar, or may include pure oxygen.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Imbert_2006-64) Decompression procedures include in-water decompression or [surface decompression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_practice "Decompression practice") in a [deck chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_chamber "Diving chamber").[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''2006Chapter_9_Air_Decompression-65)

A [wet bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell#Structure_of_a_typical_wet_bell "Diving bell") with a gas filled dome provides more comfort and control than a stage and allows for longer time in water. Wet bells are used for air and mixed gas, and divers can decompress on oxygen at 12 metres (40 ft).[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Imbert_2006-64) Small [closed bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell#Structure_of_a_typical_closed_bell "Diving bell") systems have been designed that can be easily mobilised, and include a two-man bell, a [launch and recovery system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_and_recovery_system_/(diving/) "Launch and recovery system (diving)") and a chamber for decompression after [transfer under pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transfer_under_pressure "Transfer under pressure") (TUP). Divers can breathe air or mixed gas at the bottom and are usually recovered with the chamber filled with air. They decompress on oxygen supplied through built in breathing systems (BIBS) towards the end of the decompression. Small bell systems support bounce diving down to 120 metres (390 ft) and for bottom times up to 2 hours.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Imbert_2006-64)

A relatively portable surface gas supply system using high pressure gas cylinders for both primary and reserve gas, but using the full diver's umbilical system with pneumofathometer and voice communication, is known in the industry as "[scuba replacement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_replacement "Scuba replacement")".[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-IMCA_D014-42)

[Compressor diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compressor_diving "Compressor diving") is a rudimentary method of surface-supplied diving used in some tropical regions such as the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines") and the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"). The divers swim with a half mask and fins and are supplied with air from an industrial low-pressure [air compressor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_compressor "Air compressor") on the boat through plastic tubes. There is no reduction valve; the diver holds the hose end in his mouth with no demand valve or [mouthpiece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mouthpiece_/(scuba/) "Mouthpiece (scuba)") and allows excess air to spill out between the lips.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Into_the_Blue-66)

The original breathing gas for diving was atmospheric air, and compressed air remains an important breathing gas for ambient pressure diving. Oxygen is limited to shallow water to avoid toxicity problems, and is usually used to accelerate decompression, or by tactical divers to provide a long endurance with a small amount of gas, and to minimise bubbles where detection would be a tactical problem. Some physiological problems of deeper diving, such as [inert gas narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inert_gas_narcosis "Inert gas narcosis") and high [work of breathing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_of_breathing "Work of breathing"), can be mitigated by the use of breathing gases based on helium, and experimental work which includes hydrogen in the mixture for extreme depths, continues. The common terminology refers to [air diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_diving "Air diving") and [gas diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas_diving "Gas diving"),[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Air_diving_system-67)[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ADAS_Air_diving-68) which includes [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen") diving,[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-mixed_gas_and_oxygen-69) and [mixed gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_gas_/(diving/) "Mixed gas (diving)") diving, which includes [nitrox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrox "Nitrox") diving, [trimix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimix_/(breathing_gas/) "Trimix (breathing gas)") diving, and [heliox diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliox_diving "Heliox diving").[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Lee_et_al_2020-70)[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-mixed_gas_and_oxygen-69)

Air is available for the cost of operating the compressor, so it is supplied on open circuit, and discharged into the surroundings on exhalation, and may be supplied through a free-flow system where this has advantages. Oxygen and nitrox are also cheap enough that it is usually economical to supply by demand open circuit except for long duration scuba operations, but helium is expensive and sometimes in short supply, so recycling can be viable for moderate usage, and essential for high volume usage. The costs of recycling by rebreathing or reclaiming helium based gases include high capital investment in the equipment, and additional running costs compared to open circuit.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-P_D_Handbook_5.3-71) The use of hydrogen as a breathing gas component is still experimental.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Fogarty_2020-72)

### Atmospheric pressure diving

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Underwater_diving&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Atmospheric pressure diving")\]

[![Image 10: A diver in an armoured diving suit stands on a launch and recovery platform on the support vessel, attended by a crewman.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Navy_Diver4.jpg/120px-Navy_Diver4.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Navy_Diver4.jpg)

US Navy Atmospheric Diving System (ADS)

[![Image 11: A large support vessel with a small rectangular profile deep submergence vehicle suspended over the water at the stern](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Limiting_Factor_to_be_prepared_for_a_dive_into_the_Atlantic_Ocean.jpg/330px-Limiting_Factor_to_be_prepared_for_a_dive_into_the_Atlantic_Ocean.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Limiting_Factor_to_be_prepared_for_a_dive_into_the_Atlantic_Ocean.jpg)

Full ocean depth rated DSV _Limiting Factor_ prepared for a dive into the Atlantic Ocean

Submersibles and rigid atmospheric diving suits (ADS) enable diving to be carried out in a dry environment at normal atmospheric pressure. An ADS is a small one-person articulated submersible which resembles a [suit of armour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_armour "Plate armour"), with elaborate joints to allow articulation by direct motion of the limbs, while maintaining an internal pressure of one atmosphere. An ADS can be used for dives of up to about 700 metres (2,300 ft) for many hours. It eliminates the majority of physiological dangers associated with deep diving – the occupant does not need to decompress, there is no need for special gas mixtures, and there is no danger of [nitrogen narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_narcosis "Nitrogen narcosis") – at the expense of higher cost, complex logistics and loss of dexterity.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-subsea_2001-73)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Thornton_2000-41) Crewed submeribles have been built rated to [full ocean depth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_ocean_depth "Full ocean depth") and have dived to the deepest known points of all the oceans.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Technology_specifications-74)[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-BBC_Molloy_2019-75)

[![Image 12: A work class remotely operated underwater vehicle working on a complex underwater installation using a manipulator arm.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/ROV_working_on_a_subsea_structure.jpg/250px-ROV_working_on_a_subsea_structure.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ROV_working_on_a_subsea_structure.jpg)

ROV working on a subsea structure

[Autonomous underwater vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_underwater_vehicle "Autonomous underwater vehicle") (AUVs) and [remotely operated underwater vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remotely_operated_underwater_vehicle "Remotely operated underwater vehicle") (ROVs) can carry out some functions of divers. They can be deployed at greater depths and in more dangerous environments. An AUV is a robot which travels underwater without requiring real-time input from an operator. AUVs constitute part of a larger group of unmanned undersea systems, a classification that includes non-autonomous ROVs, which are controlled and powered from the surface by an operator/pilot via an umbilical or using remote control. In military applications AUVs are often referred to as unmanned undersea vehicles (UUVs).[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ROVCAT-76)[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-AUV-77)

[![Image 13: Helmeted surface-supplied diver using a coated electrode to arc-weld a steel patch to the underwater hull of a landing craft.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Working_Diver_01.jpg/250px-Working_Diver_01.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Working_Diver_01.jpg)

[![Image 14: A scuba diver swims over a reef with a large still camera in an underwater housing with dome port and electronic strobes.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/US_Navy_120209-N-XD935-302_Mass_Communication_Specialist_1st_Class_Shane_Tuck%2C_assigned_to_the_Expeditionary_Combat_Camera_Underwater_Photo_Team%2C_c.jpg/330px-US_Navy_120209-N-XD935-302_Mass_Communication_Specialist_1st_Class_Shane_Tuck%2C_assigned_to_the_Expeditionary_Combat_Camera_Underwater_Photo_Team%2C_c.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Navy_120209-N-XD935-302_Mass_Communication_Specialist_1st_Class_Shane_Tuck,_assigned_to_the_Expeditionary_Combat_Camera_Underwater_Photo_Team,_c.jpg)

People may dive for various reasons, both personal and professional. While a newly qualified recreational diver may dive purely for the experience of diving, most divers have some additional reason for being underwater. [Recreational diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_diving "Recreational diving") is purely for enjoyment and has several specialisations and [technical disciplines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_diving "Technical diving") to provide more scope for varied activities for which specialist training can be offered, such as [cave diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_diving "Cave diving"), [wreck diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wreck_diving "Wreck diving"), [ice diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_diving "Ice diving") and [deep diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving "Deep diving").[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Technical_diving-78)[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-richardson1999-79) Several [underwater sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_sports "Underwater sports") are available for exercise and competition.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-CMAS_Sports_committee-80)

There are various aspects of [professional diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_diving "Professional diving") that range from part-time work to lifelong careers. Professionals in the recreational diving industry include instructor trainers, [diving instructors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_instructor "Diving instructor"), assistant instructors, [divemasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divemaster "Divemaster"), dive guides, and scuba technicians. A [scuba diving tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_diving_tourism "Scuba diving tourism") industry has developed to service recreational diving in regions with popular dive sites. Commercial diving is industry related and includes [engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering "Engineering") tasks such as in [hydrocarbon exploration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrocarbon_exploration "Hydrocarbon exploration"), [offshore construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offshore_construction "Offshore construction"), dam maintenance and harbour works. Commercial divers may also be employed to perform tasks related to marine activities, such as [naval diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_diving "Naval diving"), [ships husbandry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ships_husbandry "Ships husbandry"), [marine salvage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_salvage "Marine salvage") or [aquaculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquaculture "Aquaculture").[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-OSHA_1910.410-81)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Careers-82)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Sokanu-83)

Other specialist areas of diving include [military diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_diving "Military diving"), with a long history of military [frogmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frogmen "Frogmen") in various roles. They can perform roles including direct combat, reconnaissance, infiltration behind enemy lines, placing mines, [bomb disposal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomb_disposal "Bomb disposal") or engineering operations.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''2006Chapter_1_History_of_Diving-84)

In civilian operations, [police diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_diving "Police diving") units perform search and rescue operations, and recover evidence. In some cases [diver rescue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_rescue "Diver rescue") teams may also be part of a [fire department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_department "Fire department"), [paramedical service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramedical_service "Paramedical service"), [sea rescue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Search_and_rescue "Search and rescue") or [lifeguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifeguard "Lifeguard") unit, and this may be classed as [public safety diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_safety_diving "Public safety diving").[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Robinson_2002-85)[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Phillips_2015-86) There are also professional [media divers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_diving "Media diving") such as [underwater photographers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_photography "Underwater photography") and [videographers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videography "Videography"), who record the underwater world, and [scientific divers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_diving "Scientific diving") in fields of study which involve the underwater environment, including [marine biologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_biology "Marine biology"), [geologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geologist "Geologist"), [hydrologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrology "Hydrology"), [oceanographers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanography "Oceanography"), [speleologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speleologists "Speleologists") and [underwater archaeologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_archaeology "Underwater archaeology").[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''NOAA_Diving_Manual''2001Chapter_1_History_of_Diving_and_NOAA_Contributions-87)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Sokanu-83)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-CoP_Scientific-88)

The choice between scuba and surface-supplied diving equipment is based on both legal and logistical constraints. Where the diver requires mobility and a large range of movement, scuba is usually the choice if safety and legal constraints allow. Higher risk work, particularly commercial diving, may be restricted to surface-supplied equipment by legislation and codes of practice.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-CoP_Inshore-58)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-CoP_Scientific-88)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-SA_Diving_Regulations_2009-89)

[![Image 15: In the centre foreground, a man in a transparent cylinder is being lowered into the water by a group of turbaned figures on a small sailing vessel.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Alexander_the_Great_diving_NOAA.jpg/250px-Alexander_the_Great_diving_NOAA.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alexander_the_Great_diving_NOAA.jpg)

[![Image 16: Monochrome view of the deck of a ship with a pair of divers, and a group of onlookers, some of which are crew of the ship. To the left is a diver in an armoured suit, and to the right the diver is in standard diving dress with copper helmet](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Tritonia_Lusitania_1935.jpg/330px-Tritonia_Lusitania_1935.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tritonia_Lusitania_1935.jpg)

Two divers, one wearing the _Tritonia_ ADS and the other standard diving dress, preparing to explore the wreck of the [RMS _Lusitania_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RMS_Lusitania "RMS Lusitania"), 1935

[Freediving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freediving "Freediving") as a widespread means of hunting and gathering, both for food and other valuable resources such as [pearls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_diving "Pearl diving") and [coral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precious_coral "Precious coral"), dates from before 4500 BCE.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Edmonds_1975-90) By [classical Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_Greece "Classical Greece") and [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome") times [commercial diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_diving "Commercial diving") applications such as [sponge diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sponge_diving "Sponge diving") and [marine salvage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_salvage "Marine salvage") were established.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Hendrickse-91) Military diving goes back at least as far as the [Peloponnesian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloponnesian_War "Peloponnesian War"),[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Thucydides-92) with recreational and [sporting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_sport "Underwater sport") applications being a recent development. Technological development in [ambient pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_pressure "Ambient pressure") diving started with stone weights ([skandalopetra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skandalopetra "Skandalopetra")) for fast descent, with rope assist for ascent.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Hendrickse-91) The diving bell is one of the earliest types of equipment for underwater work and exploration.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Bevan1999-93) Its use was first described by [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle") in the 4th century BCE.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Bachrach1998-94) In the 16th and 17th centuries CE, [diving bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell "Diving bell") became more useful when a renewable supply of air could be provided to the diver at depth,[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Kindwall_2004-95) and progressed to [surface-supplied diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving "Surface-supplied diving") helmets – in effect miniature diving bells covering the diver's head and supplied with compressed air by [manually operated pumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_air_pump "Diving air pump") – which were improved by attaching a waterproof suit to the helmet.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Kindwall_2004-95)[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Slight-96) In the early 19th century these became the [standard diving dress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_diving_dress "Standard diving dress"),[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Kindwall_2004-95) which made a far wider range of marine civil engineering and salvage projects practicable.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Kindwall_2004-95)[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Broadwater_2016-97)[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Acott1999-98)

Limitations in mobility of the surface-supplied systems encouraged the development of both [open circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_circuit_scuba "Open circuit scuba") and [closed circuit scuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebreather_diving "Rebreather diving") in the 20th century, which allow the diver a much greater autonomy.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Rouquayrol-99)[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-What_is_a_rebreather-100)[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-quick-101) These became popular during the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") for [clandestine military operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frogman "Frogman"), and post-war for [scientific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_diving "Scientific diving"), search and rescue, [media diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_diving "Media diving"), recreational and [technical diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_diving "Technical diving"). The heavy free-flow surface-supplied copper helmets evolved into [lightweight demand helmets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_helmet#Lightweight_demand_helmet "Diving helmet"),[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Kindwall_2004-95) which are more economical with breathing gas, important for deeper dives using expensive [helium based breathing mixtures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliox "Heliox"). [Saturation diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving "Saturation diving") reduced the risks of decompression sickness for deep and long exposures.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''2006Chapter_1_History_of_Diving-84)[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-davis1955-102)[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Kindwall_2004-95)

An alternative approach was the development of the ADS or armoured suit, which isolates the diver from the pressure at depth, at the cost of mechanical complexity and limited dexterity. The technology first became practicable in the middle 20th century.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Thornton_2000-41)[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Carmagnolle-103) Isolation of the diver from the environment was taken further by the development of [remotely operated underwater vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remotely_operated_underwater_vehicle "Remotely operated underwater vehicle") (ROV or ROUV) in the late 20th century, where the operator controls the ROV from the surface, and [autonomous underwater vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_underwater_vehicle "Autonomous underwater vehicle") (AUV), which dispense with an operator altogether. All of these modes are still in use and each has a range of applications where it has advantages over the others, though diving bells have largely been relegated to a means of transport for surface-supplied divers. In some cases combinations are particularly effective, such as the simultaneous use of surface orientated or saturation surface-supplied diving equipment and work or observation class remotely operated vehicles.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Acott1999-98)[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-pieds-lourds-104)

### Physiological discoveries

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Underwater_diving&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Physiological discoveries")\]

[![Image 17: A full height monochrome portrait of a middle-aged white man with a receding hairline and a bushy moustache.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/John_Scott_Haldane_1902.jpg/250px-John_Scott_Haldane_1902.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Scott_Haldane_1902.jpg)

John Scott Haldane, 1902

By the late 19th century, as salvage operations became deeper and longer, an unexplained malady began afflicting the divers; they would suffer breathing difficulties, dizziness, joint pain and paralysis, sometimes leading to death. The problem was already well known among workers building tunnels and bridge footings operating under pressure in [caissons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caisson_/(engineering/) "Caisson (engineering)") and was initially called _caisson disease_; it was later renamed _the bends_ because the joint pain typically caused the sufferer to [stoop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grecian_bend "Grecian bend"). Early reports of the disease had been made at the time of [Charles Pasley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Pasley "Charles Pasley")'s salvage operation, but scientists were still ignorant of its causes.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Acott1999-98)

French [physiologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology") [Paul Bert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bert "Paul Bert") was the first to understand it as decompression sickness (DCS). His work, _La Pression barométrique_ (1878), was a comprehensive investigation into the physiological effects of air pressure, both above and below the normal.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Bert-105) He determined that inhaling pressurised air caused [nitrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen "Nitrogen") to dissolve into the [bloodstream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloodstream "Bloodstream"); rapid depressurisation would then release the nitrogen into its gaseous state, forming bubbles that could block the [blood circulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_circulation "Blood circulation") and potentially cause paralysis or death. Central nervous system [oxygen toxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity "Oxygen toxicity") was also first described in this publication and is sometimes referred to as the "Paul Bert effect".[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Bert-105)[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Acott2-106)

[John Scott Haldane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Scott_Haldane "John Scott Haldane") designed a [decompression chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_chamber "Decompression chamber") in 1907, and he produced the first [decompression tables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_tables "Decompression tables") for the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") in 1908 after extensive experiments with animals and human subjects.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-acott-107)[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Boycott_Damant_and_Haldane_1908-108)[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Timetables-109) These tables established a method of [decompression in stages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_practice#Staged_decompression "Decompression practice") – it remains the basis for decompression methods to this day. Following Haldane's recommendation, the maximum safe operating depth for divers was extended to 61 metres (200 ft).[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''2006Chapter_1_History_of_Diving-84)

The US Navy continued research into decompression, and in 1915 the first [Bureau of Construction and Repair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Construction_and_Repair "Bureau of Construction and Repair") decompression tables were developed by French and Stilson.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-CarlstonMathias2012-110) Experimental dives were conducted in the 1930s, forming the basis for the 1937 US Navy air decompression tables. Surface decompression and oxygen use were also researched in the 1930s. The US Navy 1957 tables were developed to correct problems found in the 1937 tables.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Huggins-111)

In 1965 [Hugh LeMessurier](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hugh_LeMessurier&action=edit&redlink=1 "Hugh LeMessurier (page does not exist)") and [Brian Andrew Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Andrew_Hills "Brian Andrew Hills") published their paper, _A [thermodynamic approach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermodynamic_model_of_decompression "Thermodynamic model of decompression") arising from a study on Torres Strait diving techniques_, which suggested that decompression following schedules based on conventional models results in asymptomatic bubble formation which must then be re-dissolved at the decompression stops before it can be eliminated. This is slower than allowing the gas to be eliminated while it is still in solution, and indicates the importance of minimising bubble phase gas for efficient decompression.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-LeMessurier_and_Hills-112)[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-RRR6176-113)

[M.P. Spencer](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=M.P._Spencer&action=edit&redlink=1 "M.P. Spencer (page does not exist)") showed that [Doppler ultrasonic methods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultrasonic_bubble_detection "Ultrasonic bubble detection") can detect venous bubbles in asymptomatic divers,[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-pmid1249001-114) and Dr Andrew Pilmanis showed that safety stops reduced bubble formation.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Huggins-111) In 1981 [D.E. Yount](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=D.E._Yount&action=edit&redlink=1 "D.E. Yount (page does not exist)") described the [Varying Permeability Model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varying_Permeability_Model "Varying Permeability Model"), proposing a mechanism of bubble formation.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Yount_1981-115) Several other [bubble models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_theory#Bubble_models "Decompression theory") followed. The [pathophysiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathophysiology "Pathophysiology") of decompression sickness is not yet fully understood, but [decompression practice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_practice "Decompression practice") has reached a stage where the risk is fairly low, and most incidents are successfully treated by [therapeutic recompression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Therapeutic_recompression "Therapeutic recompression") and [hyperbaric oxygen therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbaric_oxygen_therapy "Hyperbaric oxygen therapy"). Mixed [breathing gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas") are used to reduce the effects of the hyperbaric environment on ambient pressure divers.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Huggins-111)[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Wienke_2002-116)[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Imbert_2004-117)

Efficient decompression requires the diver to ascend fast enough to establish as high a decompression gradient, in as many tissues as safely possible, without provoking the development of symptomatic bubbles. This is facilitated by the highest acceptably safe oxygen partial pressure in the breathing gas, and avoiding gas changes that could cause [counterdiffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isobaric_counterdiffusion "Isobaric counterdiffusion") bubble formation or growth. The development of schedules that are both safe and efficient has been complicated by the large number of variables and uncertainties, including personal variation in response under varying environmental conditions and workload.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Mitchell_2020-118)

The dive site is cordoned off with a red and white tape, and other members of the support team stand to the side, with onlookers outside the cordon.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Plong%C3%A9e_sous_glace_VJ.JPG/250px-Plong%C3%A9e_sous_glace_VJ.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plong%C3%A9e_sous_glace_VJ.JPG)

Ice diving

The diving environment is limited by accessibility and risk, but includes water and occasionally other liquids. Most underwater diving is done in the shallower coastal parts of the oceans, and inland bodies of fresh water, including lakes, dams, quarries, rivers, springs, flooded caves, reservoirs, tanks, swimming pools, and canals, but may also be done in large bore ducting and sewers, power station cooling systems, cargo and [ballast tanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballast_tank "Ballast tank") of ships, and liquid-filled industrial equipment. The environment may affect gear configuration: for instance, freshwater is less dense than saltwater, so less added weight is needed to achieve diver neutral buoyancy in freshwater dives.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Graver2010-119) Water temperature, [visibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_vision "Underwater vision") and movement also affect the diver and the dive plan.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Jablonski_2006-120) Diving in liquids other than water may present special problems due to density, viscosity and chemical compatibility of diving equipment, as well as possible environmental hazards to the diving team.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-High_risk-121)

[Benign conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benign_water "Benign water"), sometimes also referred to as [confined water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confined_water_/(diving/) "Confined water (diving)"), are environments of low risk, where it is extremely unlikely or impossible for the diver to get lost or entrapped, or be exposed to hazards other than the basic underwater environment. These conditions are suitable for initial training in the critical survival skills, and include swimming pools, training tanks, aquarium tanks and some shallow and protected shoreline areas.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-CoP_Benign-122)

[Open water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_water_/(diving/) "Open water (diving)") is unrestricted water such as a sea, lake or [flooded quarry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_dive_sites#Quarry_dive_sites "Recreational dive sites"), where the diver has unobstructed direct vertical access to the surface of the water in contact with the atmosphere.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Aus_Part_3-123) [Open-water diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-water_diving "Open-water diving") implies that if a problem arises, the diver can directly ascend vertically to the atmosphere to breathe air.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Divers_dictionary-124) [Wall diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_diving "Wall diving") is done along a near vertical face. [Blue-water diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-water_diving "Blue-water diving") is done in good visibility in [mid-water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-water "Mid-water") where the bottom is out of sight of the diver and there may be no fixed visual reference.[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Haddock_and_Heine-125) [Black-water diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black-water_diving "Black-water diving") is mid-water diving at night, particularly on a moonless night.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Black-water-126)[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Indigo-127)

An overhead or [penetration diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penetration_diving "Penetration diving") environment is where the diver enters a space from which there is no direct, purely vertical ascent to the safety of breathable atmosphere at the surface. [Cave diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_diving "Cave diving"), [wreck diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wreck_diving "Wreck diving"), [ice diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_diving "Ice diving") and diving inside or under other natural or artificial underwater structures or enclosures are examples. The restriction on direct ascent increases the risk of diving under an overhead, and this is usually addressed by adaptations of procedures and use of equipment such as redundant breathing gas sources and [guide lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guide_line "Guide line") to indicate the route to the exit.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-CoP_Scientific-88)[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-High_risk-121)[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Jablonski_2006-120)

[Night diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_diving "Night diving") can allow the diver to experience a different [underwater environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_environment "Underwater environment"), because many [marine animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_animal "Marine animal") are [nocturnal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nocturnal "Nocturnal").[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-BSAC-128) [Altitude diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude_diving "Altitude diving"), for example in mountain lakes, requires modifications to the decompression schedule because of the reduced atmospheric pressure.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Jackson_2000-129)[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''2006Chapter_9,_Section_13_-_Diving_at_altitude-130)

He is breathing from a rebreather and carrying a side-slung 80 cubic foot aluminium bailout cylinder on each side. A second diver is partly visible to the left.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Trevor_Jackson_returns_from_SS_Kyogle.jpg/250px-Trevor_Jackson_returns_from_SS_Kyogle.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trevor_Jackson_returns_from_SS_Kyogle.jpg)

The recreational diving depth limit set by the EN 14153-2 / ISO 24801-2 level 2 "[Autonomous Diver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_Diver "Autonomous Diver") " standard is 20 metres (66 ft).[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-EUF-131) The recommended depth limit for more extensively trained recreational divers ranges from 30 metres (98 ft) for PADI divers,[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-padi1-132) (this is the depth at which nitrogen narcosis symptoms generally begin to be noticeable in adults), to 40 metres (130 ft) specified by [Recreational Scuba Training Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_Scuba_Training_Council "Recreational Scuba Training Council"),[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-padi1-132) 50 metres (160 ft) for divers of the [British Sub-Aqua Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Sub-Aqua_Club "British Sub-Aqua Club") and [Sub-Aqua Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Aqua_Association "Sub-Aqua Association") breathing air,[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Cole_2008-133) and 60 metres (200 ft) for teams of 2 to 3 French Level 3 recreational divers, breathing air.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Code_du_sport-134)

For technical divers, the recommended maximum depths are greater on the understanding that they will use less narcotic gas mixtures. 100 metres (330 ft) is the maximum depth authorised for divers who have completed Trimix Diver certification with [IANTD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IANTD "IANTD")[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-IANTD-135) or Advanced Trimix Diver certification with [TDI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_Diving_International "Technical Diving International").[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-TDI-136) 332 metres (1,089 ft) is the world record depth on scuba (2014).[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-GuinnessGabr-137) Commercial divers using saturation techniques and heliox breathing gases routinely exceed 100 metres (330 ft), but they are also limited by physiological constraints. [Comex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compagnie_maritime_d%27expertises "Compagnie maritime d'expertises") Hydra 8 experimental dives reached a record open water depth of 534 metres (1,752 ft) in 1988.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Hydra_8-138) Atmospheric pressure diving suits are mainly constrained by the technology of the articulation seals, and a US Navy diver has dived to 610 metres (2,000 ft) in one.[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Depth_record-139)[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Nuytco-140)
