The [Blue Hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Hole_/(Red_Sea/) "Blue Hole (Red Sea)") in [Dahab, Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahab "Dahab"), a world-renowned recreational dive site

The common term for a place at which one may dive is a dive site. As a general rule, professional diving is done where the work needs to be done, and recreational diving is done where conditions are suitable. There are many recorded and publicised [recreational dive sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_dive_sites "Recreational dive sites") which are known for their convenience, points of interest, and frequently favourable conditions. Diver training facilities for both professional and recreational divers generally use a small range of dive sites which are familiar and convenient, and where conditions are predictable and the environmental risk is relatively low.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-CoP_Training-141)

Due to the inherent risks of the environment and the necessity to operate the equipment correctly, both under normal conditions and during incidents where failure to respond appropriately and quickly can have fatal consequences, standardised procedures are used in preparation of the equipment, preparation to dive, during the dive if all goes according to plan, after the dive, and in the event of a reasonably foreseeable contingency. The standard procedures are not necessarily the only course of action that will have a satisfactory outcome, but they are generally procedures which have been found by experiment and experience to work well and reliably when applied in response to the given circumstances.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Larn_and_Whistler_1993-142) All formal diver training is based on the learning of standardised skills and procedures, and in many cases the [over-learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Over-learning "Over-learning") of critical skills until the procedures can be performed without hesitation even when distracting circumstances exist. Where reasonably practicable, [checklists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checklist "Checklist") may be used to ensure that preparatory procedures are carried out in the correct sequence and that no steps are inadvertently omitted.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Ranapurwala_et_al_2015-143)[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-DAN_Checklists-144)[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ADCI_2016-145)

Some procedures are common to all manned modes of diving, but most are specific to the mode of diving and many are specific to the equipment in use.[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Class_4_training_standard-146)[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Class_II_diver_training_standard-147)[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ADCI_2016-145) Diving procedures are those which are directly relevant to diving safety and efficiency, but do not include task specific skills. Standard procedures are particularly helpful where communication is by hand or rope signal – the [hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_communications#Hand_signals "Diver communications") and [line signals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_communications#Line_signals "Diver communications") are examples of standard procedures themselves – as the communicating parties have a better idea of what the other is likely to do in response. Where [voice communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_communications#Voice_communication "Diver communications") is available, [standardised communications protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_communications#Voice_communication_protocol "Diver communications") reduces the time needed to convey necessary information and the error rate in transmission.[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-P_D_Handbook_6.2-148)

Diving procedures generally involve the correct application of the appropriate diving skills in response to the current circumstances, and range from selecting and testing equipment to suit the diver and the dive plan, to the rescue of oneself or another diver in a life-threatening emergency. In many cases, what might be a life-threatening emergency to an untrained or inadequately skilled diver, is a mere annoyance and minor distraction to a skilled diver who applies the correct procedure without hesitation. Professional diving operations tend to adhere more rigidly to [standard operating procedures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_operating_procedures "Standard operating procedures") than recreational divers, who are not legally or contractually obliged to follow them, but the prevalence of diving accidents is known to be strongly correlated to human error, which is more common in divers with less training and experience.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Ranapurwala_et_al_2015-143) The [Doing It Right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doing_It_Right_/(scuba_diving/) "Doing It Right (scuba diving)") philosophy of [technical diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_diving "Technical diving") is strongly supportive of common standard procedures for all members of a [dive team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doing_It_Right_/(scuba_diving/)#Unified_team "Doing It Right (scuba diving)"), and prescribes the procedures and equipment configuration which may affect procedures to the members of their organisations.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Jablonski_2006-120)

The terms _diving skills_ and _diving procedures_ are largely interchangeable, but a procedure may require the ordered application of several skills, and is a broader term. A procedure may also conditionally branch or require repeated applications of a skill, depending on circumstances. Diver training is structured around the learning and practice of standard procedures until the diver is assessed as competent to apply them reliably in reasonably foreseeable circumstances, and the certification issued limits the diver to environments and equipment that are compatible with their training and assessed skill levels. The teaching and assessment of diving skills and procedures is often restricted to registered [instructors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_instructor "Diving instructor"), who have been assessed as competent to teach and assess those skills by the [certification or registration agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_certification_agencies "Diver certification agencies"), who take the responsibility of declaring the diver competent against their [assessment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educational_assessment "Educational assessment") criteria. The teaching and assessment of other task oriented skills does not generally require a diving instructor.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ADCI_2016-145)

There is considerable difference in the diving procedures of professional divers, where a diving team with formally appointed members in specific roles and with recognised competence is required by law,[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Diving_at_Work_Regulations_1997-43) and recreational diving, where in most jurisdictions the diver is not constrained by specific laws, and in many cases is not required to provide any evidence of competence.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-OSHA_1910.410-81)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-SA_Diving_Regulations_2009-89)

[![Image 21: A group of about 12 divers on the shore of a flooded quarry preparing surface-supplied diving equipment for diver training exercises. Several umbilicals are laid out for use in figure 8 coils.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Commercial_diver_training_at_Blue_Rock_Quarry_P3233799.JPG/250px-Commercial_diver_training_at_Blue_Rock_Quarry_P3233799.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Commercial_diver_training_at_Blue_Rock_Quarry_P3233799.JPG)

Commercial diver training in a flooded [quarry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarry "Quarry")

Underwater diver training is normally given by a qualified [instructor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_instructor "Diving instructor") who is a member of one of many [diver training agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diver_certification_organizations "List of diver certification organizations") or is registered with a government agency. Basic diver training entails the learning of skills required for the safe conduct of activities in an underwater environment, and includes procedures and skills for the use of diving equipment, safety, emergency self-help and rescue procedures, dive planning, and use of [dive tables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dive_tables "Dive tables").[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ISO-149)[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-IDSA-150) [Diving hand signals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_communications#Hand_signals "Diver communications") are used to communicate underwater. Professional divers will also learn other methods of communication.[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ISO-149)[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-IDSA-150)

An [entry level diver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entry_level_diver "Entry level diver") must learn the techniques of breathing underwater through a demand regulator, including clearing it of water and recovering it if dislodged from the mouth, and clearing the mask if it is flooded. These are critical survival skills, and if not competent the diver is at a high risk of drowning. A related skill is sharing breathing gas with another diver, both as the donor and the recipient. This is usually done with a secondary demand valve carried for this purpose. Technical and professional divers will also learn how to use a backup gas supply carried in an independent scuba set, known as the emergency gas supply or [bailout cylinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailout_cylinder "Bailout cylinder").[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ISO-149)[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-IDSA-150)

To avoid injury during descent, divers must be competent at [equalising the ears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ear_clearing "Ear clearing"), sinuses and mask; they must also learn not to hold their breath while ascending, to avoid barotrauma of the lungs. The speed of ascent must be controlled to avoid decompression sickness, which requires buoyancy control skills. Good [buoyancy control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_skills#Buoyancy_control "Scuba skills") and [trim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_trim "Diver trim") also allow the diver to manoeuvre and move about safely, comfortably and efficiently, using [swimfins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimfins "Swimfins") for propulsion.[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ISO-149)[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-IDSA-150)

Some knowledge of [physiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology") and the [physics of diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_physics "Diving physics") is considered necessary by most diver certification agencies, as the diving environment is alien and relatively hostile to humans. The physics and physiology knowledge required is fairly basic, and helps the diver to understand the effects of the diving environment so that informed acceptance of the associated risks is possible. The physics mostly relates to gases under pressure, [buoyancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buoyancy "Buoyancy"), heat loss, and [light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light "Light") underwater. The physiology relates the physics to the effects on the human body, to provide a basic understanding of the causes and risks of [barotrauma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barotrauma "Barotrauma"), decompression sickness, gas toxicity, [hypothermia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothermia "Hypothermia"), [drowning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drowning "Drowning") and sensory variations. More advanced training often involves first aid and rescue skills, skills related to specialised diving equipment, and underwater work skills.[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ISO-149)[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-IDSA-150) Further training is required to develop the skills necessary for diving in a wider range of environments, with specialised equipment, and to become competent to perform a variety of underwater tasks.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-High_risk-121)[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Jablonski_2006-120)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''NOAA_Diving_Manual''2001Chapter_7_Diver_and_Support_Personnel_Training-57)[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''2006Chapter_1_History_of_Diving-84)

Medical aspects of diving
-------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Underwater_diving&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Medical aspects of diving")\]

The medical aspects of diving and hyperbaric exposure include examination of divers to establish medical fitness to dive, diagnosis and treatment of [diving disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_disorders "Diving disorders"), treatment by recompression and [hyperbaric oxygen therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbaric_oxygen_therapy "Hyperbaric oxygen therapy"), toxic effects of gases in a hyperbaric environment,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ECHM-EDTM_2011-1) and treatment of injuries incurred while diving which are not directly associated with immersion, depth, or pressure.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Kindwall_2004-95)

Medical fitness to dive is the medical and physical suitability of a diver to function safely in the underwater environment using underwater diving equipment and procedures. As a general principle, fitness to dive is dependent on the absence of conditions which would constitute an unacceptable risk for the diver, and for professional divers, to any member of the diving team. General physical fitness requirements are also often specified by a certifying agency, and are usually related to ability to swim and perform the activities that are associated with the relevant type of diving. The general hazards of diving are much the same for recreational divers and professional divers, but the risks vary with the diving procedures used. These risks are reduced by appropriate skills and equipment. Medical fitness to dive generally implies that the diver has no known medical conditions that limit the ability to do the job or jeopardise the safety of the diver or the team, that might get worse as an consequence of diving, or unacceptably predispose the diver to diving or occupational illness.[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-EDTC_fitness_standard-151)

Depending on the circumstances, fitness to dive may be established by a signed statement by the diver that he or she does not suffer from any of the disqualifying conditions and is able to manage the ordinary physical requirements of diving, by a detailed medical examination by a physician registered as a [medical examiner of divers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_medicine#Education_and_registration_of_practitioners "Diving medicine") following a prescribed procedural checklist, attested by a legal document of fitness to dive issued by the medical examiner and recorded on a national database, or by alternatives between these extremes.[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Fitness_2001-152)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-SA_Diving_Regulations_2009-89)

[Psychological fitness to dive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_fitness_to_dive "Psychological fitness to dive") is not normally evaluated before recreational or commercial diver training, but can influence the safety and success of a diving career.[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Campbell_2000-153)

[![Image 22: Photograph of the cramped interior of a cylinder containing two benches and two diver trainees](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Decompression_chamber.jpg/250px-Decompression_chamber.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Decompression_chamber.jpg)

Military and commercial divers are trained in the procedures for use of a [recompression chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recompression_chamber "Recompression chamber") to treat [diving disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_disorders "Diving disorders").

[Diving medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_medicine "Diving medicine") is the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of conditions caused by exposing divers to the underwater environment. It includes the effects of pressure on gas filled spaces in and in contact with the body, and of partial pressures of breathing gas components, the diagnosis and treatment of conditions caused by marine hazards and how fitness to dive and the side effects of drugs used to treat other conditions affects a diver's safety. [Hyperbaric medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbaric_medicine "Hyperbaric medicine") is another field associated with diving, since recompression in a hyperbaric chamber with hyperbaric oxygen therapy is the definitive treatment for two of the most important diving-related illnesses, [decompression sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_sickness "Decompression sickness") and [arterial gas embolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_embolism#Decompression_illness "Air embolism").[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''US_Navy_Diving_Manual''2006Chapter_20_Diagnosis_and_Treatment_of_Decompression_Sickness_and_Arterial_Gas_Embolism-154)[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Bove_2013-155)

Diving medicine deals with medical research on issues of diving, the prevention of [diving disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_disorders "Diving disorders"), treatment of diving accident injuries and diving fitness. The field includes the effect on the human body of breathing gases and their contaminants under high pressure, and the relationship between the state of physical and psychological health of the diver and safety. In diving accidents it is common for multiple disorders to occur together and interact with each other, both causatively and as complications. Diving medicine is a branch of [occupational medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupational_medicine "Occupational medicine") and [sports medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_medicine "Sports medicine"), and first aid and recognition of symptoms of diving disorders are important parts of diver education.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ECHM-EDTM_2011-1)

[![Image 23: A drawing of a flag with white hoist and blue swallowtail fly](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Alfa_flag.svg/250px-Alfa_flag.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alfa_flag.svg)

[![Image 24: A drawing of a red flag with a white diagonal band from the top of the hoist to the bottom of the fly](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Pavillon_rouge_avec_une_diagonale_blanche.svg/250px-Pavillon_rouge_avec_une_diagonale_blanche.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pavillon_rouge_avec_une_diagonale_blanche.svg)

Risk is a combination of hazard, vulnerability and likelihood of occurrence, which can be the probability of a specific undesirable consequence of a hazard, or the combined probability of undesirable consequences of all the hazards of an activity.[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Coppola_2015-156)

The presence of a combination of several hazards simultaneously is common in diving, and the effect is generally increased risk to the diver, particularly where the occurrence of an incident due to one hazard triggers other hazards with a resulting cascade of incidents. Many diving fatalities are the result of a cascade of incidents overwhelming the diver, who should be able to manage any single reasonably foreseeable incident and its probable direct consequences.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Blumenberg_1996-157)[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Lock_2011-158)[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Barsky_2003-159)

Commercial diving operations may expose the diver to more and sometimes greater hazards than recreational diving, but the associated occupational health and safety legislation is less tolerant of risk than recreational, particularly technical divers, may be prepared to accept.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Blumenberg_1996-157)[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Lock_2011-158) Commercial diving operations are also constrained by the physical realities of the operating environment, and expensive engineering solutions are often necessary to control risk. A formal hazard identification and risk assessment is a standard and required part of the planning for a commercial diving operation, and this is also the case for offshore diving operations. The occupation is inherently hazardous, and great effort and expense are routinely incurred to keep the risk within an acceptable range. The [standard methods of reducing risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierarchy_of_hazard_controls "Hierarchy of hazard controls") are followed where possible.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Blumenberg_1996-157)[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Lock_2011-158)[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-DAWR-160)

Statistics on injuries related to commercial diving are normally collected by national regulators. In the UK the [Health and Safety Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_and_Safety_Executive "Health and Safety Executive") (HSE) is responsible for the overview of about 5,000 commercial divers; in Norway the corresponding authority is the [Petroleum Safety Authority Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_Safety_Authority_Norway "Petroleum Safety Authority Norway") (PSA), which has maintained the DSYS database since 1985, gathering statistics on over 50,000 diver-hours of commercial activity per year.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-QinetiQ-161)[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-DSYS-162) The risks of dying during [recreational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_diving "Recreational diving"), [scientific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_diving "Scientific diving") or [commercial diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_diving "Commercial diving") are small, and for [scuba diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_diving "Scuba diving"), deaths are usually associated with poor [gas management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_skills#Breathing_gas_management "Scuba skills"), poor [buoyancy control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_skills#Buoyancy_control,_trim_and_stability "Scuba skills"), equipment misuse, entrapment, rough water conditions and pre-existing health problems. Some fatalities are inevitable and caused by unforeseeable situations escalating out of control, but the majority of diving fatalities can be attributed to human error on the part of the victim.[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Concannon_2011-163) During 2006 to 2015 there were an estimated 306 million recreational dives made by US residents and 563 recreational diving deaths from this population. The fatality rate was 1.8 per million recreational dives, and 47 deaths for every 1000 emergency department presentations for scuba injuries.[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Buzzacott_2018-164)

[Scuba diving fatalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_diving_fatalities "Scuba diving fatalities") have a major financial impact by way of lost income, lost business, insurance premium increases and high litigation costs.[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Concannon_2011-163) Equipment failure is rare in [open circuit scuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_circuit_scuba "Open circuit scuba"), and when the cause of death is recorded as [drowning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drowning "Drowning"), it is usually the consequence of an uncontrollable series of events in which drowning is the endpoint because it occurred in water, while the initial cause remains unknown.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Ange_2010-165) Where the triggering event is known, it is most commonly a shortage of breathing gas, followed by buoyancy problems.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Denoble_et_al_2008-166) Air embolism is also frequently cited as a cause of death, often as a consequence of other factors leading to an uncontrolled and badly managed [ascent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_skills#Ascents_and_descents "Scuba skills"), occasionally aggravated by medical conditions. About a quarter of diving fatalities are associated with cardiac events, mostly in older divers. There is a fairly large body of data on diving fatalities, but in many cases the data are poor due to the standard of investigation and reporting. This hinders research which could improve diver safety.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Ange_2010-165)[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Caruso_2011-167)

Artisanal fishermen and gatherers of marine organisms in less developed countries may expose themselves to relatively high risk using diving equipment if they do not understand the physiological hazards, particularly if they use inadequate equipment.[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Westin_2005-168)

Divers operate in an environment for which the human body is not well suited. They face special physical and health risks when they go underwater or use high pressure breathing gas. The consequences of diving incidents range from merely annoying to rapidly fatal, and the result often depends on the equipment, skill, response and fitness of the diver and diving team. The hazards include [the aquatic environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diving_hazards_and_precautions#The_aquatic_environment "List of diving hazards and precautions"), the use of [breathing equipment in an underwater environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diving_hazards_and_precautions#Use_of_breathing_equipment_in_an_underwater_environment "List of diving hazards and precautions"), [exposure to a pressurised environment and pressure changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diving_hazards_and_precautions#Exposure_to_a_pressurised_environment_and_pressure_changes "List of diving hazards and precautions"), particularly pressure changes during descent and ascent, and breathing gases at high ambient pressure. [Diving equipment other than breathing apparatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diving_hazards_and_precautions#Failure_of_diving_equipment_other_than_breathing_apparatus "List of diving hazards and precautions") is usually reliable, but has been known to fail, and loss of buoyancy control or thermal protection can be a major burden which may lead to more serious problems. There are also hazards of [the specific diving environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diving_hazards_and_precautions#The_specific_diving_environment "List of diving hazards and precautions"), which include strong water movement and local pressure differentials, and hazards related to access to and egress from the water, which vary from place to place, and may also vary with time. Hazards inherent in the diver include [pre-existing physiological and psychological conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diving_hazards_and_precautions#Pre-existing_physiological_and_psychological_conditions_in_the_diver "List of diving hazards and precautions") and the [personal behaviour and competence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diving_hazards_and_precautions#Diver_behaviour_and_competence "List of diving hazards and precautions") of the individual. For those pursuing other activities while diving, there are additional [hazards of task loading, of the dive task and of special equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diving_hazards_and_precautions#Hazards_of_the_dive_task_and_special_equipment "List of diving hazards and precautions") associated with the task.[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-General_Hazards-169)[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Hazards_and_Solutions-170)

The major factors influencing diving safety are the environment, the diving equipment and the performance of the diver and the dive team. The underwater environment is alien, both physically and psychologically stressful, and usually not amenable to control, though divers can be selective of the conditions in which they are willing to dive. The other factors must be controlled to mitigate the overall stress on the diver and allow the dive to be completed in acceptable safety. The equipment is critical to diver safety for life support, but is generally reliable, controllable and predictable in its performance.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Blumenberg_1996-157)

[Human factors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_factors "Human factors") are the physical or [cognitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive "Cognitive") properties of individuals, or social behaviour specific to humans, which influence functioning of technological systems as well as human-environment equilibrium.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Blumenberg_1996-157) Human error is inevitable and everyone makes mistakes at some time, and the consequences of these errors are varied and depend on many factors. Most errors are minor and do not cause harm, but in a high risk environment, such as in diving, errors are more likely to have catastrophic consequences. Examples of human error leading to accidents are available in vast numbers, as it is the direct cause of 60% to 80% of all accidents.[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Perrow_1984-171) [Human error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_error "Human error") and [panic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic "Panic") are considered to be the leading causes of diving accidents and fatalities. A study by William P. Morgan indicates that over half of all divers in the survey had experienced panic underwater at some time during their diving career,[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Morgan_1995-172) and these findings were independently corroborated by a survey that suggested 65% of recreational divers have panicked under water.[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Staff_1996-173) Panic frequently leads to errors in a diver's judgement or performance, and may result in an accident.[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Lock_2011-158)[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Morgan_1995-172)[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Elliott_1984-174)[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Shelanski_1996-175)[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Vorosmarti_1987-176) The [safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety "Safety") of underwater diving operations can be improved by reducing the frequency of human error and the consequences when it does occur.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Blumenberg_1996-157)

Only 4.46% of the recreational diving fatalities in a 1997 study were attributable to a single contributory cause.[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-PARAS_1997-177) The remaining fatalities probably arose as a result of a progressive sequence of events involving two or more procedural errors or equipment failures, and since procedural errors are generally avoidable by a well-trained, intelligent and alert diver, working in an organised structure, and not under excessive stress, it was concluded that the low accident rate in professional scuba diving is due to this factor.[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Tetlow_2006-178) The study also concluded that it would be impossible to eliminate all minor contraindications of scuba diving, as this would result in overwhelming bureaucracy and bring all diving to a halt.[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-PARAS_1997-177)

[Human factors in diving equipment design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_factors_in_diving_equipment_design "Human factors in diving equipment design") is the influence of the interaction between the diver and the equipment on the design of the equipment on which the diver relies to stay alive and in reasonable comfort, and to perform the planned tasks during a dive. The design of the equipment can strongly influence its effectiveness in performing the desired functions. Divers vary considerably in [anthropometric dimensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropometry "Anthropometry"), [physical strength](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_strength "Physical strength"), joint flexibility, and other physiological characteristics within the range of acceptable fitness to dive. [Diving equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_equipment "Diving equipment") should allow as full a range of function as reasonably practicable, and should be matched to the diver, the environment, and the task. [Diving support equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_support_equipment "Diving support equipment") is usually shared by a wide range of divers, and must work for them all.[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Bitterman-179)

The most difficult stages of a dive for [recreational divers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_diver "Recreational diver") are out of water activities and transitions between water and the surface site such as carrying equipment on shore, exiting from water to boat and shore, surface swimming, and dressing into the equipment. Safety and reliability, adjustability to fit the individual, performance, and simplicity were rated the most important features for diving equipment by recreational divers.[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Bitterman-179)[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Bitterman_et_al_2009-180) The [professional diver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_diver "Professional diver") is supported by a [surface team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_team "Diving team"), who are available to assist with the out-of-water activities to the extent necessary to reduce the risk associated with them to a level acceptable in terms of the governing regulations and codes of practice.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-CoP_Inshore-58)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-SA_Diving_Regulations_2009-89)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Diving_at_Work_Regulations_1997-43)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-IMCA_D014-42)

[![Image 25: A diver is carrying two cylinders, one on his back and the other at his side.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Peter_Southwood_2.jpg/250px-Peter_Southwood_2.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Peter_Southwood_2.jpg)

Solo diver managing risk of breathing gas supply failure by carrying a bailout cylinder (slung at the diver's left side)

[Risk management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risk_management "Risk management") of diving operations involves the usual measures of [engineering controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering_controls "Engineering controls"),[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Engineering-182) [administrative controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_controls "Administrative controls") and procedures,[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Administration-183) and [personal protective equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_protective_equipment "Personal protective equipment"),[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-PPE-184) including [hazard identification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard_identification "Hazard identification") and [risk assessment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risk_assessment "Risk assessment") (HIRA), [protective equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protective_equipment "Protective equipment"), [medical screening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screening_/(medicine/) "Screening (medicine)"), [training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Training "Training") and [standardised procedures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_operating_procedure "Standard operating procedure").[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Risk_management-185)[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-OHS_answers-181) Professional divers are generally legally obliged to carry out and formally record these measures,[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-DAWR-160) and though recreational divers are not legally required to do many of them,[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-SA_Diving_Regulations_2009-89) competent recreational divers, and particularly technical divers, generally perform them informally but routinely, and they are an important part of technical diver training. For example, a medical statement or examination for fitness, pre-dive site assessment and briefing, safety drills, thermal protection, equipment redundancy, [alternative air source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_air_source "Alternative air source"), buddy checks, [buddy or team diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_diving "Buddy diving") procedures, [dive planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dive_planning "Dive planning"), use of [dive computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dive_computer "Dive computer") to monitor and record the dive profile and decompression status, [underwater hand signals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_communications "Diver communications"), and carrying [first aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_aid "First aid") and [oxygen administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_therapy "Oxygen therapy") equipment are all routinely part of technical diving.[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Gurr_2008-186)

Inshore and inland commercial and military diving is regulated by legislation in many countries. Responsibility of the employer, client and diving personnel is specified in these cases;[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-SA_Diving_Regulations_2009-89)[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-DAWR-160) offshore commercial diving may take place in international waters, and is often done following the guidelines of a voluntary membership organisation such as the [International Marine Contractors Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Marine_Contractors_Association "International Marine Contractors Association") (IMCA), which publishes [codes of accepted best practice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_practice "Code of practice") which their member organisations are expected to follow.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-IMCA_D014-42)[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-IMCA-187)

Recreational diver training and dive leading are industry regulated in some countries, and only directly regulated by government in a subset of them. In the UK, HSE legislation includes recreational diver training and dive leading for reward;[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-DAWR-160) in the US and South Africa industry regulation is accepted, though non-specific health and safety legislation still applies.[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-29_CFR_1910.424-188)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-SA_Diving_Regulations_2009-89) In Israel recreational diving activities are regulated by the Recreational Diving Act, 1979.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Rec_Diving_Act_1979-189)

The legal responsibility for recreational diving service providers is usually limited as far as possible by [waivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waiver "Waiver") which they require the customer to sign before engaging in any diving activity. The extent of [duty of care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duty_of_care "Duty of care") of recreational [buddy divers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_diving "Buddy diving") is unclear and has been the subject of considerable litigation. It is probable that it varies between jurisdictions. In spite of this lack of clarity, buddy diving is recommended by [recreational diver training agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diver_certification_organizations "List of diver certification organizations") as safer than [solo diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo_diving "Solo diving"), and some service providers insist that customers dive in buddy pairs.[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Coleman-190)[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-SPUMShalstead-191)[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Powell_2011-192)

Scuba diving tourism is the industry based on servicing the requirements of [recreational divers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_diver "Recreational diver") at destinations other than where they live. It includes aspects of training, equipment sales, rental and service, guided experiences and [environmental tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_tourism "Environmental tourism").[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Dimmock_et_al_2013-193)[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Dimmock_and_Musa_2015-194) Provision of transport to and from dive sites without convenient shore entry may be provided by basic, day excursion, and live-aboard [dive boats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dive_boat "Dive boat").[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-BSAC_Sport_Diving_1985-195)

Motivations to travel for scuba diving are complex and may vary considerably during the diver's development and experience. Participation can vary from once off to multiple dedicated trips per year over several decades. The popular destinations fall into several groups, including tropical reefs, shipwrecks and cave systems, each frequented by its own group of enthusiasts, with some overlap. Customer satisfaction is largely dependent on the quality of services provided, and personal communication has a strong influence on the popularity of specific service providers in a region.[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Dimmock_et_al_2013-193)

[Professional diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_diving "Professional diving") includes a wide range of applications, of varying economic impact. All of them are in support of specific sectors of industry, commerce, defence, or public service, and their economic impacts are closely related to their importance to the relevant sector, and their effects on the diving equipment manufacturing and support industries. The importance of diving to the scientific community is not well recorded, but analysis of publications shows that diving supports scientific research largely through efficient and targeted sampling.[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Sayer_2007-196)

Most modes of diving are equipment intensive, and much of the equipment is either life-support or specialised equipment for the application. This has led to a manufacturing industry in support of both recreational and professional diving, where developments in one mode often find applications in another. In terms of total numbers of divers, the recreational diving industry has a far larger market, but the costs of equipment and relatively large manning requirements of professional diving make that market substantial in its own right. The international [Diving Equipment and Marketing Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_Equipment_and_Marketing_Association "Diving Equipment and Marketing Association"), (DEMA), exists to promote the scuba diving and snorkeling industry.[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-DEMA-197)

The number of active scuba divers is not recorded systematically, but has been estimated on occasions with varying levels of confidence. One of the problems is the lack of a generally accepted definition of what constitutes an active scuba diver. The situation for freedivers and snorkelers is even less clear, as most freedivers have no qualification registered anywhere.[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Sadler_et_al_2020-198)

The [Diving Equipment and Marketing Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_Equipment_and_Marketing_Association "Diving Equipment and Marketing Association") (DEMA) estimate from 2.5 to 3.5 million active scuba divers in the US and up to 6 million worldwide, about 11 million snorkelers in the US, and about 20 million snorkelers worldwide.[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-DEMA_2021-199) The [Sports and Fitness Industry Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_and_Fitness_Industry_Association&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sports and Fitness Industry Association (page does not exist)") (SFIA) reported 2,351,000 casual participants, and 823,000 core participants in 2019, also in the US. [Divers Alert Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divers_Alert_Network "Divers Alert Network") (DAN), reported 2019 membership numbers worldwide: DAN US/Canada, 274,708; DAN Europe, 123,680; DAN Japan, 18,137; DAN World Asia Pacific, 12,163; DAN World Latin America/Brazil, 8,008; DAN South Africa, 5,894.[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Sadler_et_al_2020-198)

The active US scuba diving population could be fewer than 1,000,000, possibly as low as 500,000, depending on the definition of _active_. Numbers outside the US are less clear.[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Sadler_et_al_2020-198) This may be compared with PADI worldwide statistics for 2021, in which they claim to have issued more than 28 million diver certifications since 1967.[\[197\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-PADI_2021_stats-200)

Entry of non-divers through certification courses also provides an indicator of numbers, though there is no record of whether a diver remains active after certification unless further training is registered. Three training and certification agencies – [Professional Association of Diving Instructors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_Association_of_Diving_Instructors "Professional Association of Diving Instructors") (PADI), [Scuba Diving International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_Diving_International "Scuba Diving International") (SDI), and [Scuba Schools International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_Schools_International "Scuba Schools International") (SSI) reported a combined average of 22,325 entry-level certifications per quarter. Estimating the number of active scuba instructors in the US and internationally is also difficult. Over 300 individual certifying agencies train and certify divers, dive leaders, and instructors, but there are also an unknown number of instructors who are registered with more than one agency. PADI reported 137,000 professional members (instructors and divemasters) worldwide in 2019. On the assumption that PADI represents 70% of the market share, the number of instructors globally may be about 195,000.[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Sadler_et_al_2020-198)

The [American Academy of Underwater Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Academy_of_Underwater_Sciences "American Academy of Underwater Sciences") (AAUS) reports 4,500 divers at 150 organisational member scientific diving programmes (2020), and the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention") (CDC) and [Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Labor_Statistics "Bureau of Labor Statistics") reported 3,380 commercial divers in the US (2018). The number of active public safety divers in the US is also uncertain, but estimated to be between 3,000 and 5,000 in 2019.[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Sadler_et_al_2020-198)

Environmental impact
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Underwater_diving&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Environmental impact")\]

[![Image 26: Diver wearing a diving helmet is sanding a repair patch on a submarine](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Working_Diver_02.jpg/250px-Working_Diver_02.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Working_Diver_02.jpg)

A diver at work on hull maintenance

The environmental impact of recreational diving is the effects of diving tourism on the marine environment. Usually these are considered to be adverse effects, and include damage to reef organisms by incompetent and ignorant divers, but there may also be positive effects as the environment is recognised by the local communities to be worth more in good condition than degraded by inappropriate use, which encourages conservation efforts. During the 20th century recreational scuba diving was considered to have generally low environmental impact, and was consequently one of the activities permitted in most marine protected areas. Since the 1970s diving has changed from an elite activity to a more accessible recreation, marketed to a very wide demographic. To some extent better equipment has been substituted for more rigorous training, and the reduction in perceived risk has shortened minimum training requirements by several training agencies. Training has concentrated on an acceptable risk to the diver, and paid less attention to the environment. The increase in the popularity of diving and in tourist access to sensitive ecological systems has led to the recognition that the activity can have significant environmental consequences.[\[198\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Hammerton_2014-201)

Recreational scuba diving has grown in popularity during the 21st century, as is shown by the number of certifications issued worldwide, which has increased to about 23 million by 2016 at about one million per year.[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Lucrezi_2016-202) Scuba diving tourism is a growth industry, and it is necessary to consider [environmental sustainability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_sustainability "Environmental sustainability"), as the expanding impact of divers can adversely affect the [marine environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_environment "Marine environment") in several ways, and the impact also depends on the specific environment. Tropical coral reefs are more easily damaged by poor diving skills than some temperate reefs, where the environment is more robust due to rougher sea conditions and fewer fragile, slow-growing organisms. The same pleasant sea conditions that allow development of relatively delicate and highly diverse ecologies also attract the greatest number of tourists, including divers who dive infrequently, exclusively on vacation and never fully develop the skills to dive in an environmentally friendly way.[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Dimmock_et_al_2013-193) [Low impact diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_impact_diving "Low impact diving") training has been shown to be effective in reducing diver contact.[\[198\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-Hammerton_2014-201)

The ecological impact of [commercial diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_diving "Commercial diving") is a small part of the impact of the specific industry supported by the diving operations, as commercial diving is not done in isolation. In most cases the impact of diving operations is insignificant in comparison with the overall project, and environmental impact assessments may be required before the project is authorised for some classes of project.[\[200\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-SAFLII-203)[\[201\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-ELaw-204) Underwater [ships husbandry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ships_husbandry "Ships husbandry") may be an exception to this general tendency, and specific precautions to limit ecological impact may be required. Several of these operations will release some quantity of harmful material into the water, particularly hull cleaning operations which will release antifouling toxins.[\[202\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-UNDS_1999-205) Alien biofouling organisms may also be released during this process.[\[202\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-UNDS_1999-205): 15  Other forms of [professional diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_diving "Professional diving"), such as [scientific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_diving "Scientific diving") and [archaeological dives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_archaeology "Underwater archaeology"), are planned to minimise impact, which may be a condition for the application for a permit.[\[203\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-NHL-206)[\[204\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-SAHRA-207)

1.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_ref-Engineering_182-0)** Engineering methods control the hazard at its source. When feasible, the work environment and the job itself are designed to eliminate hazards or reduce exposure to hazards: If feasible, the hazard is removed or substituted by something that is not hazardous. If removal is not feasible, the hazard is enclosed to prevent exposure during normal operations. Where complete enclosure is not feasible, barriers are established to limit exposure during normal operations.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-OHS_answers-181)
2.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_ref-Administration_183-0)** Safe work practices, appropriate training, medical screening and limiting exposure by rotation of workers, breaks and limits on shift length are forms of administrative controls. They are intended to limit the effect of the hazard on the worker when it cannot be eliminated.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-OHS_answers-181)
3.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_ref-PPE_184-0)** Personal protective clothing and equipment are required in diving operations as exposure to the inherent hazards cannot be engineered out of normal operations, and safe work practices and management controls cannot provide sufficient protection from exposure. Personnel protective controls assume the hazard will be present and the equipment will prevent injury to those exposed.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving#cite_note-OHS_answers-181)

Atmospheric diving suit
Atmospheric diving suit
AcronymADS
Other namesHard suit, JIM suit
UsesDeep diving
Related itemsSubmersible
[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Newtsuit_atmospheric_diving_suit.jpg/250px-Newtsuit_atmospheric_diving_suit.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Newtsuit_atmospheric_diving_suit.jpg) The [Newtsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtsuit "Newtsuit") has fully articulated, rotary joints in the arms and legs. These provide high mobility, while remaining largely unaffected by high pressures. An **atmospheric diving suit** (**ADS**), **atmospheric pressure diving suit** or **single atmosphere diving suit** is a small one-person articulated [submersible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submersible "Submersible") which resembles a [suit of armour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_armour "Plate armour"), with pressure-tight joints to allow articulation while maintaining a constant internal volume and an internal pressure of one atmosphere. An ADS can enable diving at depths of up to 2,300 feet (700 m) for many hours by eliminating the majority of significant physiological dangers associated with [deep diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving "Deep diving").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) The occupant of an ADS does not need to [decompress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_/(diving/) "Decompression (diving)"), and there is no need for special [breathing gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas") mixtures, so there is no danger of [decompression sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_sickness "Decompression sickness") or [nitrogen narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_narcosis "Nitrogen narcosis") when the ADS is functioning properly.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Wasp_specifications-2) An ADS can permit less-skilled swimmers to complete deep dives, albeit at the expense of dexterity. Atmospheric diving suits in current use include the [Newtsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtsuit "Newtsuit"), Exosuit, Hardsuit and the WASP, all of which are self-contained hard suits that incorporate propulsion units. The Hardsuit is constructed from [cast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casting "Casting") aluminum ([forged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forging "Forging") aluminum in a version constructed for the US Navy for submarine rescue); the upper torso hull is made from cast [aluminum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminum "Aluminum"), while the bottom dome is machined aluminum. The WASP is of [glass-reinforced plastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass-reinforced_plastic "Glass-reinforced plastic") (GRP) body tube construction.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) Definition and classification ----------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Definition and classification")\] An atmospheric diving suit is a small one-person submersible with articulated limbs encasing the diver. Water- and pressure-tight joints allow articulation while maintaining an internal pressure of one atmosphere. Mobility may be through thrusters for mid-water operation, though this is not a requirement, and articulated legs may be provided for walking on the substrate.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) Thornton (2000) distinguishes an ADS from a submersible in that the ADS has human powered articulated limbs, as opposed to remotely operated articulated limbs.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) It is not clear whether this would exclude servo-assisted limbs encasing those of the operator, as a powered exoskeleton, but it might be reasonable to include them as atmospheric diving suits. An atmospheric diving suit may be classified as a crewed submersible and a self-propelled, crewed, one-atmosphere underwater intervention device, but has also been classified as an atmospheric diving system.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) A characteristic of single atmosphere internal pressure is that the suit cannot passively vent gas to ambient pressure. The options are to recycle breathing gas internally, adding oxygen and removing carbon dioxide,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Machine_Design-4) to vent surface supplied gas back to the surface through a hose which can safely withstand the external ambient pressure, or to pump it out by compressing it to ambient pressure before venting.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-5) Purpose and requirements ------------------------ \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Purpose and requirements")\] See also: [Human factors in diving equipment design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_factors_in_diving_equipment_design "Human factors in diving equipment design") The [underwater environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_environment "Underwater environment") exerts major [physiological stresses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_physiology_of_underwater_diving "Human physiology of underwater diving") on the diver, which increase with depth, and appear to impose an absolute limit to diving depth at ambient pressure. An atmospheric diving suit is a small submersible with a pressure hull which accommodates a single occupant at an internal pressure of about one atmosphere. The provision of hollow arm spaces with pressure-resistant joints to carry manually operated manipulators, and usually separate leg spaces, similarly articulated for locomotion, makes a suit resemble a bulky suit of [plate armour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_armour "Plate armour"), or an [exoskeleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exoskeleton "Exoskeleton"), with elaborate joint seals to allow articulation while maintaining internal pressure.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) An atmospheric diving suit is equipment intended primarily to isolate the occupant from the ambient pressure of the underwater environment, and provide any necessary [life-support](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life-support_system "Life-support system") while the suit is in use. While using the suit, the diver will expect to perform useful work, and get to and from the place where the work is to be done. These functions require sufficient mobility, dexterity and sensory input to do the job, and this will vary depending on the details of the work. Consequently, the work possible in an atmospheric suit is limited by the suit construction.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) Mobility at the surface and on deck can be managed by [launch and recovery systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_and_recovery_system_/(diving/) "Launch and recovery system (diving)"), Mobility underwater generally requires neutral or moderately negative buoyancy, and either the ability to walk or swim, or the use of finely controllable [thrusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thruster_/(marine_/) "Thruster (marine )"). Both walking and thruster propulsion have been applied with some success. Swimming has not been effective.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) The dexterity to perform useful work is limited by joint mobility and geometry, inertia, and friction, and has been one of the more difficult engineering challenges. [Haptic perception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haptic_perception "Haptic perception") through manipulators is a major limitation on finer control, as the friction of the joints and seals greatly reduces the sensitivity available.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) Operator visual input is relatively easy to provide directly by using transparent [viewports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viewport_/(diving/) "Viewport (diving)"). A wide field of view can be achieved simply and structurally effectively by using a transparent partial dome over the diver's head. Close-up views of the manipulators are limited by joint flexibility and geometry of the suit's arms. External sound and temperature perception are greatly attenuated, and there is no sense of touch through the suit. [Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_communication#Voice_communications "Diver communication") must be provided by technology, as there is normally no-one else in the immediate vicinity.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) ### Design constraints \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Design constraints")\] The main environmental factors affecting design are the ambient hydrostatic pressure of the maximum operating depth, and ergonomic considerations regarding the potential range of operators.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) The structure and mechanics of the suit must reliably withstand the external pressure, without collapsing or deforming sufficiently to cause seals to leak or joints to experience excessive friction, and the full range of movement must not change the internal or external displaced volume, as this would have consequences for the amount of force required to move the joints in addition to the friction of the joint seals. Insulation is relatively simple, and can be applied to the inside of the suit and in the form of clothing on the diver. Active heating and cooling are also possible using well established technology. Mass changes can be used to provide initial and emergency buoyancy conditions by way of fixed and ditchable ballast weights.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) Ergonomic considerations include the size and strength of the user. The interior dimensions must fit or be modifiable to fit a reasonable range of operators, and operating forces on joints must be reasonably practicable. The field of vision is constrained by the helmet design or viewport positioning, though closed circuit video can extend it considerably in any direction. General underwater conditions of visibility and water movement must be manageable for the range of conditions in which the suit is expected to be used. Marine thrusters may be mounted on the suit to help with maneuvering and positioning,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) and sonar and other scanning technologies may help provide an augmented external view.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) Factors affecting the design and construction:[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6) * Pressure hull form – Sufficient volume for necessary internal systems, constrained by size and shape of human operator, and by shapes with high resistance to collapse under external pressure.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6) * Displacement – Need for neutral buoyancy at work and positive buoyancy in emergencies[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6) * Hydrodynamics – cruise speed[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6) * Propulsion – Thruster type and arrangement[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6) * Ergonomics – Anthropometry, joint design for limb articulation under external pressure. * Working depth rating – Strength, rigidity and density of materials.
