\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Operator requirements")\] * The operator must fit inside the suit, be able to move their limbs effectively, and be able to get out again.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6) * The operator must be able to reach and to operate electronics panels and life support systems, be able to jettison ballast, operate umbilical and thruster cable cutters.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6) * The operator must be physically, medically and psychologically fit for the work.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6) ### Hazards and failure modes \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Hazards and failure modes")\] The primary structural failure modes of an ADS are [buckling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckling "Buckling") collapse in compression, leaks, and lockup of joints. Leaks and buckling in compression both cause a reduction in buoyancy. Joint leaks and locking of articulating joints may be reversible when pressure is reduced. Electrically ignited fire is also possible. Systems failures may include loss of power, communications, or propulsion, or life-support systems failure, such as failure of scrubbing the carbon dioxide from the breathing air, or failure of internal temperature control. Recovery from most of these would be by aborting the dive and making an emergency ascent. Bailout to emergency breathing system and ditching of ballast to establish positive buoyancy may be necessary. If the ADS is tethered it can be lifted. The most dangerous consequence is catastrophic leakage, which is likely to be fatal. There has been one fatal incident involving an ADS. A WASP was dropped 80 feet (25 m) in August 1999 due to a structural failure in a recently tested launch and recovery system, and the diver was killed by the impact with the launch platform. This is in the context of tens of thousands of operational man-hours by WASPs without serious incidents.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) Comparison with alternative technologies ---------------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Comparison with alternative technologies")\] Several advantages over ambient pressure diving are claimed, but dexterity is less. There are also advantages and disadvantages in comparison with [remotely operated underwater vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remotely_operated_underwater_vehicle "Remotely operated underwater vehicle") (ROVs): * No decompression is required. Decompression from saturation takes approximately 1 day per 30 [msw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre_sea_water "Metre sea water") plus 1 day, during which time the divers are unproductive. This is particularly expensive when the total dive time is relatively short.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) * Consecutive dives can be made to any depths within the operating range. Saturation divers are very limited in safe excursion range from storage depth.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) An ADS depth excursions are limited only by maximum working depth.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6) * Lateral range is comparable with ROVs.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6) * Thrusters, when provided, can provide moderate mid-water and current capability.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) * Manipulatory capacity and dexterity are better than ROVs. Less special tooling is required for most work. Depth perception of the diver is better than remote viewing via a ROV cameras.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) * Deep applications are possible compared with ambient pressure diving. The industry-accepted maximum depth for routine saturation diving is 300 msw. ADS operations can go deeper.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) However, ROVs and crewed submersibles can go much deeper. Maximum depth capability for ROV and crewed submersibles is [full ocean depth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_ocean_depth "Full ocean depth").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Technology_specifications-7) For some work the most effective method can be a combination of ADS and ROV; in other cases, ADS and ambient pressure diver.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) History ------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: History")\] See also: [History of underwater diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_underwater_diving "History of underwater diving") ### Early designs \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=12 "Edit section: Early designs")\] [![Image 6: Drawing of a one-person tapered submarine like vessel with sealed holes for operator's arms shown with rope slings](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Jacob_Rowe%27s_diving_machine.jpg/250px-Jacob_Rowe%27s_diving_machine.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jacob_Rowe%27s_diving_machine.jpg) [Jacob Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jacob_Rowe&action=edit&redlink=1 "Jacob Rowe (page does not exist)")'s copper diving dress, built in the 1710s [![Image 7: Tapered one-person submarine like wooden vessel with sealed holes for operator's arms held aloft by rope slings in a museum display](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/John_Lethbridge_diving_apparatus_replica_%281715%29.jpg/250px-John_Lethbridge_diving_apparatus_replica_%281715%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Lethbridge_diving_apparatus_replica_/(1715/).jpg) Modern replica on display at the [History of Diving Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Diving_Museum "History of Diving Museum"), Florida In 1715, British inventor [John Lethbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lethbridge "John Lethbridge") constructed a "diving engine". Essentially a wooden barrel about 6 feet (1.8 m) in length with two holes for the diver's arms sealed with leather cuffs, and a 4-inch (100 mm) viewport of thick glass. It was reportedly used to dive as deep as 60 feet (18 m), and was used to salvage substantial quantities of [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver") from the wreck of the [East Indiaman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Indiaman "East Indiaman") [_Vansittart_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vansittart_/(1718_EIC_ship/) "Vansittart (1718 EIC ship)"), which sank in 1719 off the [Cape Verde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Verde "Cape Verde") islands.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-tanads-8) A similar design made of copper was used by Jacob Rowe on the same salvage contract.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Ratcliffe_2011-9) The first armored suit with real joints, designed as leather pieces with rings in the shape of a spring (also known as accordion joints), was designed by Englishman W. H. Taylor in 1838. The diver's hands and feet were covered with leather. Taylor also devised a ballast tank attached to the suit that could be filled with water to attain negative [buoyancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buoyancy "Buoyancy"). While it was patented, the suit was never actually produced. It is considered that its weight and bulk would have rendered it nearly immobile underwater.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-tanads-8) Lodner D. Phillips designed the first completely enclosed ADS in 1856. His design comprised a barrel-shaped upper torso with domed ends with ball and socket joints in the articulated arms and legs. The arms had joints at shoulder and elbow, and the legs at knee and hip. The suit included a ballast tank, a viewing port, entrance through a [manhole cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhole_cover "Manhole cover") on top, a hand-cranked propeller, and rudimentary manipulators at the ends of the arms. Breathing air was to be supplied from the surface via hose. There is no indication that Phillips' suit was ever constructed.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-tanads-8) [![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Scaphandre_Carmagnolle_MnM_Paris.jpg/250px-Scaphandre_Carmagnolle_MnM_Paris.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scaphandre_Carmagnolle_MnM_Paris.jpg) Suit built by Carmagnolle brothers in 1882 was the first anthropomorphic design. The first properly anthropomorphic design of ADS, built by the [Carmagnolle brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carmagnolle_brothers&action=edit&redlink=1 "Carmagnolle brothers (page does not exist)") of [Marseille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marseille "Marseille"), France in 1882, featured rolling convolute joints consisting of closely fitting concentric spherical sections sealed by watertight cloth membranes. The suit had 22 of these joints: four in each leg, six in each arm, and two in the torso. The helmet had 25 individual 2-inch (50 mm) glass viewports spaced at the average separation of the human eyes.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Historic_diving_times_2005-10) Weighing 830 pounds (380 kg), the Carmagnole ADS never worked properly and its joints never were entirely waterproof. It is now on display at the [French National Navy Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_national_de_la_Marine "Musée national de la Marine") in Paris.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-pieds-lourds-11) Another design was patented in 1894 by inventors John Buchanan and Alexander Gordon from [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne"), Australia. The construction was based on a frame of spiral wires covered with waterproof material. The design was improved by Alexander Gordon by attaching the suit to the helmet and other parts and incorporating jointed [radius rods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radius_rod "Radius rod") in the limbs. This resulted in a flexible suit which could withstand high pressure. The suit was manufactured by British firm [Siebe Gorman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siebe_Gorman "Siebe Gorman") and trialed in Scotland in 1898.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] US Navy 1913 ADS [![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/1913_US_Navy_ADS_at_Man_in_the_Sea_Museum_Panama_City_with_mechanical_lobster_claws_Bhargav.jpg/250px-1913_US_Navy_ADS_at_Man_in_the_Sea_Museum_Panama_City_with_mechanical_lobster_claws_Bhargav.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1913_US_Navy_ADS_at_Man_in_the_Sea_Museum_Panama_City_with_mechanical_lobster_claws_Bhargav.jpg) 1913 US Navy ADS at Man in the Sea Museum, Panama City, FL with the lobster claws [![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/2_jawed_grasper_on_1913_US_Navy_armored_diving_suit.jpg/250px-2_jawed_grasper_on_1913_US_Navy_armored_diving_suit.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2_jawed_grasper_on_1913_US_Navy_armored_diving_suit.jpg) Close up view of two-jawed grasper and pitch-yaw wrist joint on 1913 US Navy armored diving suit American designer Macduffee constructed the first suit to use ball bearings to provide joint movement in 1914; it was tested in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") to a depth of 214 feet (65 m), but was not very successful. A year later, Harry L. Bowdoin of [Bayonne, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayonne,_New_Jersey "Bayonne, New Jersey"), made an improved ADS with oil-filled rotary joints. Each joint has a small duct to its interior to allow equalization of pressure. The suit was designed to have eighteen joints: four in each arm and leg, and one in each thumb. Four viewing ports and a chest-mounted lamp were intended to assist underwater vision. There is no evidence that Bowdoin's suit was ever built, or that it would have worked if it had been.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-tanads-8) Atmospheric diving suits built by [Neufeldt and Kuhnke](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neufeldt_and_Kuhnke&action=edit&redlink=1 "Neufeldt and Kuhnke (page does not exist)") of Germany were used during the salvage of gold and silver bullion from the wreck of the British ship [SS _Egypt_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Egypt "SS Egypt"), an 8,000 ton [P&O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%26O "P&O") liner that sank in May 1922. The suit was relegated to duties as an observation chamber at the wreck's depth of 560 feet (170 m),[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Pickford-12) and was successfully used to direct mechanical grabs which opened up the bullion storage. In 1917, [Benjamin F. Leavitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Benjamin_F._Leavitt&action=edit&redlink=1 "Benjamin F. Leavitt (page does not exist)") of [Traverse City, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traverse_City,_Michigan "Traverse City, Michigan"), dived on the [SS _Pewabic_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Pewabic "SS Pewabic") which sank to a depth of 182 feet (55 m) in [Lake Huron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Huron "Lake Huron") in 1865, salvaging 350 tons of copper ore. In 1923, he went on to salvage the wreck of the British schooner _Cape Horn_ which lay in 220 feet (67 m) of water off [Pichidangui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pichidangui "Pichidangui"), Chile, salvaging $600,000 worth of copper. Leavitt's suit was of his own design and construction. The most innovative aspect of Leavitt's suit was the fact that it was completely self-contained and needed no umbilical, the breathing mixture being supplied from a tank mounted on the back of the suit. The breathing apparatus incorporated a [scrubber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrubber "Scrubber") and an oxygen [regulator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_regulator "Diving regulator") and could last for up to a full hour.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Marx_1990-13) In 1924 the _[Reichsmarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reichsmarine "Reichsmarine")_ tested the second generation of the Neufeldt and Kuhnke suit to 530 feet (160 m), but limb movement was very difficult and the joints were judged not to be [fail-safe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fail-safe "Fail-safe"), in that if they were to fail, there was a possibility that the suit's integrity would be violated. However, these suits were used by the Germans as armored divers during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") and were later taken by the [Western Allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") after the war. From 1929 to 1931 two atmospheric pressure one-person submersible "suits" designed by Carl Wiley were used in the successful salvage of the steamship _[Islander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Islander "SS Islander")_ which sank in the [Stevens Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stevens_Passage&action=edit&redlink=1 "Stevens Passage (page does not exist)") near [Juneau, Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juneau,_Alaska "Juneau, Alaska") on 15 August 1901, with a large amount of gold dust in the cargo. The suits operated at a maximum depth of 365 feet (111 m). They were each equipped with a mechanical arm with a grasping claw at the end operated from inside the suit. The suits were capable of traversing a hard, reasonably smooth substrate on wheels, and were used to place the steel cables used to raise the wreck by [tidal lift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_lift "Tidal lift") (with an 18-foot or 5-metre tide range) under a catamaran barge in stages, while it was towed to shallow water. The suits had electrical power, and the diver/pilot used an oxygen rebreather. These suits have also been described as diving bells and observation chambers, as they do not match the usual definition of an atmospheric diving suit, but they were more than just observation chambers, being capable of work, and were independently mobile, so do not match the usual definition of a diving bell either. They were an unusual type of tethered crewed submersible.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Popular_Mechanics_Oct_1931-14) In 1952, [Alfred A. Mikalow](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_A._Mikalow&action=edit&redlink=1 "Alfred A. Mikalow (page does not exist)") constructed an ADS using ball and socket joints, specifically for the purpose of locating and salvaging sunken treasure. The suit was reported to be capable of diving to 1,000 feet (300 m) depth and was successfully used to dive on the wreck of [SS _City of Rio de Janeiro_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_City_of_Rio_de_Janeiro "SS City of Rio de Janeiro") near [Fort Point, San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Point,_San_Francisco "Fort Point, San Francisco") at a depth of 330 feet (100 m). Mikalow's suit had various interchangeable instruments which could be mounted on the end of the arms in place of the original manipulators. It carried seven 90-cubic foot high pressure cylinders to provide breathing gas and control buoyancy. The ballast compartment covered the gas cylinders. For communication, the suit used [hydrophones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrophone "Hydrophone").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Burke_1966-15) ### The modern suit \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: The modern suit")\] #### Peress' _Tritonia_ \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Peress' Tritonia")\] [![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Tritonia_Lusitania_1935.jpg/330px-Tritonia_Lusitania_1935.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tritonia_Lusitania_1935.jpg) Two divers, one wearing the "Tritonia" ADS and the other standard diving dress, preparing to explore the wreck of the [RMS _Lusitania_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RMS_Lusitania "RMS Lusitania"), 1935 Although various atmospheric suits had been developed during the [Victorian era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era "Victorian era"), none of these suits overcame the basic design problem of constructing a joint which would remain flexible and watertight at depth without seizing up under pressure. Pioneering British diving engineer, [Joseph Salim Peress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Salim_Peress "Joseph Salim Peress"), invented the first truly usable atmospheric diving suit, the _Tritonia_, in 1932 and was later involved in the construction of the famous [JIM suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JIM_suit "JIM suit"). Having a natural talent for engineering design, he challenged himself to construct an ADS that would keep divers dry and at atmospheric pressure, even at great depth. In 1918, Peress began working for WG Tarrant at [Byfleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byfleet "Byfleet"), United Kingdom, where he was given the space and tools to develop his ideas about constructing an ADS. His first attempt was an immensely complex prototype machined from solid [stainless steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stainless_steel "Stainless steel"). In 1923, Peress was asked to design a suit for salvage work on the wreck of [SS _Egypt_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Egypt "SS Egypt") which had sunk in the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel"). He declined, on the grounds that his prototype suit was too heavy for a diver to handle easily, but was encouraged by the request to begin work on a new suit using lighter materials. By 1929 he believed he had solved the weight problem, by using cast magnesium instead of steel, and had also managed to improve the design of the suit's joints by using a trapped cushion of oil to keep the surfaces moving smoothly. The oil was virtually non-compressible and readily displaceable, which would allow the limb joints to move freely even under great pressure. Peress claimed the Tritonia suit could function at 1,200 ft (370 m), where the pressure was 520 psi (35 atm), although this was never proven.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-loftas1973-16) [![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Luciana_Civico_risalita_record_ARA_meno_80_stringe_pinza_scafandro_Verardi.jpg/250px-Luciana_Civico_risalita_record_ARA_meno_80_stringe_pinza_scafandro_Verardi.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Luciana_Civico_risalita_record_ARA_meno_80_stringe_pinza_scafandro_Verardi.jpg) Luciana Civico ascending from the dive of the depth record at 269 feet (82 m) on 11 November 1962 in the vicinity of Capo Miseno in the Gulf of Pozzuoli tightens the pincer of the diving suit operated by the s. Lieutenant Benito Velardi In 1930, Peress revealed the Tritonia suit.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-dive_hx-17) By May it had completed trials and was publicly demonstrated in a tank at [Byfleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byfleet "Byfleet"). In September Peress' assistant [Jim Jarret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Jarret "Jim Jarret") dived in the suit to a depth of 404 ft (123 m) in [Loch Ness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Ness "Loch Ness"). The suit performed perfectly, the joints proving resistant to pressure and moving freely even at depth. The suit was offered to the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") which turned it down, stating that Navy divers never needed to descend below 300 ft (90 m). In October 1935 Jarret made a successful deep dive to more than 300 ft (90 m) on the wreck of the [RMS _Lusitania_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RMS_Lusitania "RMS Lusitania") off south Ireland, followed by a shallower dive to 200 feet (60 m) in the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel") in 1937 after which, due to lack of interest, the Tritonia suit was retired.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] The development in atmospheric pressure suits stagnated in the 1940s through 1960s, as efforts were concentrated on solving the problems of deep diving by dealing with the physiological problems of ambient pressure diving instead of avoiding them by isolating the diver from the pressure. Although the advances in ambient pressure diving (in particular, with [scuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_set "Scuba set") gear) were significant, the limitations brought renewed interest to the development of the ADS in the late 1960s.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-loftas1973-16) #### The JIM suit \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: The JIM suit")\] Main article: [JIM suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JIM_suit "JIM suit") The _Tritonia_ suit spent about 30 years in an engineering company's warehouse in [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow"), where it was discovered, with Peress' help, by two partners in the British firm Underwater Marine Equipment, Mike Humphrey and Mike Borrow, in the mid-1960s.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-loftas1973-16)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-scribe71-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-divernet-19) UMEL would later classify Peress' suit as the "A.D.S Type I", a designation system that would be continued by the company for later models. In 1969, Peress was asked to become a consultant to the new company created to develop the JIM suit, named in honour of the diver Jim Jarret.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Carter_1976-20) [![Image 13](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/JIM_suit_in_Naval_Undersea_Museum.jpg/250px-JIM_suit_in_Naval_Undersea_Museum.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JIM_suit_in_Naval_Undersea_Museum.jpg) JIM suit in Naval Undersea Museum The first JIM suit was completed in November 1971 and underwent sea trials from [HMS _Reclaim_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Reclaim "HMS Reclaim") in early 1972. In 1976, it set a record of five hours and 59 minutes for the longest working dive below 490 feet (150 m), at a depth of 905 feet (276 m). The first JIM suits were constructed from cast magnesium for its high strength-to-weight ratio and weighed approximately 1,100 pounds (500 kg) in air, including the occupant. They were 6 feet 6 inches (1.98 m) in height and had a maximum operating depth of 1,500 feet (460 m). The suit had a positive buoyancy of 15 to 50 pounds-force (67 to 222 N). Ballast was attached to the suit's front and could be jettisoned from inside, allowing the suit to ascend to the surface at approximately 100 feet per minute (30 m/min).[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Kesling_2011-21) The suit also incorporated a communication link and an umbilical connection that could be released by the diver. The original JIM suit had eight annular oil-supported universal joints, one at each hip, knee, shoulder and lower arm. The JIM operator received air through an oral/nasal mask that attached to a lung-powered scrubber that had a life support duration of approximately 72 hours.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-nedu76-22) Operations in arctic conditions with water temperatures of 28.9 °F (−1.7 °C) for over 5 hours were successfully carried out using woolen thermal protection and neoprene boots. In 86 °F (30 °C) water the suit was reported to be uncomfortably hot during heavy work.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Curley_and_Bachrach_1982-23) [![Image 14](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/JIM_suitRoyal_Navy_Submarine_Museum.jpg/250px-JIM_suitRoyal_Navy_Submarine_Museum.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JIM_suitRoyal_Navy_Submarine_Museum.jpg) A [JIM suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JIM_suit "JIM suit") on display at the [Royal Navy Submarine Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy_Submarine_Museum "Royal Navy Submarine Museum"), Gosport As technology improved and operational knowledge grew, Oceaneering upgraded their fleet of JIMs. The magnesium construction was replaced with [glass-reinforced plastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass-reinforced_plastic "Glass-reinforced plastic") (GRP) and the single joints with segmented ones, each allowing seven degrees of motion, and when added together giving the operator a very great range of motion. In addition, the four-port domed top of the suit was replaced by a transparent acrylic dome as used on WASP, which provided a much better field of vision. Trials were also carried out by the [Ministry of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_/(United_Kingdom/) "Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)") on a flying Jim suit powered from the surface through an umbilical cable. This resulted in a hybrid suit with the ability of working on the sea bed as well as mid water.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Curley_and_Bachrach_1982-23) In addition to upgrades to the JIM design, other variations of the original suit were constructed. The first, named the SAM Suit (designated A.D.S III), was a completely aluminium model. A smaller and lighter suit, it was more anthropomorphic than the original JIMs and was depth-rated to 1,000 feet (300 m). Attempts were made to limit corrosion by the use of a chromic anodizing coating applied to the arm and leg joints, which gave them an unusual green color. The SAM suit stood at 6 feet 3 inches (1.91 m) in height, and had a life support duration of 20 hours. Only three SAM suits would be produced by UMEL before the design was shelved. The second, named the JAM suit (designated A.D.S IV), was constructed of [glass-reinforced plastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass-reinforced_plastic "Glass-reinforced plastic") (GRP) and was depth-rated for around 2,000 feet (610 m).[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Nuytten_1998-24) ### WASP \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=16 "Edit section: WASP")\] [![Image 15](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/WASP_at_the_OSEL_Testing_tank_Gt_Yarmouth%2C_UK.JPG/250px-WASP_at_the_OSEL_Testing_tank_Gt_Yarmouth%2C_UK.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WASP_at_the_OSEL_Testing_tank_Gt_Yarmouth,_UK.JPG) WASP at the OSEL Testing tank [Great Yarmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Yarmouth "Great Yarmouth"), UK The WASP atmospheric diving system is partway between a one-person submersible and an atmospheric diving suit, in that there are articulated arms which contain and are moved by the operator's arms, but the operator's legs are contained in a rigid housing. Mobility is provided by two vertical and two horizontal foot-switch controlled electrical [marine thrusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_thruster "Marine thruster"). Operating depth was quoted as 2,300 feet (700 m)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Wasp_specifications-2) WASP is 84 inches (2.1 m) high, 42 inches (1.1 m) wide, and 34 inches (0.86 m) front to back. Ballasted weight in air approximately 2,200 pounds (1,000 kg), for neutral buoyancy in water, but buoyancy can be increased by up to 35 pounds (16 kg) during operation, and ballast can be jettisoned in an emergency. WASP is transported on a support frame.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Wasp_specifications-2) Current suits ------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit§ion=17 "Edit section: Current suits")\] Exosuit [![Image 16](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Exosuit_Side.jpg/250px-Exosuit_Side.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Exosuit_Side.jpg) Side view of Exosuit [![Image 17](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Exosuit_Back.jpg/250px-Exosuit_Back.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Exosuit_Back.jpg) Back view of Exosuit In 1987, the "[Newtsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtsuit "Newtsuit")" was developed by the Canadian engineer [Phil Nuytten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Nuytten "Phil Nuytten"), and a version was put into production as the "Hardsuit" by [Hardsuits International](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hardsuits_International&action=edit&redlink=1 "Hardsuits International (page does not exist)").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Ratcliffe_2011-9) The Newtsuit is constructed to function like a 'submarine you can wear', allowing the diver to work at normal atmospheric pressure even at depths of over 1,000 feet (300 m). Made of wrought [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium"), it had fully articulated joints so the diver can move more easily underwater. The [life support system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_support_system "Life support system") provides 6–8 hours of air, with an emergency back-up supply of an additional 48 hours. The Hardsuit was used to salvage the bell from the wreck of the [SS _Edmund Fitzgerald_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Edmund_Fitzgerald "SS Edmund Fitzgerald") in 1995. The latest version of the Hardsuit designed by [Oceanworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oceanworks&action=edit&redlink=1 "Oceanworks (page does not exist)"), the "Quantum 2", uses higher power commercially available ROV thrusters for better reliability and more power as well as an atmospheric monitoring system to monitor the environmental conditions in the cabin. A more recent design by Nuytten is the Exosuit, a relatively lightweight and low powered suit intended for marine research.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Gizmodo-25) It was first used in 2014 at the Bluewater and Antikythera underwater research expeditions.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Exosuit-27) [![Image 18](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Navy_Diver4.jpg/250px-Navy_Diver4.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Navy_Diver4.jpg) US Navy ADS 2000 on launch and recovery platform after a certification dive in August 2006 The [ADS 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ADS_2000&action=edit&redlink=1 "ADS 2000 (page does not exist)") was developed jointly with OceanWorks International and the US Navy in 1997,[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-oceanworks-28) as an evolution of the Hardsuit to meet US Navy requirements. The ADS 2000 provides increased depth capability for the US Navy's Submarine Rescue Program. Manufactured from forged T6061 aluminum alloy, it uses an advanced articulating joint design based on the Hardsuit joints. Capable of operating in up to 2,000 feet (610 m) of seawater for a normal mission of up to six hours, it has a self-contained, automatic life support system.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Logico_2006b-29) Additionally, the integrated dual thruster system allows the pilot to navigate easily underwater. It became fully operational and certified by the US Navy off southern California on 1 August 2006, when Chief Navy Diver Daniel Jackson submerged to 2,000 feet (610 m).[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Logico_2006-30) From the project's beginning until 2011, the US navy spent $113 million on the ADS An **atmospheric diving suit (ADS)** is an articulated, anthropomorphic submersible device designed as a one-person vehicle that maintains an internal pressure of one atmosphere regardless of external water pressure, allowing the operator to perform underwater tasks at depths up to several hundred feet without experiencing decompression sickness or requiring a breathing gas mixture.\[1\] Unlike traditional diving suits that compress with depth, an ADS encloses the entire body in a rigid, armored structure with movable joints, functioning essentially as a small submarine controlled by the human inside.\[2\] The concept of atmospheric diving suits originated in the early 18th century, with the first notable design being John Lethbridge's "diving engine" in 1715, a barrel-like device that allowed brief submersion without air supply from the surface.\[2\] Significant advancements occurred in the 19th century, including the Carmagnolle brothers' steel-and-glass suit around 1882, which featured articulated limbs for mobility.\[2\] In the 20th century, Joseph Peress developed the first practical modern ADS, the Tritonia suit, in 1922, capable of depths over 300 feet.\[2\] Post-World War II innovations included U.S. experimental suits in the 1950s and the British JIM suit in the 1960s, which reached operational depths of 1,500 feet and were used for salvage and rescue operations.\[3\] Key features of ADS include pressure-resistant materials like steel or composites for the body and limbs, rotary or ball-and-socket joints for articulation, and life support systems providing breathable air, heating, and communication via an umbilical tether to the surface.\[2\] Advantages over conventional scuba or hard-hat diving encompass no risk of nitrogen narcosis or decompression illness, extended bottom times limited only by umbilical length and fatigue, and enhanced safety in hazardous environments such as cold or contaminated waters.\[1\] However, limitations include high weight (often over 500 pounds), restricted mobility due to joint friction, and the need for support vessels for deployment.\[4\] Notable modern examples include the U.S. Navy's NOMOADS, a modified ADS tested in the 1980s and 1990s for submarine rescue up to 2,000 feet, and the Canadian Exosuit developed in the early 2000s by Nuytco Research and first certified for 1,000 feet in 2012, used in scientific and commercial diving.\[3\] Current developments, such as the U.S. Navy's DSEND project initiated in the 2020s, focus on lightweight materials, improved joint flexibility, and integration of augmented reality displays to extend operational depths beyond 300 feet of seawater while reducing diver fatigue.\[4\] ADS remain vital for military, offshore oil, and underwater construction tasks where precision manipulation at depth is required.\[2\]

Definition and fundamentals
---------------------------

### Definition and classification

An atmospheric diving suit (ADS) is a one-person articulated submersible that maintains an internal pressure of one atmosphere, equivalent to surface conditions, thereby protecting the operator from the external hydrostatic pressure encountered at depth without the need for decompression upon ascent.\[1\] This design allows the diver to perform tasks in a shirt-sleeve environment, avoiding the physiological stresses associated with changes in ambient pressure, such as decompression sickness.\[5\] Unlike ambient-pressure diving suits, which equalize internal and external pressure, an ADS encapsulates the operator in a rigid or semi-rigid enclosure that withstands the full differential pressure.\[3\] The fundamental physics of an ADS relies on pressure isolation, where the suit's exterior structure resists the compressive forces of the surrounding water—approximately one atmosphere (about 14.7 psi or 101 kPa) added per 10 meters of depth—while the interior remains at ambient surface pressure.\[5\] This principle eliminates the need for the operator's body to adapt to high-pressure environments, as nitrogen and other gases in the bloodstream do not dissolve excessively or form harmful bubbles during rapid pressure changes.\[1\] ADS are classified primarily as hard suits, which are fully rigid enclosures made of metal or composite materials with articulated joints for mobility, though variations include soft-hard hybrids and distinctions based on functionality. Hard suits, such as the HARDSUIT or EXOSUIT, feature pressure-resistant rotary joints to enable limb movement while maintaining structural integrity against depths typically rated from 100 to 600 meters.\[1\] Patented designs for soft-hard hybrids propose incorporating flexible fabric elements, often using advanced materials like shape memory alloys for joints that transition between rigid and compliant states, allowing enhanced dexterity at shallower depths (e.g., 25-185 meters) without compromising pressure containment.\[6\] In broader terms, ADS can overlap with crewed submersibles equipped with manipulator arms, but they are distinguished by their anthropomorphic form for direct human manipulation; further categorizations include mobility levels (e.g., fully articulated versus limited fixed positioning), depth ratings, and power sources, such as tethered umbilicals for unlimited supply versus self-contained systems with onboard batteries and thrusters for untethered operation.\[3\]

### Purpose and applications

Atmospheric diving suits (ADS) are primarily designed to enable human operators to perform complex underwater tasks at significant depths while maintaining internal pressure at one atmosphere, thereby avoiding the physiological effects of high ambient pressure encountered in traditional diving methods.\[7\] This capability supports core purposes such as deep-sea salvage, structural inspection, equipment maintenance, scientific research, and commercial operations where conventional scuba, surface-supplied, or saturation diving becomes inefficient or hazardous due to depth limitations exceeding 50 meters.\[8\] By eliminating the need for decompression stops, ADS allow for immediate surface return after missions, reducing operational downtime and associated risks.\[9\] In the oil and gas sector, ADS find extensive application in offshore platform and pipeline inspections, anode replacements, cathodic protection installations, and maintenance of subsea manifolds and wet trees, often in challenging environments like the North Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Arctic waters.\[7\] For instance, the JIM suit has been deployed since the 1970s for exploratory drilling support and repair tasks at depths up to 610 meters.\[7\] Subsea construction and salvage operations, including recovery of wellheads and debris, also benefit from the suits' articulated manipulators, which provide dexterity comparable to human hands for precise handling.\[8\] In scientific research, ADS facilitate oceanographic studies and deep-water sampling, as demonstrated by the Exosuit's use in expeditions reaching 305 meters for biological and geological surveys.\[10\] Military applications include submarine rescue missions and hull inspections, where ADS like the Hardsuit 2000 enable rapid intervention at depths up to 610 meters without exposing operators to decompression sickness.\[11\] The U.S. Navy has integrated such systems into submarine rescue protocols, allowing divers to attach lifting devices or perform emergency repairs on distressed vessels.\[12\] Archaeological dives represent another niche, with the Exosuit supporting underwater excavations at sites like ancient shipwrecks, where prolonged dexterity at depths beyond recreational limits is essential.\[13\] ADS are particularly suited to environments requiring high manual precision and extended mission durations at depths where decompression obligations would otherwise limit productivity, offering economic advantages through reduced setup times compared to hyperbaric chamber systems for saturation diving.\[7\] For example, operations in the offshore industry have shown cost savings by minimizing surface support infrastructure and enabling quicker task turnaround.\[7\] However, their bulkiness and high acquisition costs—often exceeding hundreds of thousands of dollars per unit as of 2016—make them impractical for shallow-water or recreational diving, where lighter equipment suffices.\[14\]

Design and components
---------------------

### Design constraints and principles

Atmospheric diving suits (ADS) must maintain internal pressure at one atmosphere while withstanding external hydrostatic pressures that increase linearly with depth, necessitating robust structural principles centered on high-strength materials to resist compression without deformation. Common materials include aluminum alloys for their balance of strength and weight, titanium for enhanced corrosion resistance and higher yield strength in advanced designs, and acrylic for transparent viewports that provide visibility while enduring pressure differentials. These materials are selected to prevent yielding or implosion, with design factors of safety typically around 2.0 to 3.0 based on yield strength, to ensure operational integrity up to rated depths.\[2\] Buoyancy compensation is critical for neutral submersion and maneuverability, achieved through integration of syntactic foam, such as AM-32 grade, which provides positive lift without significant compression under pressure, or detachable ballast weights that allow fine adjustments. For instance, suits are often configured with 2 cubic feet of syntactic foam, such as AM-32 grade, along with ballast weights to achieve slightly negative buoyancy for stability. Depth limits are governed by material properties, with aluminum-constructed suits typically rated to 1,000 feet (305 meters) and fiberglass-reinforced plastic versions extending to 2,000 feet (610 meters), constrained by buckling resistance in elongated components like limbs modeled as slender columns. The critical buckling pressure PcrP\_{cr} for such members is given by Euler's formula: Pcr\=π2EIL2P\_{cr} = \\frac{\\pi^2 E I}{L^2} where EE is the modulus of elasticity, II is the cross-sectional moment of inertia, and LL is the effective length; this establishes the compressive load at which instability occurs, informing limb thickness and aspect ratios to avoid failure at operational depths.\[2\] Mobility presents significant engineering challenges, as articulated joints must permit 6-7 degrees of freedom approximating human kinematics while maintaining pressure integrity through rotary seals or oil-supported mechanisms that minimize friction and leakage. These joints, often rotary or ball-and-socket types, align the suit's geometric axes closely with the operator's anatomical joints to reduce torque and enable natural movement, but scaling suit size upward increases moment of inertia, amplifying control effort and fatigue during tasks.\[2\] Ergonomic principles prioritize human-scale proportions to accommodate operators within the 5th to 95th percentile for athletic males and 50th to 95th percentile for athletic females, based on anthropometric data, ensuring sufficient internal volume for posture and reach without excessive leverage that could exacerbate muscle strain over extended missions. This sizing minimizes fatigue by optimizing joint leverage and workspace, allowing operators to perform dexterous work with reduced metabolic cost compared to oversized or rigid configurations.\[2\]

### Key systems and technologies

Atmospheric diving suits (ADS) incorporate advanced life support systems to maintain a breathable environment at surface pressure, typically using closed-circuit oxygen rebreathers or umbilically supplied air to avoid decompression sickness. These systems often employ soda lime canisters for CO2 scrubbing, enabling extended operations of up to 50 hours in self-contained configurations, as seen in suits like the Exosuit developed by Nuytco Research. Thermal regulation is achieved through insulated inner layers and, in some designs, integrated heaters to counteract cold deep-water conditions, ensuring operator comfort without compromising suit integrity.\[15\]\[10\] Mobility and control in ADS are facilitated by articulated joints and propulsion mechanisms, allowing precise navigation in underwater environments. Thrusters, such as the four 2-horsepower units on the Wrangler ADS, or fin-like propulsors provide directional control, while rotary joints in the arms and legs enable natural movement unaffected by external pressure. Manipulator arms equipped with interchangeable end-effectors, like grippers or hand pods, support task execution such as object manipulation or tool handling. Power for these components derives from onboard batteries for electrical systems or hydraulic pumps for mechanical actuation, with emergency backups ensuring reliability during missions.\[16\]\[2\]\[17\] Communication and monitoring systems in ADS rely on umbilicals for wired voice and data transmission or acoustic hydrophones for wireless links in untethered operations, enabling real-time interaction with surface support. Internal sensors, including pressure gauges and leak detectors, continuously assess suit integrity and environmental conditions, often integrated into a topside monitoring console that tracks life support parameters and diver vitals. These setups, as in the HARDSUIT, use distributed control systems like PLCs for automated oversight and fault detection.\[2\]\[18\] Recent technological advancements enhance ADS functionality with integrated high-definition cameras and sonar for improved visibility, as incorporated in SMP's atmospheric suits for situational awareness during low-light dives. LED lighting arrays provide efficient illumination without excessive power draw, while emerging designs explore haptic feedback mechanisms to relay tactile information from manipulators to the operator, improving precision in complex tasks; such features are under development in U.S. Navy next-generation prototypes. These integrations build on depth-rated components to support operations beyond 300 meters.\[15\]

Operation and human factors
---------------------------

### Operating procedures and skills

Pre-dive procedures for atmospheric diving suits (ADS) begin with suit assembly, where components such as joints, seals, and life support systems are inspected and secured to ensure structural integrity.\[19\] Pressure testing follows, involving pressurization of the suit to verify its ability to maintain one atmosphere internally against external hydrostatic forces, typically conducted in a controlled environment like a hyperbaric chamber or on a test stand.\[2\] Calibration of controls, including thrusters, manipulators, and communication systems, is then performed to align with operator inputs, often using diagnostic software or manual adjustments.\[18\] Integration with support vessels or remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) includes tether attachment for power, gas supply, and data transmission, with checklists typically taking about one hour to complete.\[19\] Dive operations commence with entry methods, where the pilot dons the suit through a rear or top hatch, followed by a lock-in process that seals the suit at surface pressure.\[19\] Deployment usually involves crane lowering from the support vessel to achieve neutral buoyancy, allowing controlled descent via thrusters for navigation in three dimensions.\[20\] Navigation techniques rely on integrated sensors like sonar and cameras for orientation, particularly in low-visibility conditions, with thrusters enabling precise positioning and hovering.\[18\] Task performance, such as object manipulation, utilizes articulated arms with end effectors compatible with standard tools, requiring adaptation to the suit's leverage for fine motor actions like grasping or cutting.\[18\] Exit follows mission completion, with crane recovery to the surface after confirming system stability. Required skills for ADS operation emphasize manual dexterity adaptation, as pilots must compensate for the suit's mechanical amplification and resistance in movements, often practicing through simulated tasks to maintain precision.\[19\] Spatial awareness is critical in low-visibility environments, honed via training in sensor interpretation and thruster control to avoid collisions or entanglement.\[21\] Basic troubleshooting, such as monitoring joint lubrication levels during missions and initiating emergency overrides, forms part of pilot competency, ensuring uninterrupted task execution.\[2\] Post-dive protocols include decontamination to remove contaminants from external surfaces and internal air systems, followed by data logging of mission parameters like depth, duration, and system performance for analysis.\[19\] Maintenance scheduling involves inspecting wear on joints and seals, typically taking 30 minutes initially, with more extensive servicing based on usage to prepare for future deployments.\[18\] These steps ensure the suit's reliability across repeated operations, typically 4-6 hours per dive without decompression.\[18\]

### Operator requirements and training

Operators of atmospheric diving suits (ADS) must meet stringent physical requirements to ensure safe and effective performance during missions that can last 8 to 12 hours or longer in confined conditions. These include a general level of physical fitness comparable to that of commercial divers, with the ability to sustain moderate to heavy exertion, such as oxygen consumption rates of 1.5 to 1.8 liters per minute during activities like walking in the suit.\[22\] Suit designs typically accommodate operators within the 5th to 95th percentile for athletic males and females based on anthropometric data, with adjustable extensions for limb compatibility to prevent mobility restrictions.\[2\] A current medical certificate is required to confirm fitness for diving, including the capacity to endure prolonged enclosure without issues related to confinement.\[21\] Mental and skill prerequisites emphasize resilience under stress, situational awareness, and technical aptitude for monitoring suit systems. Candidates typically need prior experience in wet diving or hyperbaric operations to understand underwater physics, physiology, and emergency protocols, often holding certifications such as commercial diver qualifications.\[23\]\[24\] Engineering knowledge is essential for overseeing life support, thruster controls, and manipulator functions, while strong teamwork skills are critical for coordination with surface support crews during operations.\[23\] Training programs for ADS pilots are structured to build proficiency progressively, often starting with theoretical instruction on atmospheric management and suit controls. Basic skills in life support operation and thruster maneuvering—such as simultaneous control of port and starboard pedals—require approximately 20 hours of initial training, followed by 10 to 20 additional sessions for manipulator use and task execution.\[21\]\[22\] Hands-on sessions progress from shallow-water or tank trials to full-depth simulations, with programs like those developed by Technical Diving International (TDI) accumulating up to 49 hours of dive time across multiple sessions.\[23\] Certification is issued by bodies such as the Australian Diver Accreditation Scheme (ADAS), which mandates a minimum age of 18 and relevant industry experience, or aligns with International Marine Contractors Association (IMCA) guidelines for offshore diving personnel.\[24\]\[23\] Unique demands of ADS operation include adaptation to reduced tactile feedback from manipulators, which limits fine motor precision to about 75% of unsuited capacity for tasks like lifting up to 50 pounds, and inherent delays in response times due to mechanical joints and control interfaces.\[22\] Pilots must also manage the psychological strain of isolation within the suit, relying on enhanced spatial awareness honed through prior diving experience to navigate and perform duties effectively.\[23\]

Safety considerations
---------------------

### Hazards and failure modes

Atmospheric diving suits (ADS) are susceptible to mechanical failures that can compromise the integrity of the pressurized habitat. Joint seal breaches represent a primary risk, where articulated joints in the arms and legs may fail due to wear, abrasion from suspended debris, or pressure-induced deformation, potentially leading to flooding if seals are compromised. Although some designs, such as the Campos joint, incorporate fail-safe mechanisms that automatically reseal upon failure to prevent water ingress, historical engineering assessments indicate that earlier seals, like linen-based ones, could tear under prolonged exposure to particulate matter. Structural implosion is another catastrophic mode, occurring if the suit exceeds its depth rating, causing the rigid shell to collapse under external hydrostatic pressure; this risk is heightened by design constraints on material strength and buoyancy control, which limit operational depths to typically 300-700 meters depending on the model. Power loss failures can result in immobility, as battery or hydraulic system outages disable propulsion thrusters and manipulator arms, stranding the operator in hazardous underwater positions without redundant manual overrides in all configurations. Environmental hazards pose additional threats to ADS operations, particularly in dynamic ocean conditions. Strong currents can entangle umbilicals used for power, gas supply, or communication in tethered models like the WASP, potentially dragging the suit into obstacles or severing connections, as observed in general subsea umbilical incidents. Biofouling accumulates on external surfaces during extended deployments, adhering marine organisms that increase drag, obscure sensors, and accelerate corrosion on joints and viewports. Thermal extremes further exacerbate seal vulnerabilities; extreme cold in deep water can embrittle elastomeric O-rings and gaskets, leading to leaks, while rapid temperature fluctuations during ascent or descent may cause differential expansion between suit materials, stressing integrity. Human-related failure modes often stem from the operator's interaction with the complex control systems. Operator error in control inputs, such as misjudging manipulator arm forces or thruster commands, can lead to unintended collisions or task failures, compounded by the suit's reduced tactile feedback compared to ambient-pressure diving. Fatigue-induced mistakes arise from prolonged missions, where physical strain from the suit's weight and limited ergonomics impairs decision-making after several hours of operation. Communication blackouts, due to umbilical damage or electronic glitches, isolate the operator from surface support, heightening disorientation risks in low-visibility environments. Failure probabilities for ADS remain low, reflecting their robust design and limited deployment history. Statistical data from operational surveys indicate no fatal or serious injuries from suit failures prior to 1999. The sole recorded fatality involving an ADS occurred in 1999 with a WASP suit, attributed to a launch platform impact rather than a pressure or systems failure, underscoring the rarity of inherent suit-related hazards as of 2025.\[2\]

### Emergency procedures and safety measures

Emergency procedures for atmospheric diving suits (ADS) emphasize rapid response to maintain operator safety, including protocols for activating backup buoyancy systems to initiate an uncontrolled ascent to the surface in cases of system failure or loss of control.\[21\] In tethered operations, operators are trained to climb the umbilical manually if power is lost, allowing a controlled return to the surface without relying on propulsion.\[21\] Surface recovery procedures incorporate emergency beacons for locating the suit and coordination with support divers or vessels for retrieval.\[18\] Built-in safety features mitigate risks such as seal failures through redundant sealing mechanisms on joints and hatches, designed to maintain internal atmospheric pressure even if primary seals are compromised.\[2\] Emergency breathing supplies, including dual oxygen systems and CO2 scrubbers with capacities up to 72 hours, ensure sustained life support during prolonged surface waits or recovery delays.\[18\] Automated shutdown systems detect pressure anomalies or power issues and initiate safe modes, such as halting movement and activating emergency buoyancy.\[25\] Support measures rely on a structured dive team, where tenders handle umbilical management and immediate assistance, while supervisors oversee operations from the surface using real-time telemetry for monitoring vital signs, suit integrity, and environmental data.\[26\] Post-incident analysis involves reviewing telemetry logs and team debriefs to identify procedural gaps and refine risk mitigation. ADS operations adhere to regulatory standards, including the International Maritime Organization's (IMO) 2023 Code of Safety for Diving Systems (resolution MSC.548(107)), which mandates comprehensive risk assessments, emergency planning, and equipment certification for ADS as submersible systems.\[27\] In the United States, compliance with Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) guidelines under 29 CFR 1910 Subpart T requires similar protocols for commercial diving, treating ADS as specialized equipment with emphasis on standby teams and evacuation plans. Additional classification by agencies like the American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) ensures structural integrity and operational safety through mandatory operations manuals detailing emergency responses.\[28\]

Historical development
----------------------

### Early concepts and designs

The origins of atmospheric diving suits (ADS) can be traced to the early 18th century, when English inventor John Lethbridge developed a wooden barrel-like enclosure in 1715 to enable underwater salvage operations. This device, known as the "diving engine," fully enclosed the operator's body except for the arms, which protruded through sealed openings, and relied on a flexible hose for surface-supplied air. Constructed from oak staves reinforced with iron hoops and lined with greased leather, it weighed approximately 240 pounds in air and allowed dives to depths of about 9-10 meters for up to 30 minutes, primarily for recovering valuables from shipwrecks off the Devon coast. However, its design severely restricted mobility, confining the user to a curled position inside the 6-foot-long barrel, and it required hoisting by ropes for entry and exit.\[29\]\[30\] In the 19th century, conceptual advancements built toward more rigid systems, with German physician Karl Heinrich Klingert patenting an early ADS prototype in 1797. Klingert's suit featured a tinplate helmet and torso cylinder connected to leather trousers and sleeves, supplied with air via a surface bellows pump through a hose, and included glass portholes for visibility. Tested successfully to 18 meters in the Vistula River near Warsaw, it represented a shift from open diving bells to enclosed, pressurized armors but was limited by unreliable air delivery and poor joint seals, restricting practical use to shallow recoveries. In 1882, French inventors Alphonse and Théodore Carmagnolle developed the first anthropomorphic ADS, a steel-and-glass suit with articulated limbs for improved mobility, though limited to shallow depths due to material constraints.\[31\]\[32\] Concurrently, British-German engineer Augustus Siebe's innovations in the 1830s provided key precursors through his closed diving helmet, bolted to an airtight rubber suit and supplied with compressed air from a surface pump. This standard diving dress enabled safer operations at depths up to 20-30 meters compared to earlier open helmets, emphasizing rigid head protection while the body suit remained flexible and pressurized, influencing later full-rigid ADS designs.\[31\]\[33\]\[34\] Early 20th-century developments addressed mobility challenges with innovations in joint mechanisms, notably by British engineer Joseph Salim Peress, who began work on ADS designs in 1914 and filed a patent in 1921 for oil-filled spherical joints that equalized internal and external pressures to prevent crushing while permitting articulation. This marked a critical transition from inflexible rigid armors to more maneuverable systems, using viscous oil in sealed chambers to lubricate and balance hydrostatic forces across limb joints. Peress's first functional prototype, the Tritonia suit completed in 1930, was a magnesium-alloy armored unit with these joints, helmet portholes, and umbilical air supply; initial tests in Loch Ness reached 123 meters (404 feet), demonstrating dry operation and basic dexterity for tasks like valve manipulation, though deeper pressure chamber trials equivalent to 400 meters revealed joint stiffening under pressure. German firm Neufeldt and Kuhnke contributed parallel efforts starting around 1912 with buoyancy-adjustable patents and a 1917 steel prototype tested to 82 meters in the Baltic Sea, employing grease-packed hinges for pressure resistance but suffering from heavy weight (over 200 kg) and limited arm swing.\[35\]\[36\]\[37\] These early designs were constrained by shallow operational depths typically under 50 meters due to joint compression and material fatigue, reliance on tethered surface air supplies without onboard reserves, and inherent low mobility from bulky construction and pressure-induced resistance, often requiring mechanical assistance for movement and precluding untethered or prolonged missions.\[38\]

### Mid-20th century advancements

In the 1930s, British engineer Joseph Peress developed the Tritonia suit, marking a major advancement in atmospheric diving suit technology with its articulated design constructed from lightweight magnesium alloy. This material choice provided strength and corrosion resistance suitable for prolonged exposure to seawater, addressing key challenges in earlier rigid suits. The suit's joints used spherical, fluid-filled mechanisms to enable movement under pressure, representing an improvement over previous non-anthropomorphic designs.\[39\] The Tritonia was first revealed in 1930 and underwent rigorous testing, including open-water dives to 400 feet (122 meters) in Loch Ness and pressure chamber simulations equivalent to depths of approximately 400 meters at 600 pounds per square inch. These tests demonstrated the suit's viability for deep operations without decompression requirements, as it maintained internal atmospheric pressure. In 1935, diver Jim Jarrett employed the Tritonia to explore the wreck of the RMS Lusitania at 312 feet (95 meters), highlighting its practical utility for wreck inspection and salvage tasks. In the 1950s, the U.S. Navy developed prototypes such as the Trexler suit, which incorporated advanced alloys and hydraulic actuators for enhanced durability and dexterity at depths up to 1,500 feet (457 meters).\[39\]\[40\]\[41\]\[2\] World War II military demands for deep-sea submarine repair and salvage operations accelerated advancements in ADS materials and designs, with Peress' innovations influencing corrosion-resistant alloys and joint technologies for enhanced durability in harsh underwater environments. Post-war efforts in the 1950s by the U.S. Navy and British developers built on these foundations, incorporating hydraulic actuators in prototypes to improve manipulator control and overall operator dexterity during tethered dives. By 1950, design milestones included pressure-tested capabilities reaching equivalents of 200 meters, paving the way for more operational untethered trials in the late 1940s.\[2\]

### Late 20th century suits

The JIM suit, developed in the late 1960s by Underwater Marine Equipment Limited (UMEL) in Britain and based on earlier designs by inventor Joseph Peress, represented a significant advancement in atmospheric diving suits (ADS) with its aluminum alloy construction and articulated joints allowing limited mobility at depths up to 450 meters (1,500 feet).\[41\]\[36\] The suit maintained internal atmospheric pressure, eliminating decompression needs, and featured oil-filled rotary joints for arm and leg movement, enabling tasks such as underwater inspection and manipulation.\[42\] Its first operational sea trials occurred in 1969, marking the initial human use of a modern ADS prototype.\[43\] In the 1970s and 1980s, the focus shifted toward enhanced mobility and mid-water capabilities, exemplified by the WASP (Workstation in Atmospheric Diving Suit Pressure), a modified version of the JIM suit developed by Graham Hawkes for powered operations.\[44\] The WASP incorporated thrusters for propulsion and a tubular lower body design, achieving a depth rating of 610 meters (2,000 feet) while prioritizing drilling support and salvage tasks in offshore environments.\[45\] Concurrently, precursor tests for the Newtsuit, led by Phil Nuytten at Oceaneering International, explored lightweight materials and improved rotary joints in the late 1970s, building on hydraulic systems from mid-century prototypes to enhance dexterity without pressure effects.\[46\] These efforts culminated in the Newtsuit's initial configurations by the early 1980s, tested for commercial viability in deep-sea interventions.\[47\] By the 1990s, ADS models saw commercial adaptations tailored for the offshore oil and gas industry, with companies like Oceaneering integrating video camera systems for real-time monitoring and enhanced seals to minimize leaks in high-pressure joints.\[2\] These upgrades allowed operators to perform precise tasks such as pipeline inspections and valve manipulations at depths exceeding 300 meters, reducing reliance on saturation diving.\[48\] Improved sealing technologies, including advanced O-rings and composite materials, addressed earlier vulnerabilities to water ingress, supporting extended deployments in harsh North Sea conditions.\[49\] A key impact of these late 20th-century developments was the transition to fully self-contained power and life support systems, which extended mission durations from hours to up to 72 hours in emergency scenarios through onboard batteries, oxygen supplies, and rebreathers.\[50\] This autonomy enabled longer, untethered operations, establishing ADS as reliable tools for industrial applications while prioritizing operator safety over traditional umbilical-dependent methods.\[2\]

Modern and current suits
------------------------

### Commercially available models

One of the prominent commercially available atmospheric diving suits (ADS) is the Exosuit developed by Nuytco Research Ltd., constructed from A536 aluminum alloy for durability under pressure.\[25\] It features a depth rating of 305 meters (1,000 feet) and incorporates 18 advanced rotary joints, including 360-degree wrist rotation, enabling enhanced dexterity for precise tasks.\[51\] The suit has been employed in scientific dives, such as the 2014 expedition to the Antikythera wreck to investigate the ancient mechanism, where it facilitated delicate artifact handling at depths beyond traditional scuba limits.\[52\] As of 2025, the Exosuit remains in production with ongoing support for life systems, including backup batteries for extended operations.\[10\] The HARDSUIT, produced by PHNX International (formerly Phoenix International), offers a depth rating of 366 meters (1,200 feet seawater) and is designed for one-person operation at ambient atmospheric pressure.\[18\] This model supports industrial applications, including 2025 offshore oilfield maintenance and inspection, repair, and maintenance (IRM) tasks on subsea infrastructure.\[53\] Its design allows for versatile tool integration, enhancing its utility in commercial underwater interventions without requiring decompression.\[54\] Another established model is the Newtsuit, originally developed by International Hard Suits Inc. and now offered by Nuytco Research Ltd., with a certified depth of 305 meters (1,000 feet) and tested to greater extremes.\[47\] Following the death of its inventor Phil Nuytten in 2023, the suit incorporates acrylic pressure windows for visibility and focuses on commercial salvage operations, providing mobility through articulated rotary joints for recovery tasks.\[47\] The suit maintains ongoing certifications for industrial use.\[47\] The market for atmospheric diving suits is experiencing growing demand, projected to expand at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 4.7% from 2023 to 2033, primarily driven by needs in offshore energy sectors such as oil and gas exploration and maintenance.\[55\] Units typically cost between $1 million and $5 million, reflecting their specialized construction and capabilities.\[56\]

### Military and research developments

The U.S. Navy has advanced its Deep Sea Expeditionary with No Decompression (DSEND) suit program, focusing on prototypes developed between 2023 and 2025 to improve diver mobility and operational depth.\[57\]\[58\] The DSEND suit incorporates lightweight, flexible materials that maintain internal atmospheric pressure, eliminating decompression requirements and enabling extended missions at depths exceeding 300 meters.\[9\] In August 2025, Navy divers conducted in-water testing of a new concept suit under the DSEND initiative, evaluating enhanced joint designs for greater dexterity and flexibility during deep-sea operations.\[59\] The U.S. Navy evaluated the Newtsuit for integration into the Submarine Rescue Diving and Recompression System (SRDRS), allowing operators to perform rescue tasks at significant depths without physiological pressure effects, though it did not fully meet all requirements.\[60\] Similarly, the UK Royal Navy supports NATO's Submarine Rescue System (NSRS) for quick-response extractions from distressed submarines, with operations up to 610 meters.\[61\] These efforts highlight rapid deployment in contested underwater environments.\[62\] Academic research has explored human-machine interfaces to enhance ADS usability, with institutions like MIT conducting studies on pilot interaction and control mechanisms for improved task performance.\[63\] Looking ahead, military ADS developments post-2020 focus on enhancing dexterity and operational range to address limitations in traditional systems.\[9\]

Comparisons and alternatives
----------------------------

### With other diving technologies

Atmospheric diving suits (ADS) differ fundamentally from ambient pressure diving systems, such as scuba and surface-supplied diving (SSD), by maintaining internal pressure at one atmosphere, thereby eliminating the risk of decompression sickness associated with exposure to elevated ambient pressures.\[18\] In contrast, scuba diving is typically limited to depths of around 40 meters (130 feet) for recreational use due to risks like nitrogen narcosis and oxygen toxicity, with no-decompression bottom times of approximately 10 minutes at 40 meters. SSD extends capabilities to approximately 60 meters on air or deeper with mixed gases, but requires extensive surface support and prolonged decompression for dives beyond no-decompression limits, sacrificing the mobility and simplicity of ADS while still exposing divers to physiological stresses. Compared to saturation diving, which allows extended bottom times at depths up to 300 meters (1,000 feet) by maintaining divers in a pressurized environment for days or weeks, ADS enables immediate return to the surface without decompression, supporting faster mission cycles despite higher per-dive costs from specialized equipment.\[64\] Saturation operations demand large support teams, hyperbaric chambers, and decompression periods of roughly one day per 100 feet of depth, making them suitable for prolonged projects but logistically intensive.\[65\] ADS, with typical operational durations of 4 to 6 hours per dive and life support capacities up to 72 hours, offers greater flexibility for shorter interventions, though it lacks the multi-diver capacity of saturation systems.\[18\]\[3\] Against unmanned systems like remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) and autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), ADS provides the advantage of human dexterity, real-time judgment, and adaptability for complex tasks requiring fine manipulation, such as precise inspections or repairs, where remote operation may fall short in unpredictable environments.\[66\] ROVs excel in repetitive, high-risk, or extreme-depth operations beyond 500 meters, offering lower costs for routine surveys and no human exposure to hazards, but they depend on tether limitations and lack the intuitive decision-making of a suited diver.\[2\] ADS is particularly efficient at depths of 100 to 500 meters, where human presence enhances task efficiency over purely robotic systems, though ROVs dominate for depths exceeding ADS crush limits around 700 meters.\[20\]

### Advantages and limitations

Atmospheric diving suits (ADS) offer significant safety advantages over traditional ambient pressure diving methods by maintaining an internal pressure of one atmosphere, thereby eliminating the risk of decompression sickness and related physiological hazards such as nitrogen narcosis or oxygen toxicity.\[2\] This sealed environment allows operators to breathe normal air mixtures and perform extended missions at depths up to several hundred meters without requiring decompression stops upon ascent, enabling rapid surface returns and bottom times of several hours without decompression, longer than scuba's short no-decompression limits but requiring shorter individual dives than saturation systems' extended stays.\[67\] Additionally, the suits provide enhanced dexterity through articulated joints, facilitating complex manipulation tasks that demand human precision, while their fully enclosed design ensures protection in contaminated or hazardous underwater environments where ambient divers would face exposure risks.\[20\] Despite these benefits, ADS face notable limitations that constrain their operational flexibility and adoption. The suits' rigid, bulky construction—often weighing several hundred kilograms—reduces agility and mobility, making navigation in confined spaces or high-current conditions challenging compared to lighter diving apparatuses.\[22\] Maintenance is complex and resource-intensive, involving specialized inspections of pressure seals, joints, and life-support systems to prevent failures under extreme conditions, which can lead to extended downtime between deployments.\[22\] Operational costs are high, with acquisition, training, and support infrastructure often exceeding hundreds of thousands of dollars per unit, limiting accessibility to well-funded military, commercial, or research programs.\[2\] Current designs are also not suited for ultra-deep operations beyond approximately 700 meters due to material strength and buoyancy constraints, nor for swarm-based missions requiring multiple coordinated units.\[68\] Overall, ADS excel in mid-depth interventions (100–500 meters) where human oversight is essential, such as precision repairs or inspections, but their trade-offs in cost and maneuverability often favor alternatives like remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) for routine tasks. Emerging hybrid systems combining ADS with ROV elements are addressing these gaps by integrating teleoperated manipulators and enhanced propulsion, potentially expanding versatility in offshore maintenance applications.\[69\] As of 2025, market analyses indicate continued growth in ADS viability, driven by investments in AI integration for automated suit control, navigation assistance, and mobility augmentation via predictive algorithms that compensate for bulkiness.\[70\]\[71\]
