4.content:
Scuba diving is a versatile and exciting activity that offers a wide range of experiences for divers of all skill levels. There are many ways of dividing up scuba diving. The most common are recreational and technical, by the target of the dive, by the environment of the dive, and much more. Bellow we will explore the different types, and highlight their key features.

Recreational Diving
-------------------

Recreational diving is the most common type of scuba diving, designed for enjoyment rather than professional or scientific purposes. Divers typically stay within the limits of open water diving depth, which is generally up to 40 meters (130 feet). This category includes activities like:

### Night Diving

Exploring underwater environments after sunset, where specialized equipment like dive lights reveals nocturnal marine life.

### Wreck Diving

Investigating sunken ships, planes, or other man-made structures, offering a mix of history and adventure.

### Drift Diving

Letting the current carry you along, providing a unique way to explore large areas with minimal effort.

![Image 1: CCR Liberty diver](http://foxer360-media-library.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/divesoft/0e9ff28f763d135cd08782af86003cc1695cd236_divesoft-photo-189.jpg)

Technical diving
----------------

The definition of [technical diving](https://www.divesoft.com/en/blog/what-is-technical-diving) can be fuzzy at times. There are multiple schools of thought, but they almost all agree that technical diving involves diving in an overhead environment, an environment in which the surface is not directly accessible. Or when mixtures other than air, or sometimes nitrox, are used.

Rebreather Diving
-----------------

[Rebreather diving](https://www.divesoft.com/en/products/ccr-liberty) is a subset of recreational diving that uses advanced equipment to recycle exhaled air, allowing for longer dives and reduced bubble production. This technology is ideal for photographing marine life, exploring fragile ecosystems without disturbing them, or diving for extended periods.

Scientific Diving
-----------------

Scientific diving involves underwater research and data collection, often conducted by marine biologists, archaeologists, or geologists. These dives require specialized training and equipment to ensure safety while performing tasks such as sample collection, habitat surveys, and underwater photography.

![Image 2: CCR Liberty diver](http://foxer360-media-library.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/divesoft/bdd08049f7155191bb0994380d616a238a68dbb8_divesoft-photo-186.jpg)

Cave Diving and Cavern Diving
-----------------------------

Cave diving involves exploring underwater caves beyond the reach of natural light, often requiring specialized gear and training. Cavern diving, a less advanced version, stays within the light zone and is more accessible to intermediate divers.

![Image 3: CCR Liberty diver](http://foxer360-media-library.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/divesoft/6a53b1ecf4349e89ecbd0da955b07c6ba55e1993_divesoft-photo-183.jpg)

Deep Sea Diving
---------------

[Deep sea diving](https://www.divesoft.com/en/blog/what-is-deep-diving) pushes beyond recreational diving limits, often exceeding depths of 40 meters. This type of diving requires technical training and specialized equipment to handle increased pressure and decompression stops.

Rescue Diving
-------------

Rescue diving focuses on training divers to manage emergencies underwater and assist other divers in distress. This type of diving is a critical skill for advanced divers and diving professionals.

Ice Diving
----------

Ice diving takes place beneath frozen surfaces, offering a unique and challenging experience. Divers must cut an entry hole in the ice and rely on safety lines to navigate the cold, dark waters.

Altitude Diving
---------------

Altitude diving occurs at locations above 300 meters (1,000 feet) sea level, such as mountain lakes. The reduced atmospheric pressure at these altitudes requires adjustments to dive planning and decompression.

River Diving
------------

River scuba diving, or simply river diving, involves navigating freshwater rivers, often with strong currents. This type of diving is excellent for exploring unique ecosystems and submerged artifacts but requires careful planning and drift-diving techniques.

Diving is a very diverse sport, and it requires proper training and [equipment](https://eshop.divesoft.com/) to practice it safely. If you want to try any of the types of diving listed above, contact your local dive center.

32.title: QXRtb3NwaGVyaWMgRGl2aW5nIFN5c3RlbSB8IE9jY3VwYXRpb25hbCBEaXZlciBDZXJ0aWZpY2F0aW9uIHwgQURBUw==
32.content:
### Overview

An Atmospheric Diving Suit or ADS is a small one-man articulated submersible similar in shape to a suit of armor.  The ADS is equipped with elaborate pressure joints to allow articulation while maintaining an internal pressure of one atmosphere.

The ADS can be used for very deep dives of up to 2300 feet (700m) for many hours, and eliminates the majority of physiological dangers associated with deep diving. There is no need for the occupant to decompress, there is no need for special gas mixtures, and there is no danger of decompression sickness or nitrogen narcosis. Divers do not even need to be skilled swimmers.

#### Underwater Work

The traditional approach to offshore maintenance, construction and inspection work has been to use either ROVs or divers.  
An ROV equipped with video and still cameras, water jetting and/or wire brush cleaning tools can be used for platform inspection. An ROV has the advantage of high speed in the water column, practically unlimited depth capability and the ability to make long horizontal excursions. The disadvantages of the ROV include poor access to structures, limited visual acuity, and limited spatial NDT tools and equipment for remote operation.

Divers offer the advantage of much improved access to structures, much improved visual acuity and a wide range of off the shelf hand held NDT inspection tools available. Marine growth cleaning for divers is achieved quickly and efficiently using water or grit blasting equipment. The disadvantages of diving include depth or decompression limitations, limited vertical and horizontal excursion capability, and in the case of saturation diving, very high equipment and operating costs coupled with extended decompression time.

The modern atmospheric diving systems (ADS) available today in many ways combine the advantages of ROVs and divers.  The ADS is capable of using a range of hand-held diver tools with little or no modifications. Marine growth cleaning is done in the same way as with divers using high pressure, surface supplied, water jets. Decompression considerations are eliminated and horizontal excursion capability is comparable to that of an ROV and vertical excursion is unlimited.

#### ADS Course

The Atmospheric Diving System (ADS) training course is intended to train pilots in the safe operation and maintenance of the ADS and to provide a sufficient amount of experience and knowledge to qualify the pilot to undertake field operations.

#### Course Overview

The program provides a safe and supervised environment where pilots can be directed and corrected in technique and understanding.  The duration of the course allows students to identify individual constraints in operating the suit and develop personalized corrective action. During the course structures and framework will be added to simulate the real working environment.  In a training course specific to a job, training will simulate the real tasks that will be encountered during operations.

#### Course Standard

AODC 022 Code of practice for the operation of manned submersible craft.

#### Student Prerequisites

Students must have demonstrated the ability to fit within the ADS and perform all necessary movements including the following:

*   Ability to control starboard and port electronic panels and life support controls quickly and efficiently.
*   Ability to remove arms from arm limb assemblies in a timely manner.
*   Of a physical stature that fits within the sizing criteria.
*   Provide a relevant medical certificate ensuring the pilot is safe to dive.
*   Be able to operate all jettison systems including umbilical cutting and jettison, thruster cable cutting and jettison.
*   18 years of age.
*   Demonstrate psychological fitness for the position, through aptitude testing.

Student candidates that are unable to meet the above criteria will not be allowed into the ADS pilot training program.

#### Competencies

Theory covers top level understanding relevant to the physical operations of the ADS and the understanding of resources available to assist in ADS understanding. An extrapolation of information is conducted during the class by the instructor. All technical information can be found within the hard copy manuals which are followed during the in class modules.

During the practical dive sessions the pilot trainee is expected to perform a number of tasks that reflect situations and operations that may be encountered in the field. Pilots require approximately 20 hours to learn basic skills and become proficient with suit life support and flying functions to allow them to focus on the work tasks. Students are introduced to the tooling with emphasis on job preparation, planning, and tool modification required for use with the ADS.

Examples of typical tasks which will be completed by students are; sizing up and buoyancy set up, overall operating procedures in water exercise, emergency procedures in water exercise, flying in and around structures, giving a set of life support system readings while hovering, thru-water communications protocols and many more.

#### Delivery And Assessment – Specific Requirements

During open water dive sessions the pilot trainee is expected to perform a number of tasks that reflect situations and operations that may be encountered in the field.

Tools applicable to these tasks are provided within the course. Courses directly leading to real operations will request the actual tools to be used in the operation be present during the course. Courses may be tailored for military sub-rescue, salvage, inspection and NDT, or typical oilfield construction.

Specific training in using tooling effectively involves a significant amount of preparation. Students are introduced to the tooling with emphasis on job preparation, planning, and tool modification required for use with the ADS.

The following are examples of typical tasks which will be completed by students and tracked within the course:

*   Sizing up and buoyancy set up
*   Overall operating procedures in water exercise
*   Overall emergency procedures in water exercise
*   Climbing umbilical (power loss, entrapment)
*   Emergency jettison systems
*   Flying in and around structure
*   Giving a set of life support system readings while hovering
*   Thru-water communications protocols
*   Rigging preparation
*   Rigging work
*   Connecting umbilical to down line
*   Shackle work on bottom and mid water
*   Carrying weight
*   Pneumatic tool use
*   Hydraulic tool use
*   Subsea Measurement
*   Tool basket management
*   Lift bag use
*   LARS operation (Optional)

All personnel will have successfully completed a training course specifying the type and extent of that training (Pilot, Supervisor, Technician). This should be signed by the Examining Supervisors. Upon completion of their training, they will have a competent working knowledge of the following subjects:

*   **Life Support**
    *   Thermal protection
    *   Gas partial pressures
    *   Gas mixtures
    *   Effects of high/low oxygen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide on human systems
    *   The body’s requirements – oxygen, food and water.
    *   Atmospheric monitoring.
    *   Cleanliness in gas systems, particularly in relation to oxygen.
    *   Colour coding and marking of gas cylinders.
    *   Carbon dioxide removal.
    *   Material compatibility with oxygen.
*   **Buoyancy and Trim Ballast Systems**
    *   Trim – centre of gravity and centre of buoyancy.
    *   Payload effects.
    *   Stability when submerged and in emergency conditions.
    *   Water density, layering.
    *   Pressure effects.
    *   Ballast systems.
*   **Movement**
    *   Propulsion systems, thrusters.
    *   Control of vertical, lateral and forward movement.
*   **Emergencies**
    *   Fires and fire extinguishing methods.
    *   Flooding.
    *   Entanglement.
    *   Life-support, toxic hazards.
    *   Loss of communications.
    *   Loss of power and sensors.
    *   Emergency communications.
    *   Emergency planning.
    *   Physical and mental effects of a prolonged period underwater when subject to sensory and thermal deprivation.
*   **Personnel Responsibilities**
    *   Chain of command, liaison, handovers.

*   **Statutory Requirements**
    *   Familiarization with codes of practice, certification requirements and relevant government regulations.

*   **Work Procedures**
    *   Operational planning.
    *   Interface with other underwater activities/operations.

*   **ADS Design and Construction**
    *   Hull shape
    *   Depth rating
    *   Materials of construction
    *   Safety systems
    *   Displacement
    *   Hydrodynamics.

To be familiar with the system’s equipment, all personnel should be conversant with the items listed below. Depending on job description, technicians will require more detailed knowledge than others.

*   **Navigation**
    *   Compasses (gyro and magnetic), including compass errors.
    *   Depth gauge
    *   Currents and tides
    *   Velocity triangles
    *   Acoustics
    *   Visibility and mid-water problems.
    *   General seamanship.
    *   Transponders, pingers and sonars.
*   **Communications**
    *   Hard wire digital system
    *   Acoustics
    *   VHF systems
    *   Emergency signals
*   **Power Sources and Electrical Systems**
    *   Batteries and other relevant primary sources.
    *   Umbilical systems.
    *   Circuit protection, electrical faults and their effects.
    *   Fault detection and elimination.
    *   Emergency power sources
    *   Hydraulic and Pneumatic Systems
    *   Pumps
    *   Accumulators
    *   Valves
    *   Compensated systems

#### Delivery And Assessment – Dive Program And Times

Time allocation of this course is as follows (per student):  
a)    Minimum 20 hours each of bottom dive time (pilot/dive).  
b)    Minimum 12 hours of supervisory training.

7.title: QXRtb3NwaGVyaWMgZGl2aW5nIHN1aXQgLSBXaWtpd2FuZA==
7.content:
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atmospheric_diving_suit&action=edit&section=0&oldformat=true)An **atmospheric diving suit** (**ADS**), **atmospheric pressure diving suit** or **single atmosphere diving suit** is a small one-person articulated [submersible](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Submersible "Submersible") which resembles a [suit of armour](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Plate_armour "Plate armour"), with pressure-tight joints to allow articulation while maintaining a constant internal volume and an internal pressure of one atmosphere. An ADS can enable diving at depths of up to 2,300 feet (700 m) for many hours by eliminating the majority of significant physiological dangers associated with [deep diving](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Deep_diving "Deep diving").[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) The occupant of an ADS does not need to [decompress](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Decompression_/(diving/) "Decompression (diving)"), and there is no need for special [breathing gas](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas") mixtures, so there is no danger of [decompression sickness](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Decompression_sickness "Decompression sickness") or [nitrogen narcosis](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Nitrogen_narcosis "Nitrogen narcosis") when the ADS is functioning properly.[\[2\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Wasp_specifications-2) An ADS can permit less-skilled swimmers to complete deep dives, albeit at the expense of dexterity.

**Quick facts** Acronym, Other names ...

[![Image 1: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Newtsuit_atmospheric_diving_suit.jpg/640px-Newtsuit_atmospheric_diving_suit.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:Newtsuit_atmospheric_diving_suit.jpg)

The [Newtsuit](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Newtsuit "Newtsuit") has fully articulated, rotary joints in the arms and legs. These provide high mobility, while remaining largely unaffected by high pressures.

Atmospheric diving suits in current use include the [Newtsuit](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Newtsuit "Newtsuit"), Exosuit, Hardsuit and the WASP, all of which are self-contained hard suits that incorporate propulsion units. The Hardsuit is constructed from [cast](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Casting "Casting") aluminum ([forged](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Forging "Forging") aluminum in a version constructed for the US Navy for submarine rescue); the upper torso hull is made from cast [aluminum](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Aluminum "Aluminum"), while the bottom dome is machined aluminum. The WASP is of [glass-reinforced plastic](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Glass-reinforced_plastic "Glass-reinforced plastic") (GRP) body tube construction.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1)

Definition and classification
-----------------------------

An atmospheric diving suit is a small one-person submersible with articulated limbs encasing the diver. Water- and pressure-tight joints allow articulation while maintaining an internal pressure of one atmosphere. Mobility may be through thrusters for mid-water operation, though this is not a requirement, and articulated legs may be provided for walking on the substrate.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3)

Thornton (2000) distinguishes an ADS from a submersible in that the ADS has human powered articulated limbs, as opposed to remotely operated articulated limbs.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) It is not clear whether this would exclude servo-assisted limbs encasing those of the operator, as a powered exoskeleton, but it might be reasonable to include them as atmospheric diving suits.

An atmospheric diving suit may be classified as a crewed submersible and a self-propelled, crewed, one-atmosphere underwater intervention device, but has also been classified as an atmospheric diving system.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3)

A characteristic of single atmosphere internal pressure is that the suit cannot passively vent gas to ambient pressure. The options are to recycle breathing gas internally, adding oxygen and removing carbon dioxide,[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Machine_Design-4) to vent surface supplied gas back to the surface through a hose which can safely withstand the external ambient pressure, or to pump it out by compressing it to ambient pressure before venting.[\[5\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-5)

Purpose and requirements
------------------------

The [underwater environment](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Underwater_environment "Underwater environment") exerts major [physiological stresses](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Human_physiology_of_underwater_diving "Human physiology of underwater diving") on the diver, which increase with depth, and appear to impose an absolute limit to diving depth at ambient pressure. An atmospheric diving suit is a small submersible with a pressure hull which accommodates a single occupant at an internal pressure of about one atmosphere. The provision of hollow arm spaces with pressure-resistant joints to carry manually operated manipulators, and usually separate leg spaces, similarly articulated for locomotion, makes a suit resemble a bulky suit of [plate armour](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Plate_armour "Plate armour"), or an [exoskeleton](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Exoskeleton "Exoskeleton"), with elaborate joint seals to allow articulation while maintaining internal pressure.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1)

An atmospheric diving suit is equipment intended primarily to isolate the occupant from the ambient pressure of the underwater environment, and provide any necessary [life-support](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Life-support_system "Life-support system") while the suit is in use. While using the suit, the diver will expect to perform useful work, and get to and from the place where the work is to be done. These functions require sufficient mobility, dexterity and sensory input to do the job, and this will vary depending on the details of the work. Consequently, the work possible in an atmospheric suit is limited by the suit construction.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3)

Mobility at the surface and on deck can be managed by [launch and recovery systems](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Launch_and_recovery_system_/(diving/) "Launch and recovery system (diving)"), Mobility underwater generally requires neutral or moderately negative buoyancy, and either the ability to walk or swim, or the use of finely controllable [thrusters](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Thruster_/(marine_/) "Thruster (marine )"). Both walking and thruster propulsion have been applied with some success. Swimming has not been effective.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1)

The dexterity to perform useful work is limited by joint mobility and geometry, inertia, and friction, and has been one of the more difficult engineering challenges. [Haptic perception](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Haptic_perception "Haptic perception") through manipulators is a major limitation on finer control, as the friction of the joints and seals greatly reduces the sensitivity available.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3)

Operator visual input is relatively easy to provide directly by using transparent [viewports](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Viewport_/(diving/) "Viewport (diving)"). A wide field of view can be achieved simply and structurally effectively by using a transparent partial dome over the diver's head. Close-up views of the manipulators are limited by joint flexibility and geometry of the suit's arms. External sound and temperature perception are greatly attenuated, and there is no sense of touch through the suit. [Communications](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Diver_communication#Voice_communications "Diver communication") must be provided by technology, as there is normally no-one else in the immediate vicinity.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3)

### Design constraints

The main environmental factors affecting design are the ambient hydrostatic pressure of the maximum operating depth, and ergonomic considerations regarding the potential range of operators.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) The structure and mechanics of the suit must reliably withstand the external pressure, without collapsing or deforming sufficiently to cause seals to leak or joints to experience excessive friction, and the full range of movement must not change the internal or external displaced volume, as this would have consequences for the amount of force required to move the joints in addition to the friction of the joint seals. Insulation is relatively simple, and can be applied to the inside of the suit and in the form of clothing on the diver. Active heating and cooling are also possible using well established technology. Mass changes can be used to provide initial and emergency buoyancy conditions by way of fixed and ditchable ballast weights.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3)

Ergonomic considerations include the size and strength of the user. The interior dimensions must fit or be modifiable to fit a reasonable range of operators, and operating forces on joints must be reasonably practicable. The field of vision is constrained by the helmet design or viewport positioning, though closed circuit video can extend it considerably in any direction. General underwater conditions of visibility and water movement must be manageable for the range of conditions in which the suit is expected to be used. Marine thrusters may be mounted on the suit to help with maneuvering and positioning,[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3) and sonar and other scanning technologies may help provide an augmented external view.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Thornton_2000-3)

Factors affecting the design and construction:[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)

*   Pressure hull form – Sufficient volume for necessary internal systems, constrained by size and shape of human operator, and by shapes with high resistance to collapse under external pressure.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
    *   Displacement – Need for neutral buoyancy at work and positive buoyancy in emergencies[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
    *   Hydrodynamics – cruise speed[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
    *   Propulsion – Thruster type and arrangement[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
    *   Ergonomics – Anthropometry, joint design for limb articulation under external pressure.
*   Working depth rating – Strength, rigidity and density of materials. Buckling, constant volume, and joint friction limiting factors[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
    *   Construction materials[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
    *   Safety[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6) .

    *   Emergency rebreather circulation systems.[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Machine_Design-4)

Buoyancy and trim ballast systems:[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)

*   Control of basic buoyancy[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
*   Adjustment of trim – control of the positions of centre of gravity and centre of buoyancy.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
*   Compensating trim and buoyancy for payload effects.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)

*   Compensation for pressure effects.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
*   Adjustable and ditchable ballast systems.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)

Movement, propulsion, and navigation systems:[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)

*   Propulsion systems, thrusters.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
*   Control of vertical, lateral and forward movement, and rotation and orientation in three dimensions.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)

Classes of emergency:\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed?oldformat=true "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

*   Leaks and flooding.

### Work skills

These may include submarine rescue, salvage, inspection and non-destructive testing, and typical oilfield construction and maintenance tasks, or a range of scientific observation and sampling activities.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)

### Operator requirements

*   The operator must fit inside the suit, be able to move their limbs effectively, and be able to get out again.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
*   The operator must be able to reach and to operate electronics panels and life support systems, be able to jettison ballast, operate umbilical and thruster cable cutters.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
*   The operator must be physically, medically and psychologically fit for the work.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)

### Hazards and failure modes

The primary structural failure modes of an ADS are [buckling](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Buckling "Buckling") collapse in compression, leaks, and lockup of joints. Leaks and buckling in compression both cause a reduction in buoyancy. Joint leaks and locking of articulating joints may be reversible when pressure is reduced. Electrically ignited fire is also possible.

Systems failures may include loss of power, communications, or propulsion, or life-support systems failure, such as failure of scrubbing the carbon dioxide from the breathing air, or failure of internal temperature control. Recovery from most of these would be by aborting the dive and making an emergency ascent. Bailout to emergency breathing system and ditching of ballast to establish positive buoyancy may be necessary. If the ADS is tethered it can be lifted. The most dangerous consequence is catastrophic leakage, which is likely to be fatal.

There has been one fatal incident involving an ADS. A WASP was dropped 80 feet (25 m) in August 1999 due to a structural failure in a recently tested launch and recovery system, and the diver was killed by the impact with the launch platform. This is in the context of tens of thousands of operational man-hours by WASPs without serious incidents.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1)

Several advantages over ambient pressure diving are claimed, but dexterity is less. There are also advantages and disadvantages in comparison with [remotely operated underwater vehicles](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Remotely_operated_underwater_vehicle "Remotely operated underwater vehicle") (ROVs):

*   No decompression is required. Decompression from saturation takes approximately 1 day per 30 [msw](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Metre_sea_water "Metre sea water") plus 1 day, during which time the divers are unproductive. This is particularly expensive when the total dive time is relatively short.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1)
*   Consecutive dives can be made to any depths within the operating range. Saturation divers are very limited in safe excursion range from storage depth.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) An ADS depth excursions are limited only by maximum working depth.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
*   Lateral range is comparable with ROVs.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-ADAS_ADS-6)
*   Thrusters, when provided, can provide moderate mid-water and current capability.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1)
*   Manipulatory capacity and dexterity are better than ROVs. Less special tooling is required for most work. Depth perception of the diver is better than remote viewing via a ROV cameras.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1)
*   Deep applications are possible compared with ambient pressure diving. The industry-accepted maximum depth for routine saturation diving is 300 msw. ADS operations can go deeper.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1) However, ROVs and crewed submersibles can go much deeper. Maximum depth capability for ROV and crewed submersibles is [full ocean depth](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Full_ocean_depth "Full ocean depth").[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Technology_specifications-7)

For some work the most effective method can be a combination of ADS and ROV; in other cases, ADS and ambient pressure diver.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Offshore-1)

### Early designs

[![Image 2: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Jacob_Rowe%27s_diving_machine.jpg/250px-Jacob_Rowe%27s_diving_machine.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:Jacob_Rowe's_diving_machine.jpg)

Jacob Rowe's copper diving dress, built in the 1710s

[![Image 3: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/John_Lethbridge_diving_apparatus_replica_%281715%29.jpg/250px-John_Lethbridge_diving_apparatus_replica_%281715%29.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:John_Lethbridge_diving_apparatus_replica_\(1715\).jpg)

In 1715, British inventor [John Lethbridge](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/John_Lethbridge "John Lethbridge") constructed a "diving engine". Essentially a wooden barrel about 6 feet (1.8 m) in length with two holes for the diver's arms sealed with leather cuffs, and a 4-inch (100 mm) viewport of thick glass. It was reportedly used to dive as deep as 60 feet (18 m), and was used to salvage substantial quantities of [silver](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Silver "Silver") from the wreck of the [East Indiaman](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/East_Indiaman "East Indiaman") [_Vansittart_](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Vansittart_/(1718_EIC_ship/) "Vansittart (1718 EIC ship)"), which sank in 1719 off the [Cape Verde](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Cape_Verde "Cape Verde") islands.[\[8\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-tanads-8) A similar design made of copper was used by Jacob Rowe on the same salvage contract.[\[9\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Ratcliffe_2011-9)

The first armored suit with real joints, designed as leather pieces with rings in the shape of a spring (also known as accordion joints), was designed by Englishman W. H. Taylor in 1838. The diver's hands and feet were covered with leather. Taylor also devised a ballast tank attached to the suit that could be filled with water to attain negative [buoyancy](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Buoyancy "Buoyancy"). While it was patented, the suit was never actually produced. It is considered that its weight and bulk would have rendered it nearly immobile underwater.[\[8\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-tanads-8)

Lodner D. Phillips designed the first completely enclosed ADS in 1856. His design comprised a barrel-shaped upper torso with domed ends with ball and socket joints in the articulated arms and legs. The arms had joints at shoulder and elbow, and the legs at knee and hip. The suit included a ballast tank, a viewing port, entrance through a [manhole cover](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Manhole_cover "Manhole cover") on top, a hand-cranked propeller, and rudimentary manipulators at the ends of the arms. Breathing air was to be supplied from the surface via hose. There is no indication that Phillips' suit was ever constructed.[\[8\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-tanads-8)

[![Image 4: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Scaphandre_Carmagnolle_MnM_Paris.jpg/640px-Scaphandre_Carmagnolle_MnM_Paris.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:Scaphandre_Carmagnolle_MnM_Paris.jpg)

Suit built by Carmagnolle brothers in 1882 was the first anthropomorphic design.

The first properly anthropomorphic design of ADS, built by the Carmagnolle brothers of [Marseille](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Marseille "Marseille"), France in 1882, featured rolling convolute joints consisting of closely fitting concentric spherical sections sealed by watertight cloth membranes. The suit had 22 of these joints: four in each leg, six in each arm, and two in the torso. The helmet had 25 individual 2-inch (50 mm) glass viewports spaced at the average separation of the human eyes.[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Historic_diving_times_2005-10) Weighing 830 pounds (380 kg), the Carmagnole ADS never worked properly and its joints never were entirely waterproof. It is now on display at the [French National Navy Museum](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Mus%C3%A9e_national_de_la_Marine "Musée national de la Marine") in Paris.[\[11\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-pieds-lourds-11)

Another design was patented in 1894 by inventors John Buchanan and Alexander Gordon from [Melbourne](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Melbourne "Melbourne"), Australia. The construction was based on a frame of spiral wires covered with waterproof material. The design was improved by Alexander Gordon by attaching the suit to the helmet and other parts and incorporating jointed [radius rods](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Radius_rod "Radius rod") in the limbs. This resulted in a flexible suit which could withstand high pressure. The suit was manufactured by British firm [Siebe Gorman](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Siebe_Gorman "Siebe Gorman") and trialed in Scotland in 1898.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed?oldformat=true "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

1913 US Navy ADS at Man in the Sea Museum, Panama City, FL with the lobster claws

[![Image 6: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/2_jawed_grasper_on_1913_US_Navy_armored_diving_suit.jpg/250px-2_jawed_grasper_on_1913_US_Navy_armored_diving_suit.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:2_jawed_grasper_on_1913_US_Navy_armored_diving_suit.jpg)

Close up view of two-jawed grasper and pitch-yaw wrist joint on 1913 US Navy armored diving suit

American designer Macduffee constructed the first suit to use ball bearings to provide joint movement in 1914; it was tested in [New York](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/New_York_City "New York City") to a depth of 214 feet (65 m), but was not very successful. A year later, Harry L. Bowdoin of [Bayonne, New Jersey](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Bayonne,_New_Jersey "Bayonne, New Jersey"), made an improved ADS with oil-filled rotary joints. Each joint has a small duct to its interior to allow equalization of pressure. The suit was designed to have eighteen joints: four in each arm and leg, and one in each thumb. Four viewing ports and a chest-mounted lamp were intended to assist underwater vision. There is no evidence that Bowdoin's suit was ever built, or that it would have worked if it had been.[\[8\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-tanads-8)

Atmospheric diving suits built by Neufeldt and Kuhnke of Germany were used during the salvage of gold and silver bullion from the wreck of the British ship [SS _Egypt_](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/SS_Egypt "SS Egypt"), an 8,000 ton [P&O](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/P&O "P&O") liner that sank in May 1922. The suit was relegated to duties as an observation chamber at the wreck's depth of 560 feet (170 m),[\[12\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Pickford-12) and was successfully used to direct mechanical grabs which opened up the bullion storage. In 1917, Benjamin F. Leavitt of [Traverse City, Michigan](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Traverse_City,_Michigan "Traverse City, Michigan"), dived on the [SS _Pewabic_](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/SS_Pewabic "SS Pewabic") which sank to a depth of 182 feet (55 m) in [Lake Huron](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Lake_Huron "Lake Huron") in 1865, salvaging 350 tons of copper ore. In 1923, he went on to salvage the wreck of the British schooner _Cape Horn_ which lay in 220 feet (67 m) of water off [Pichidangui](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Pichidangui "Pichidangui"), Chile, salvaging $600,000 worth of copper. Leavitt's suit was of his own design and construction. The most innovative aspect of Leavitt's suit was the fact that it was completely self-contained and needed no umbilical, the breathing mixture being supplied from a tank mounted on the back of the suit. The breathing apparatus incorporated a [scrubber](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Scrubber "Scrubber") and an oxygen [regulator](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Diving_regulator "Diving regulator") and could last for up to a full hour.[\[13\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Marx_1990-13)

In 1924 the _[Reichsmarine](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Reichsmarine "Reichsmarine")_ tested the second generation of the Neufeldt and Kuhnke suit to 530 feet (160 m), but limb movement was very difficult and the joints were judged not to be [fail-safe](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fail-safe "Fail-safe"), in that if they were to fail, there was a possibility that the suit's integrity would be violated. However, these suits were used by the Germans as armored divers during [World War II](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/World_War_II "World War II") and were later taken by the [Western Allies](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") after the war.

From 1929 to 1931 two atmospheric pressure one-person submersible "suits" designed by Carl Wiley were used in the successful salvage of the steamship _[Islander](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/SS_Islander "SS Islander")_ which sank in the Stevens Passage near [Juneau, Alaska](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Juneau,_Alaska "Juneau, Alaska") on 15 August 1901, with a large amount of gold dust in the cargo. The suits operated at a maximum depth of 365 feet (111 m). They were each equipped with a mechanical arm with a grasping claw at the end operated from inside the suit. The suits were capable of traversing a hard, reasonably smooth substrate on wheels, and were used to place the steel cables used to raise the wreck by [tidal lift](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tidal_lift "Tidal lift") (with an 18-foot or 5-metre tide range) under a catamaran barge in stages, while it was towed to shallow water. The suits had electrical power, and the diver/pilot used an oxygen rebreather. These suits have also been described as diving bells and observation chambers, as they do not match the usual definition of an atmospheric diving suit, but they were more than just observation chambers, being capable of work, and were independently mobile, so do not match the usual definition of a diving bell either. They were an unusual type of tethered crewed submersible.[\[14\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Popular_Mechanics_Oct_1931-14)

In 1952, Alfred A. Mikalow constructed an ADS using ball and socket joints, specifically for the purpose of locating and salvaging sunken treasure. The suit was reported to be capable of diving to 1,000 feet (300 m) depth and was successfully used to dive on the wreck of [SS _City of Rio de Janeiro_](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/SS_City_of_Rio_de_Janeiro "SS City of Rio de Janeiro") near [Fort Point, San Francisco](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fort_Point,_San_Francisco "Fort Point, San Francisco") at a depth of 330 feet (100 m). Mikalow's suit had various interchangeable instruments which could be mounted on the end of the arms in place of the original manipulators. It carried seven 90-cubic foot high pressure cylinders to provide breathing gas and control buoyancy. The ballast compartment covered the gas cylinders. For communication, the suit used [hydrophones](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Hydrophone "Hydrophone").[\[15\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Burke_1966-15)

### The modern suit

#### Peress' _Tritonia_

[![Image 7: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Tritonia_Lusitania_1935.jpg/640px-Tritonia_Lusitania_1935.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:Tritonia_Lusitania_1935.jpg)

Two divers, one wearing the "Tritonia" ADS and the other standard diving dress, preparing to explore the wreck of the [RMS _Lusitania_](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/RMS_Lusitania "RMS Lusitania"), 1935

Although various atmospheric suits had been developed during the [Victorian era](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Victorian_era "Victorian era"), none of these suits overcame the basic design problem of constructing a joint which would remain flexible and watertight at depth without seizing up under pressure.

Pioneering British diving engineer, [Joseph Salim Peress](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Joseph_Salim_Peress "Joseph Salim Peress"), invented the first truly usable atmospheric diving suit, the _Tritonia_, in 1932 and was later involved in the construction of the famous [JIM suit](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/JIM_suit "JIM suit"). Having a natural talent for engineering design, he challenged himself to construct an ADS that would keep divers dry and at atmospheric pressure, even at great depth. In 1918, Peress began working for WG Tarrant at [Byfleet](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Byfleet "Byfleet"), United Kingdom, where he was given the space and tools to develop his ideas about constructing an ADS. His first attempt was an immensely complex prototype machined from solid [stainless steel](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Stainless_steel "Stainless steel").

In 1923, Peress was asked to design a suit for salvage work on the wreck of [SS _Egypt_](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/SS_Egypt "SS Egypt") which had sunk in the [English Channel](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/English_Channel "English Channel"). He declined, on the grounds that his prototype suit was too heavy for a diver to handle easily, but was encouraged by the request to begin work on a new suit using lighter materials. By 1929 he believed he had solved the weight problem, by using cast magnesium instead of steel, and had also managed to improve the design of the suit's joints by using a trapped cushion of oil to keep the surfaces moving smoothly. The oil was virtually non-compressible and readily displaceable, which would allow the limb joints to move freely even under great pressure. Peress claimed the Tritonia suit could function at 1,200 ft (370 m), where the pressure was 520 psi (35 atm), although this was never proven.[\[16\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-loftas1973-16)

[![Image 8: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Luciana_Civico_risalita_record_ARA_meno_80_stringe_pinza_scafandro_Verardi.jpg/320px-Luciana_Civico_risalita_record_ARA_meno_80_stringe_pinza_scafandro_Verardi.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:Luciana_Civico_risalita_record_ARA_meno_80_stringe_pinza_scafandro_Verardi.jpg)

Luciana Civico ascending from the dive of the depth record at 269 feet (82 m) on 11 November 1962 in the vicinity of Capo Miseno in the Gulf of Pozzuoli tightens the pincer of the diving suit operated by the s. Lieutenant Benito Velardi

In 1930, Peress revealed the Tritonia suit.[\[17\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-dive_hx-17) By May it had completed trials and was publicly demonstrated in a tank at [Byfleet](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Byfleet "Byfleet"). In September Peress' assistant [Jim Jarret](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Jim_Jarret "Jim Jarret") dived in the suit to a depth of 404 ft (123 m) in [Loch Ness](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Loch_Ness "Loch Ness"). The suit performed perfectly, the joints proving resistant to pressure and moving freely even at depth. The suit was offered to the [Royal Navy](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") which turned it down, stating that Navy divers never needed to descend below 300 ft (90 m). In October 1935 Jarret made a successful deep dive to more than 300 ft (90 m) on the wreck of the [RMS _Lusitania_](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/RMS_Lusitania "RMS Lusitania") off south Ireland, followed by a shallower dive to 200 feet (60 m) in the [English Channel](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/English_Channel "English Channel") in 1937 after which, due to lack of interest, the Tritonia suit was retired.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed?oldformat=true "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

The development in atmospheric pressure suits stagnated in the 1940s through 1960s, as efforts were concentrated on solving the problems of deep diving by dealing with the physiological problems of ambient pressure diving instead of avoiding them by isolating the diver from the pressure. Although the advances in ambient pressure diving (in particular, with [scuba](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Scuba_set "Scuba set") gear) were significant, the limitations brought renewed interest to the development of the ADS in the late 1960s.[\[16\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-loftas1973-16)

#### The JIM suit

The _Tritonia_ suit spent about 30 years in an engineering company's warehouse in [Glasgow](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Glasgow "Glasgow"), where it was discovered, with Peress' help, by two partners in the British firm Underwater Marine Equipment, Mike Humphrey and Mike Borrow, in the mid-1960s.[\[16\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-loftas1973-16)[\[18\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-scribe71-18)[\[19\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-divernet-19) UMEL would later classify Peress' suit as the "A.D.S Type I", a designation system that would be continued by the company for later models. In 1969, Peress was asked to become a consultant to the new company created to develop the JIM suit, named in honour of the diver Jim Jarret.[\[20\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Carter_1976-20)

[![Image 9: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/JIM_suit_in_Naval_Undersea_Museum.jpg/640px-JIM_suit_in_Naval_Undersea_Museum.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:JIM_suit_in_Naval_Undersea_Museum.jpg)

JIM suit in Naval Undersea Museum

The first JIM suit was completed in November 1971 and underwent sea trials from [HMS _Reclaim_](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/HMS_Reclaim "HMS Reclaim") in early 1972. In 1976, it set a record of five hours and 59 minutes for the longest working dive below 490 feet (150 m), at a depth of 905 feet (276 m). The first JIM suits were constructed from cast magnesium for its high strength-to-weight ratio and weighed approximately 1,100 pounds (500 kg) in air, including the occupant. They were 6 feet 6 inches (1.98 m) in height and had a maximum operating depth of 1,500 feet (460 m). The suit had a positive buoyancy of 15 to 50 pounds-force (67 to 222 N). Ballast was attached to the suit's front and could be jettisoned from inside, allowing the suit to ascend to the surface at approximately 100 feet per minute (30 m/min).[\[21\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Kesling_2011-21) The suit also incorporated a communication link and an umbilical connection that could be released by the diver. The original JIM suit had eight annular oil-supported universal joints, one at each hip, knee, shoulder and lower arm. The JIM operator received air through an oral/nasal mask that attached to a lung-powered scrubber that had a life support duration of approximately 72 hours.[\[22\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-nedu76-22) Operations in arctic conditions with water temperatures of 28.9 °F (−1.7 °C) for over 5 hours were successfully carried out using woolen thermal protection and neoprene boots. In 86 °F (30 °C) water the suit was reported to be uncomfortably hot during heavy work.[\[23\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Curley_and_Bachrach_1982-23)

[![Image 10: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/JIM_suitRoyal_Navy_Submarine_Museum.jpg/640px-JIM_suitRoyal_Navy_Submarine_Museum.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:JIM_suitRoyal_Navy_Submarine_Museum.jpg)

A [JIM suit](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/JIM_suit "JIM suit") on display at the [Royal Navy Submarine Museum](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Royal_Navy_Submarine_Museum "Royal Navy Submarine Museum"), Gosport

As technology improved and operational knowledge grew, Oceaneering upgraded their fleet of JIMs. The magnesium construction was replaced with [glass-reinforced plastic](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Glass-reinforced_plastic "Glass-reinforced plastic") (GRP) and the single joints with segmented ones, each allowing seven degrees of motion, and when added together giving the operator a very great range of motion. In addition, the four-port domed top of the suit was replaced by a transparent acrylic dome as used on WASP, which provided a much better field of vision. Trials were also carried out by the [Ministry of Defence](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ministry_of_Defence_/(United_Kingdom/) "Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)") on a flying Jim suit powered from the surface through an umbilical cable. This resulted in a hybrid suit with the ability of working on the sea bed as well as mid water.[\[23\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Curley_and_Bachrach_1982-23)

In addition to upgrades to the JIM design, other variations of the original suit were constructed. The first, named the SAM Suit (designated A.D.S III), was a completely aluminium model. A smaller and lighter suit, it was more anthropomorphic than the original JIMs and was depth-rated to 1,000 feet (300 m). Attempts were made to limit corrosion by the use of a chromic anodizing coating applied to the arm and leg joints, which gave them an unusual green color. The SAM suit stood at 6 feet 3 inches (1.91 m) in height, and had a life support duration of 20 hours. Only three SAM suits would be produced by UMEL before the design was shelved. The second, named the JAM suit (designated A.D.S IV), was constructed of [glass-reinforced plastic](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Glass-reinforced_plastic "Glass-reinforced plastic") (GRP) and was depth-rated for around 2,000 feet (610 m).[\[24\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Nuytten_1998-24)

### WASP

[![Image 11: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/WASP_at_the_OSEL_Testing_tank_Gt_Yarmouth%2C_UK.JPG/640px-WASP_at_the_OSEL_Testing_tank_Gt_Yarmouth%2C_UK.JPG)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:WASP_at_the_OSEL_Testing_tank_Gt_Yarmouth,_UK.JPG)

WASP at the OSEL Testing tank [Great Yarmouth](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Great_Yarmouth "Great Yarmouth"), UK

The WASP atmospheric diving system is partway between a one-person submersible and an atmospheric diving suit, in that there are articulated arms which contain and are moved by the operator's arms, but the operator's legs are contained in a rigid housing. Mobility is provided by two vertical and two horizontal foot-switch controlled electrical [marine thrusters](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Marine_thruster "Marine thruster"). Operating depth was quoted as 2,300 feet (700 m)[\[2\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Wasp_specifications-2)

WASP is 84 inches (2.1 m) high, 42 inches (1.1 m) wide, and 34 inches (0.86 m) front to back. Ballasted weight in air approximately 2,200 pounds (1,000 kg), for neutral buoyancy in water, but buoyancy can be increased by up to 35 pounds (16 kg) during operation, and ballast can be jettisoned in an emergency. WASP is transported on a support frame.[\[2\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Wasp_specifications-2)

[![Image 12: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Exosuit_Side.jpg/250px-Exosuit_Side.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:Exosuit_Side.jpg)

Side view of Exosuit

[![Image 13: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Exosuit_Back.jpg/250px-Exosuit_Back.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:Exosuit_Back.jpg)

Back view of Exosuit

In 1987, the "[Newtsuit](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Newtsuit "Newtsuit")" was developed by the Canadian engineer [Phil Nuytten](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Phil_Nuytten "Phil Nuytten"), and a version was put into production as the "Hardsuit" by Hardsuits International.[\[9\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Ratcliffe_2011-9) The Newtsuit is constructed to function like a 'submarine you can wear', allowing the diver to work at normal atmospheric pressure even at depths of over 1,000 feet (300 m). Made of wrought [aluminium](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Aluminium "Aluminium"), it had fully articulated joints so the diver can move more easily underwater. The [life support system](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Life_support_system "Life support system") provides 6–8 hours of air, with an emergency back-up supply of an additional 48 hours. The Hardsuit was used to salvage the bell from the wreck of the [SS _Edmund Fitzgerald_](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/SS_Edmund_Fitzgerald "SS Edmund Fitzgerald") in 1995. The latest version of the Hardsuit designed by Oceanworks, the "Quantum 2", uses higher power commercially available ROV thrusters for better reliability and more power as well as an atmospheric monitoring system to monitor the environmental conditions in the cabin. A more recent design by Nuytten is the Exosuit, a relatively lightweight and low powered suit intended for marine research.[\[25\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Gizmodo-25) It was first used in 2014 at the Bluewater and Antikythera underwater research expeditions.[\[26\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Exosuit-27)

[![Image 14: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Navy_Diver4.jpg/640px-Navy_Diver4.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:Navy_Diver4.jpg)

US Navy ADS 2000 on launch and recovery platform after a certification dive in August 2006

The ADS 2000 was developed jointly with OceanWorks International and the US Navy in 1997,[\[28\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-oceanworks-28) as an evolution of the Hardsuit to meet US Navy requirements. The ADS 2000 provides increased depth capability for the US Navy's Submarine Rescue Program. Manufactured from forged T6061 aluminum alloy, it uses an advanced articulating joint design based on the Hardsuit joints. Capable of operating in up to 2,000 feet (610 m) of seawater for a normal mission of up to six hours, it has a self-contained, automatic life support system.[\[29\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Logico_2006b-29) Additionally, the integrated dual thruster system allows the pilot to navigate easily underwater. It became fully operational and certified by the US Navy off southern California on 1 August 2006, when Chief Navy Diver Daniel Jackson submerged to 2,000 feet (610 m).[\[30\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Logico_2006-30)

From the project's beginning until 2011, the US navy spent $113 million on the ADS 2000.[\[31\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmospheric_diving_suit#cite_note-Budget_2011-31)

[![Image 15: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/US_Navy_090802-N-1580K-028_Chief_of_Navy_Reserve_Vice_Adm._Dirk_Debbink_asks_Cmdr._Brian_Granger_nd_Chief_Navy_Diver_Eric_Taylor_about_the_capabilities_of_the_atmospheric_diving_system.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/atmospheric_diving_suit#/media/File:US_Navy_090802-N-1580K-028_Chief_of_Navy_Reserve_Vice_Adm._Dirk_Debbink_asks_Cmdr._Brian_Granger_nd_Chief_Navy_Diver_Eric_Taylor_about_the_capabilities_of_the_atmospheric_diving_system.jpg)

The deepest no-limit freedive (male) is 253 m (830 ft) and was achieved by Herbert Nitsch (Austria), in Santorini, Greece, on 6 June 2012.

Nitsch achieved the incredible dive on a project called "Extreme 800". After the dive, he experienced severe decompression sickness.

Records change on a daily basis and are not immediately published online. For a full list of record titles, please use our Record Application Search. (You will need to register / login for access)

![Image 1](https://images.theoutdoorwire.com/2023/04/06/a809e990-30e2-40ba-988b-382384c83745_600x400.jpeg)

The world’s deepest dive on open circuit scuba stands at 332.35m (1,090ft). It was undertaken by Ahmed Gabr in Dahab in the Red Sea on 18/19 September 2014 after nearly a decade of preparation. The descent took only 15 minutes while the ascent lasted 13 hours 35 minutes. Ahmed was helped by a 30-strong support team, including nine divers as well as technicians, medical staff, and media representatives.

The record had previously been held by South Africa’s Nuno Gomes with a 2005 dive to 318.25m (1,044ft) also at Dahab. He still holds the official world record for the deepest cave dive after diving to a depth of 282m (927ft) in the Boemansgat cave in South Africa in 1996.  
Advertisement

The same cave was the scene for the deepest scuba dive by a female set in 2004 when Verna van Schaik dived down to 221m (725ft).

discipline in which the diver descends and ascends using their method of choice **No Limit apnea** is a discipline of competitive [freediving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freediving "Freediving"), also known as competitive apnea, in which the freediver descends and ascends with the method of their choice.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-limits_apnea#cite_note-RRR8947-1) Often, a heavy metal bar or "sled" grasped by the diver descends fixed to a line, reaching great depths. The most common ascension assistance is via a solid or inflatable lifting device, which allow for rapid surfacing. The dives may be performed head-first or feet-first. The freediving organization [AIDA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDA_International "AIDA International") was the first to name this discipline No Limit (NLT) and to document world records in it.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-limits_apnea#cite_note-2) This form of diving is considered extremely dangerous by diving professionals.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-limits_apnea#cite_note-3) No Limit has claimed the lives of several divers.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-limits_apnea#cite_note-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-limits_apnea#cite_note-5) In 2025 the discipline is not recognized by either [AIDA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDA_International "AIDA International") or [CMAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conf%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_Mondiale_des_Activit%C3%A9s_Subaquatiques "Confédération Mondiale des Activités Subaquatiques").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-limits_apnea#cite_note-6) Challenges ---------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=No-limits_apnea&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Challenges")\] The three main differences between free diving disciplines that involve diving to depth and those that occur at the surface are that you cannot interrupt the dive, there are periods where work is performed and the diver is impacted by [direct effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysbarism#Effects_of_pressure_on_the_body "Dysbarism") of pressure.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-limits_apnea#cite_note-pmid22183699-7) Records ------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=No-limits_apnea&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Records")\] The current No Limit world record holder is [Herbert Nitsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Nitsch "Herbert Nitsch") with a depth of 214 metres (702 ft) set on 9 June 2007, in [Spetses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spetses "Spetses"), [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece"),[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-limits_apnea#cite_note-8) however, in a subsequent dive on 6 June 2012 in [Santorini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santorini "Santorini"), [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece") to break his own record, he went down to 253.2 metres (831 ft), a Guinness World Record,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-limits_apnea#cite_note-9) but suffered severe [decompression sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_sickness "Decompression sickness") afterwards.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-limits_apnea#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-limits_apnea#cite_note-11) See also -------- 21.title: U3VyZmFjZS1zdXBwbGllZCBkaXZpbmc=
21.content:
Surface-supplied diving is a mode of [underwater diving](https://grokipedia.com/page/Underwater_diving) in which the diver is supplied with [breathing gas](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breathing_gas), such as [compressed air](https://grokipedia.com/page/Compressed_air) or mixed gases, from the surface via a flexible umbilical hose that also provides communication lines, hot water for thermal protection, and a strength member for support.\[1\] This technique enables operations at greater depths—typically up to 190 feet of [seawater](https://grokipedia.com/page/Seawater) (fsw) for air diving, with extensions to 300 fsw using mixed gases—and longer durations than self-contained [underwater breathing apparatus](https://grokipedia.com/page/Underwater_breathing_apparatus) (SCUBA), as the surface supply offers virtually unlimited gas volume.\[2\] It is the primary method for professional applications, including commercial salvage, underwater construction, [military](https://grokipedia.com/page/Military) operations, and scientific [research](https://grokipedia.com/page/Research), due to its enhanced [safety](https://grokipedia.com/page/Safety) features like continuous monitoring and emergency gas reserves.\[1\] The historical roots of surface-supplied diving trace back over 5,000 years to ancient free-diving aids like hollow reeds, evolving significantly with the invention of the [diving bell](https://grokipedia.com/page/Diving_bell) in 1535 by [Guglielmo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Guglielmo) de Lorena\[3\] and the development of armored diving suits in the early [18th century](https://grokipedia.com/page/18th_century).\[1\] By the [19th century](https://grokipedia.com/page/19th_century), Augustus Siebe's introduction of the [standard diving dress](https://grokipedia.com/page/Standard_diving_dress) in 1837 marked a pivotal advancement, featuring a [copper](https://grokipedia.com/page/Copper) and brass [helmet](https://grokipedia.com/page/Helmet) connected to surface air pumps, which was widely used for wrecks like the HMS Royal George in 1843.\[4\] The U.S. [Navy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Navy) adopted the [Mark](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mark) V [helmet](https://grokipedia.com/page/Helmet) [system](https://grokipedia.com/page/System) in 1916, which remained in service through [World War II](https://grokipedia.com/page/World_War_II) for salvage operations, and further innovations in the 1930s, such as helium-oxygen mixtures, enabled deeper dives like the 1939 USS Squalus rescue at 243 fsw.\[1\] Modern systems, including lightweight helmets like the MK 21 and full-face masks like the MK 20, emerged in the mid-20th century, improving mobility and communication while adhering to standards from organizations like the U.S. [Navy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Navy) and [Occupational Safety and Health Administration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Occupational_Safety_and_Health_Administration) (OSHA).\[1\] Key equipment in surface-supplied diving includes the umbilical—a bundled [hose](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hose) delivering gas at pressures up to 225 pounds per square inch ([psi](https://grokipedia.com/page/Psi)) for depths beyond 190 fsw—and helmets or [masks](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Masks) with demand regulators that supply gas on [inhalation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Inhalation).\[5\] Support systems on the surface comprise air compressors, gas storage flasks, and control consoles for monitoring [diver](https://grokipedia.com/page/Diver) depth, gas flow, and voice communication, often supplemented by [emergency](https://grokipedia.com/page/Emergency) gas supplies (EGS) providing 10-15 minutes of bailout air.\[1\] For deeper or [saturation diving](https://grokipedia.com/page/Saturation_diving), dive bells and [decompression](https://grokipedia.com/page/Decompression) chambers are integrated, allowing divers to work at pressures up to 1000 fsw with surface [decompression](https://grokipedia.com/page/Decompression) protocols.\[1\] Safety in surface-supplied diving is prioritized through rigorous team structures, requiring a minimum of six personnel including a dive supervisor, console operator, [tender](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tender), and standby diver, with operations limited to 190 fsw unless authorized otherwise.\[2\] Risks such as [decompression sickness](https://grokipedia.com/page/Decompression_sickness), [nitrogen narcosis](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nitrogen_narcosis), and umbilical entanglement are mitigated by adherence to [decompression](https://grokipedia.com/page/Decompression) tables, mixed-gas usage below 150 fsw, and emergency procedures like rapid ascent to 10 fsw with EGS activation.\[1\] Regulations mandate safety harnesses with positive buckles, air purity standards (20-22% oxygen, less than 1,000 ppm CO2), and a [decompression](https://grokipedia.com/page/Decompression) chamber ready for use at the dive location.\[6\] Compared to [SCUBA](https://grokipedia.com/page/Scuba), this method reduces physiological stresses through better thermal protection via hot water suits and enhanced oversight, making it the preferred choice for demanding professional environments.\[1\]

Overview
--------

### Definition and principles

Surface-supplied diving is a diving technique in which the [diver](https://grokipedia.com/page/Diver) receives [breathing gas](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breathing_gas) continuously from the surface through a [hose](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hose) or umbilical connected to the [diver's](https://grokipedia.com/page/Diver) [breathing apparatus](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breathing_apparatus), such as a [helmet](https://grokipedia.com/page/Helmet) or [mask](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mask), thereby eliminating the need to carry self-contained gas cylinders and enabling prolonged underwater operations.\[1\] This method supports depths up to 190 feet of seawater (fsw) for air diving and 300 fsw for mixed-gas applications, with emergency extensions to 380 fsw, depending on the system.\[1\] The fundamental principles revolve around gas flow mechanics and [pressure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pressure) regulation to ensure safe [respiration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Respiration) at depth. [Breathing gas](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breathing_gas), which may include air, mixed gases like helium-oxygen, or oxygen-enriched mixtures, is pressurized at the surface by compressors to match the ambient hydrostatic [pressure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pressure) experienced by the [diver](https://grokipedia.com/page/Diver), preventing [lung](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lung) squeeze or overexpansion.\[1\] Umbilicals serve as the primary conduit, delivering the gas along with communications, electrical [power](https://grokipedia.com/page/Power), and sometimes hot water for [thermal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Thermal) [protection](https://grokipedia.com/page/Protection), while being tended to avoid entanglement or excessive tension.\[1\] The basic setup typically involves a surface [compressor](https://grokipedia.com/page/Compressor) (reciprocating low- or high-pressure types), reinforced hoses forming the umbilical, and the [diver](https://grokipedia.com/page/Diver)'s apparatus like the KM-37 or MK V [helmet](https://grokipedia.com/page/Helmet) for gas intake and exhaust management via demand regulators and valves.\[1\] A key physical principle underlying the pressurization of surface-supplied gas is [Boyle's law](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boyle's_law), which states that for a fixed [mass](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mass) of gas at constant [temperature](https://grokipedia.com/page/Temperature), the [pressure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pressure) and [volume](https://grokipedia.com/page/Volume) are inversely proportional: P1V1\=P2V2P\_1 V\_1 = P\_2 V\_2 This [equation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Equation) illustrates why surface gas must be compressed to maintain adequate [volume](https://grokipedia.com/page/Volume) and [density](https://grokipedia.com/page/Density) at depth—for instance, at 99 fsw (4 atmospheres absolute), the gas [volume](https://grokipedia.com/page/Volume) compresses to one-fourth its surface value, quadrupling its [density](https://grokipedia.com/page/Density) and affecting consumption rates.\[1\]\[7\]

### Advantages over scuba

Surface-supplied diving provides an unlimited supply of [breathing gas](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breathing_gas) from the surface, eliminating the constraints of finite [scuba](https://grokipedia.com/page/Scuba) cylinders that typically limit dives to 40-60 minutes at recreational depths. This [continuous delivery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Continuous_delivery) via the umbilical allows for extended bottom times of several hours or even days in [saturation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Saturation) operations, enabling more productive underwater work without frequent resurfacing or gas management interruptions.\[8\] Safety is significantly enhanced compared to [scuba](https://grokipedia.com/page/Scuba), as surface teams can continuously monitor gas quality and pressure, detect contaminants or supply issues in [real-time](https://grokipedia.com/page/Real-time), and provide immediate [emergency](https://grokipedia.com/page/Emergency) support. The umbilical facilitates rapid abort procedures, including [emergency](https://grokipedia.com/page/Emergency) cutoff valves that can isolate the diver's supply if needed, while also serving as a lifeline for location and rescue; additionally, hot water can be pumped through the hose to maintain diver comfort in cold environments, reducing [hypothermia](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hypothermia) risks during prolonged exposures. [Bailout](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bailout) bottles integrated into the system offer redundant air for ascent if the primary supply fails.\[9\]\[10\]\[8\] Divers using surface-supplied systems benefit from increased payload capacity, as they do not need to carry heavy gas cylinders, freeing up [buoyancy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Buoyancy) and strength for transporting tools and equipment essential for demanding tasks like underwater welding, cutting, or [construction](https://grokipedia.com/page/Construction). This contrasts with [scuba](https://grokipedia.com/page/Scuba), where cylinder weight and limited capacity restrict the amount of gear a [diver](https://grokipedia.com/page/Diver) can manage effectively.\[11\]\[12\] Operations can extend to greater depths beyond recreational scuba limits of around 40 meters, with surface-supplied mixed-gas diving supporting work up to 300 meters or more in [saturation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Saturation) configurations, where helium-oxygen mixtures mitigate narcosis and toxicity issues.\[13\] In practice, surface-supplied diving is particularly advantageous for [offshore](https://grokipedia.com/page/Offshore) oil rig maintenance, where [scuba](https://grokipedia.com/page/Scuba)'s depth and time restrictions would render tasks like subsea [pipeline](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pipeline) inspection or repair inefficient and hazardous; for instance, teams can complete complex interventions in a single dive that might require multiple scuba entries.\[14\]\[8\]

### Limitations and risks

Surface-supplied diving imposes significant mobility restrictions on the diver due to the tethered umbilical, which connects the [diver](https://grokipedia.com/page/Diver) to the surface supply and limits free movement compared to untethered [scuba](https://grokipedia.com/page/Scuba) systems. This [tether](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tether), typically consisting of hoses for gas, communications, and sometimes hot water, can become entangled or snagged on underwater obstacles, leading to immobility or restricted actions that increase the risk of accidents.\[1\]\[15\] The method's heavy reliance on surface support introduces vulnerabilities such as potential gas supply failures from compressor malfunctions or hose damage, as well as exposure to surface emergencies that could abruptly terminate the dive. Umbilical snags, for instance, can immobilize the [diver](https://grokipedia.com/page/Diver) and necessitate immediate [intervention](https://grokipedia.com/page/Intervention) from surface tenders, heightening the overall operational hazards.\[2\]\[1\] Depth limitations further constrain surface-supplied air diving, with a practical maximum of approximately 60 meters (197 feet of [seawater](https://grokipedia.com/page/Seawater)) for non-saturation air dives due to decompression requirements and physiological risks like [nitrogen narcosis](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nitrogen_narcosis).
