#### Emergency procedures \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Surface-supplied_diving&action=edit§ion=50 "Edit section: Emergency procedures")\] The diver must be able to deal with the following emergencies. Some are life-threatening, whereas others are more inconveniences.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-CDM_9-40)[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-CDM_10-77)[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-C2DTS-78) * Bailout to back gas, in the case of a failure of gas supply from the umbilical, or if the main air supply is contaminated. * Pneumo breathing, if the main air supply is cut, but the pneumo hose is intact. Pneumo gas can also be supplied by the standby diver * Voice communications failure is not usually an emergency, but can adversely affect work effectiveness and expose the diver to higher risk if anything else goes wrong. Ability to communicate with line signals can help here, particularly to assist in the decision whether the dive should be aborted, and if there are other more urgent problems. * Helmet flood. Depending on the severity of the flood, this can range from an annoyance to an emergency. A slow leak can be controlled by opening the free flow valve, which will drive a moderate flow of water out of the exhaust valve. A neck dam failure usually has this effect. * Broken faceplate. This is a real emergency, but very unlikely as the faceplate is usually a highly impact-resistant polymer and should not shatter. It can be mitigated by opening the free flow valve and holding the opening level, facing down, and breathing very carefully. a small hole or crack can be covered with a hand to slow the leak. * Demand valve failure. This is a minor problem if there is a free flow valve, but the dive will normally be terminated, as the bailout will not last long if needed. * Exhaust valve failure, like demand valve failure, can be dealt with by opening the free flow valve and ensuring a constant outflow of air. * Vomiting in the helmet. This can be a real emergency and life-threatening in a demand helmet with an orinasal mask if not handled effectively, as the diver can aspirate the vomit and asphyxiate. Once again, the action is to open the free flow valve, preferably before vomiting, and to inhale as carefully as possible. If there is no free flow valve, as on a full face mask, the purge button should clear the demand valve and orinasal mask, and the mask can be rinsed by lifting the bottom edge away from the face to let in some water, before purging again. With a free-flow helmet it is more a nuisance than an emergency. * Hot water supply failure. This can be life-threatening for deep heliox diving, and there is not much the diver can do but head back to the bell immediately. #### Wet bell and stage emergency procedures \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Surface-supplied_diving&action=edit§ion=51 "Edit section: Wet bell and stage emergency procedures")\] Emergency procedures for wet bell and diving stages include:[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-C2DTS-78)[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-CDM_11-79)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-IMCACoP-28) * [Loss of main gas supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving_skills#Surface_gas_supply_failure "Surface-supplied diving skills") to the bell * [Recovery of a distressed diver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving_skills#Rescue_of_the_working_diver "Surface-supplied diving skills") to the bell * [Abandonment of the bell or stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving_skills#Bell_abandonment "Surface-supplied diving skills") * Deployment of a surface standby diver * [Loss of heated water supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving_skills#Hot_water_supply_failure "Surface-supplied diving skills") for [hot water suits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_suit#Hot_water_suits "Diving suit") * [Voice communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diver_communications#Voice_communications "Diver communications") failures * [Dynamic positioning alarm and runout response for bell divers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_positioning#Dynamic_positioning_alarm_and_runout_response_for_bell_divers "Dynamic positioning"): Yellow and Red alerts. The standby diver will be prepared in the same way as the working diver, but will not enter the water until needed. He will usually be prepared to the stage of readiness to enter the water, and then will remove his mask, or have his helmet removed and will then sit in as comfortable a place as can be found, so that in case of an emergency he can be readied for action in as short a time as possible.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-BuRec_dive_manual-80) This often means setting up some form of shelter from the weather, and heat and sunshine are usually more of a problem than cold and wet. It is frequently necessary to cool the standby diver to avoid overheating, and dehydration can also be a problem.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-CADC_2015-81) When the working diver is using a helmet, the stand-by diver may use a full face mask or bandmask, as this makes it quicker to get into the water in an emergency. The stand-by diver's job is to wait until something goes wrong, and then be sent in to sort it out. For this reason a stand by diver should be one of the best divers on the team regarding diving skills and strength, but does not have to be expert at the work skills for the specific job. When deployed, the standby diver will normally follow the umbilical of the diver who is in trouble, as unless it has been severed, it will reliably lead to the correct diver. The standby diver must maintain communications with the supervisor throughout the dive and is expected to give a running commentary of progress so that the supervisor and surface crew know as much as possible what is happening and can plan accordingly, and must take the necessary steps to resolve incidents, which may involve supply of emergency air or locating and rescuing an injured or unconscious diver. In bell diving, the bellman is the primary standby diver, and may have to recover a distressed diver to the bell and give first aid if necessary and possible. There will generally also be a surface standby diver in a bell operation, as some types of assistance are provided from the surface.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-Standby_diver-82)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-IMCACoP-28)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-SSBA_Standby-83) A rescue tether or rescue strop is a short length of rope or webbing with a clip at one or both ends, which the stand-by diver uses to clip the unresponsive diver to his harness to free up both hands during a recovery. This can be useful if he needs to climb a structure, shotline or topographical feature, and the umbilicals can not be safely used to lift the divers due to snags or sharp edges.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-SSBA_Standby-83) A bellman is a stand-by diver who tends the working diver's umbilical from a wet or closed bell, and is ready to go to the diver's assistance at all times. The bellman must be in effective voice communication with the supervisor.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-IMCA_D022_2016-56) ### Underwater tending point \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Surface-supplied_diving&action=edit§ion=54 "Edit section: Underwater tending point")\] For some operations it is necessary to control the umbilical at a point underwater. This is known as an underwater tending point, and it may be done by another diver or by the diver passing through a closed [fairlead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairlead "Fairlead") placed in the required position. This is usually done to prevent inadvertent access to a known hazard by making the length of the umbilical extending beyond the tending point too short to let the diver get to the hazard. The fairlead must constrain the umbilical laterally and vertically, while allowing free passage away from and back to the bell or stage, and should not interfere with the bellman's ability to pay out or take up slack when the diver travels to the workplace and back. It may be held in position by suspending a weighted hoop from a crane, resting a frame on the bottom, or other methods as may suit the job. Underwater tending may also be used for penetrations of enclosed spaces, such as wrecks, caves, penstocks, sewers, culverts and the like. A diving stage or basket is a by default an underwater tending point, as the umbilical passes through it from the surface to the diver, which also serves as a guide line for the diver to get back to the stage. A diving bell is also an underwater tending point, as the [excursion umbilical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excursion_umbilical "Excursion umbilical") is tended from the bell by the bellman.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-IMCA_D022_2016-56) Occupational health and safety issues ------------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Surface-supplied_diving&action=edit§ion=55 "Edit section: Occupational health and safety issues")\] [Divers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving "Underwater diving") face specific physical and [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health "Health") risks when they go [underwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater "Underwater") with [diving equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_equipment "Diving equipment"), or use high pressure [breathing gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas"). A [hazard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard "Hazard") is any agent or situation that poses a level of threat to life, health, property, or environment. Most hazards remain dormant or potential, with only a theoretical risk of harm, and when a hazard becomes active, and produces undesirable consequences, it is called an incident and may culminate in an emergency or accident.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-CCOHS_Hazard-84) Hazard and vulnerability interact with likelihood of occurrence to create risk, which can be the probability of a specific undesirable consequence of a specific hazard, or the combined probability of undesirable consequences of all the hazards of a specific activity.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-CCOHS_Risk-85) A hazard that is understood and acknowledged may present a lower risk if appropriate precautions are taken, and the consequences may be less severe if mitigation procedures are planned and in place.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-Hazard_and_Risk-86) The presence of a combination of several hazards simultaneously is common in diving, and the effect is generally increased risk to the diver, particularly where the occurrence of an incident due to one hazard triggers other hazards with a resulting cascade of incidents. Many diving fatalities are the result of a cascade of incidents overwhelming the diver, who should be able to manage any single reasonably foreseeable incident.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-Lock_2011-87) The use of surface supplied breathing gas reduces one of the most significant hazards in diving, that of loss of breathing gas supply, and mitigates that risk by the use of a suitable emergency gas supply, usually in the form of a scuba bailout set, which is intended to provide the diver with sufficient breathing gas to reach a place of relative safety with more breathing gas available.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-IMCACoP-28)[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-CoP_Inshore-88) The risk of the diver getting lost or being unable to call for assistance is also drastically reduced in comparison with most scuba, as the diver is physically connected to the surface control point by the umbilical, making it relatively simple for the standby diver to get to a diver in distress, and the standard application of hard-wired voice communications allows the surface team to constantly monitor the diver's breathing sounds.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-IMCA_D022_2016_\(5\)-89) The assessed risk of a dive would generally be considered unacceptable if the diver is not expected to cope with any single reasonably foreseeable incident with a significant probability of occurrence during that dive. Precisely where the line is drawn depends on circumstances. Professional diving operations tend to be less tolerant of risk than recreational, particularly technical divers, who are less constrained by occupational health and safety legislation and codes of practice.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-IMCACoP-28): 35  This is one of the factors driving the use of surface supplied equipment where reasonably practicable for professional work. [Diving disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_disorders "Diving disorders") are [medical conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_conditions "Medical conditions") specifically arising from [underwater diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving "Underwater diving"). The [signs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sign "Medical sign") and [symptoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symptoms "Symptoms") of these may present during a dive, on surfacing, or up to several hours after a dive. Surface supplied divers have to breathe a gas which is at the same pressure as their surroundings ([ambient pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_pressure "Ambient pressure")), which can be much greater than on the surface. The ambient pressure underwater increases by 1 [standard atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_/(unit/) "Atmosphere (unit)") (100 kPa) for every 10 metres (33 ft) of depth.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-BE9-90) The principal disorders are: [decompression illness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_illness "Decompression illness") (which covers [decompression sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_sickness "Decompression sickness") and [arterial gas embolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arterial_gas_embolism "Arterial gas embolism")); [nitrogen narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_narcosis "Nitrogen narcosis"); [high pressure nervous syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_pressure_nervous_syndrome "High pressure nervous syndrome"); [oxygen toxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity "Oxygen toxicity"); and [pulmonary barotrauma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulmonary_barotrauma "Pulmonary barotrauma") (burst lung). Although some of these may occur in other settings, they are of particular concern during diving activities.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-BE9-90) Long term diving disorders include [dysbaric osteonecrosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysbaric_osteonecrosis "Dysbaric osteonecrosis"), which is associated with decompression sickness. These disorders are caused by [breathing gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas") at the high pressures encountered at depth, and divers may breathe a gas mixture different from air to mitigate these effects. [Nitrox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrox "Nitrox"), which contains more [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen") and less [nitrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen "Nitrogen"), is commonly used as a breathing gas to reduce the risk of decompression sickness at depths to about 40 metres (130 ft). [Helium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helium "Helium") may be added to reduce the amount of nitrogen and oxygen in the gas mixture when diving deeper, to reduce the effects of narcosis and to avoid the risk of oxygen toxicity. This is complicated at depths beyond about 150 metres (500 ft), because a helium–oxygen mixture ([heliox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliox "Heliox")) then causes high pressure nervous syndrome.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-BE9-90) More exotic mixtures such as [hydreliox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydreliox "Hydreliox"), a hydrogen–helium–oxygen mixture, are used at extreme depths to counteract this.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-Abraini1994-91) "Compressor diving" is a method of surface-supplied diving used in some tropical sea areas including the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines") and the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"). The divers swim with a [half mask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_mask "Diving mask") covering the eyes and nose and (often home-made) fins and are supplied air from the boat by plastic hoses from an industrial low-pressure [air compressor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_compressor "Air compressor") of the type commonly used to supply [jackhammers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackhammer "Jackhammer"). There is no reduction valve; the diver holds the hose end in his mouth with no demand valve or [mouthpiece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mouthpiece_/(scuba/) "Mouthpiece (scuba)"). Excess air spills out through the nose or lips. If several people are compressor diving from the same boat, several line tenders are needed in the boat to stop the airlines from getting tangled and blocked by kinks.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-Into_the_blue-15) Compressor diving is the most common method used to fish for Caribbean spiny lobster (_[Panulirus argus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panulirus_argus "Panulirus argus")_) in the Caribbean.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-Herrera-Moreno_and_Betancourt_2003a-92) However, it is illegal because it contributes to overfishing, is environmentally destructive, and is harmful to the health of the fishermen.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-Herrera-Moreno_and_Betancourt_2003b-93) When using compressors, fishermen use either gaffs or harpoons to spear lobsters immediately upon sight, killing or injuring the lobsters before they can be checked for eggs or assessed as legally sized. Compressors allow fishermen to remain in deeper waters for longer periods of time, facilitating reef damage by fishermen seeking lobsters hidden underneath corals and other living refuges. The misuse of compressors has also resulted in health problems for many fishermen, such as respiratory problems, limb paralysis, and death due to [decompression illness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_illness "Decompression illness").[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-WWF_2006-94) This method of diving is commonly used in [Philippine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines") waters for _pa-aling_ fishing, which is fishing with big nets on coral reef areas where a surface-dragged net would snag on coral; the compressor air hoses are also used to make a curtain of bubbles to corral and herd the fish into the nets, since _[muro-ami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muro-ami "Muro-ami")_ fishing was stopped in the area. At least one _pa-aling_ fishing fleet has been found and arrested in a protected fishery area. Compressor diving was shown, and so called, used for _pa-aling_ fishing, in episode 1 (Oceans: Into the Blue) of the [BBC television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_television "BBC television") series _[Human Planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Planet "Human Planet")_. The cameramen used ordinary [scuba gear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_gear "Scuba gear"), but one of them had a trial-dive with the crew's compressor-diving gear.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-Into_the_blue-15) Training and registration ------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Surface-supplied_diving&action=edit§ion=57 "Edit section: Training and registration")\] Almost all surface-supplied diving is done by professional divers, and consequently the training is done by schools which specialise in the training of professional divers. Registration of professional divers is generally subject to national or state legislation, though international recognition is available for some qualifications.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-Diving_at_Work_Regulations_1997-95)[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-SA_Diving_Regulations_2009-96)[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving#cite_note-IDSA-97) [![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Trevor_Jackson_returns_from_SS_Kyogle.jpg/250px-Trevor_Jackson_returns_from_SS_Kyogle.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trevor_Jackson_returns_from_SS_Kyogle.jpg) Wreck diver [Trevor Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Jackson_/(diver/) "Trevor Jackson (diver)") using a [re­breather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_rebreather "Diving rebreather") with open circuit bail­out cylinders returning from a 600-foot (180 m) dive. **Deep diving** is [underwater diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_diving "Underwater diving") to a depth beyond the normal range accepted by the associated community. In some cases this is a prescribed limit established by an authority, while in others it is associated with a level of certification or training, and it may vary depending on whether the diving is [recreational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_diving "Recreational diving"), [technical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_diving "Technical diving") or [commercial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_diving "Commercial diving"). [Nitrogen narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_narcosis "Nitrogen narcosis") becomes a hazard below 30 metres (98 ft) and [hypoxic breathing gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas#Classification_by_oxygen_fraction "Breathing gas") is required below 60 metres (200 ft) to lessen the risk of [oxygen toxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity "Oxygen toxicity"). For some recreational diving agencies, "Deep diving", or "Deep diver" may be a certification awarded to divers that have been trained to dive to a specified depth range, generally deeper than 30 metres (98 ft). However, the [Professional Association of Diving Instructors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_Association_of_Diving_Instructors "Professional Association of Diving Instructors") (PADI) defines anything from 18 to 30 metres (59 to 98 ft) as a "deep dive" in the context of recreational diving (other diving organisations vary), and considers _deep diving_ a form of [technical diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_diving "Technical diving").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-padi1-1)\[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_\] In [technical diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_diving "Technical diving"), a depth below about 60 metres (200 ft) where hypoxic [breathing gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas") becomes necessary to avoid [oxygen toxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity "Oxygen toxicity") may be considered a deep dive. In [professional diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_diving "Professional diving"), a depth that requires special equipment, procedures, or advanced training may be considered a deep dive. Deep diving can mean something else in the commercial diving field. For instance early experiments carried out by [COMEX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compagnie_maritime_d%27expertises "Compagnie maritime d'expertises") using [heliox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliox "Heliox") and [trimix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimix_/(breathing_gas/) "Trimix (breathing gas)") attained far greater depths than any recreational technical diving. One example being its "Janus 4" open-sea dive to 501 metres (1,640 ft) in 1977.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-comex2000-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-3) The open-sea diving depth record was achieved in 1988 by a team of COMEX and French Navy divers who performed pipeline connection exercises at a depth of 534 metres (1,750 ft) in the Mediterranean Sea as part of the "Hydra 8" programme employing [heliox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliox "Heliox") and [hydrox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrox_/(breathing_gas/) "Hydrox (breathing gas)"). The latter avoids the [high-pressure nervous syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-pressure_nervous_syndrome "High-pressure nervous syndrome") (HPNS) caused by helium and eases breathing due to its lower density.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-comex2000-2)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Hydra_8-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-5) These divers needed to breathe special gas mixtures because they were exposed to very high ambient pressure (more than 54 times atmospheric pressure). An [atmospheric diving suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suit "Atmospheric diving suit") (ADS) allows very deep dives of up to 700 metres (2,300 ft).[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-6) These suits are capable of withstanding the pressure at great depth permitting the diver to remain at normal atmospheric pressure. This eliminates the problems associated with breathing pressurised gases. In 2006 Chief Navy Diver Daniel Jackson set a record of 610 metres (2,000 ft) in an ADS.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-8) On 20 November 1992 COMEX's "Hydra 10" experiment simulated a dive in an onshore [hyperbaric chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_chamber#Out_of_water_use "Diving chamber") with [hydreliox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydreliox "Hydreliox"). [Théo Mavrostomos](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theo_Mavrostomos "fr:Theo Mavrostomos") spent two hours at a simulated depth of 701 metres (2,300 ft).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-comex2000-2)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-OTC-6073-MS-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-12) Depth ranges in underwater diving --------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Deep_diving&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Depth ranges in underwater diving")\] Assumed is the surface of the waterbody to be at or near sea level and underlies atmospheric pressure. Not included are the differing ranges of [freediving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freediving "Freediving") – without breathing during a dive.
Depth[nb 1]Comments
12 m (39 ft)Recreational diving limit for divers aged under 12 years old and EN 14153-1 / ISO 24801-1 level 1 (Supervised Diver) standard.[13]
18 m (60 ft)Recreational diving limit for Open Water Divers (e.g. PADI, NAUI).
20 m (66 ft)Recreational diving limit for EN 14153-2  ISO 24801-2 level 2 "Autonomous Diver" standard.[14]
21 m (69 ft)GUE Recreational Diver Level 1.[15]
30 m (98 ft)Recommended recreational diving limit for PADI Advanced Open Water divers[1][page needed] and GUE Recreational Diver Level 2.[15] Average depth at which nitrogen narcosis symptoms begin to be noticeable in adults.
40 m (130 ft)Depth limit for divers specified by Recreational Scuba Training Council[1][page needed] and GUE Recreational Diver Level 3.[15] Depth limit for a French level 2 diver accompanied by an instructor (level 4 diver), breathing air.[citation needed]
50 m (160 ft)Depth limit for divers breathing air specified by the British Sub-Aqua Club and Sub-Aqua Association.[16]
60 m (200 ft)Depth limit for a group of 2 to 3 French Level 3 recreational divers, breathing air.[17]
66 m (217 ft)Depth at which breathing compressed air exposes the diver to an oxygen partial pressure of 1.6 bar (23 psi). Greater depth is considered to expose the diver to an unacceptable risk of oxygen toxicity.[nb 2]
100 m (330 ft)One of the recommended technical diving limits. Maximum depth authorised for divers who have completed Trimix Diver certification with IANTD[18] or Advanced Trimix Diver certification with TDI.[19]
156 m (512 ft)Deepest scuba dive on compressed air (July 1999 in Puerto Galera, Philippines).[20]
200 m (660 ft)Limit for surface light penetration sufficient for plant growth in clear water, though some visibility may be possible farther down.[nb 3]
230 m (750 ft)First dive on a hydrox-rebreather (14 February 2023 in the Pearse Resurgence, New Zealand).[21]
290 m (950 ft)Deepest ocean dive on a rebreather (23 March 2014 in Gili Trawangan, Indonesia).[22]
312 m (1,024 ft)Deepest cave diving on a rebreather (6 January 2024 in Font Estramar, France).
316 m (1,037 ft)Deepest dive on a rebreather (10 October 2018 in Lake Garda, Italy).[23]
332 m (1,089 ft)Deepest scuba dive, deepest dive on trimix (18 September 2014 in Dahab, Egypt).[24][25]
534 m (1,752 ft)COMEX Hydra 8 dives on hydreliox (February 1988 offshore Marseille, France).[2][4][10]
Particular problems associated with deep dives ---------------------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Deep_diving&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Particular problems associated with deep dives")\] Deep diving has more hazards and greater risk than basic [open-water diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-water_diving "Open-water diving").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-29) [Nitrogen narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_narcosis "Nitrogen narcosis"), the "narks" or "rapture of the deep", starts with feelings of euphoria and over-confidence but then leads to numbness and memory impairment similar to [alcohol intoxication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_intoxication "Alcohol intoxication").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-padi1-1)\[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_\] [Decompression sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_sickness "Decompression sickness"), or the "bends", can happen if a diver ascends too rapidly, when excess [inert gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inert_gas#Diving "Inert gas") leaves solution in the blood and tissues and forms bubbles. These bubbles produce mechanical and biochemical effects that lead to the condition. The onset of symptoms depends on the severity of the tissue gas loading and may develop during ascent in severe cases, but is frequently delayed until after reaching the surface.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-padi1-1)\[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_\] Bone degeneration ([dysbaric osteonecrosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysbaric_osteonecrosis "Dysbaric osteonecrosis")) is caused by the bubbles forming inside the bones; most commonly the upper arm and the thighs. Deep diving involves a much greater danger of all of these, and presents the additional risk of [oxygen toxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity "Oxygen toxicity"), which may lead to convulsions underwater. Very deep diving using a helium-oxygen mixture ([heliox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliox "Heliox")) or a hydrogen-helium-oxygen mixture ([hydreliox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydreliox "Hydreliox")) carries the risk of [high-pressure nervous syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-pressure_nervous_syndrome "High-pressure nervous syndrome") and [hydrogen narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_narcosis "Hydrogen narcosis"). Coping with the physical and physiological stresses of deep diving requires good [physical conditioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_fitness "Physical fitness").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-30) Using [open-circuit scuba equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_set "Scuba set"), consumption of [breathing gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas") is proportional to [ambient pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_pressure "Ambient pressure") – so at 50 metres (164 ft), where the pressure is 6 bars (87 psi), a diver breathes six times as much as on the surface (1 bar, 14.5 psi). Heavy physical exertion makes the diver breathe even more gas, and gas becomes [denser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density "Density") requiring increased effort to breathe with depth, leading to increased risk of [hypercapnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercapnia "Hypercapnia") – an excess of [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") in the blood. The need to do [decompression stops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_stop "Decompression stop") increases with depth. A diver at 6 metres (20 ft) may be able to dive for many hours without needing to do decompression stops. At depths greater than 40 metres (131 ft), a diver may have only a few minutes at the deepest part of the dive before decompression stops are needed. In the event of an emergency, the diver cannot make an immediate ascent to the surface without risking [decompression sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_sickness "Decompression sickness"). All of these considerations result in the amount of breathing gas required for deep diving being much greater than for shallow open water diving. The diver needs a disciplined approach to planning and conducting dives to minimise these additional risks. Many of these problems are avoided by the use of surface supplied breathing gas, closed [diving bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell "Diving bell"), and [saturation diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving "Saturation diving"), at the cost of logistical complexity, reduced maneuverability of the diver, and greater expense. In ambient pressure diving the [work of breathing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_of_breathing "Work of breathing") is a major limitation. Carbon dioxide elimination is limited by the capacity of the diver to cycle breathing gas through the lungs, and when this reaches the maximum, carbon dioxide will build up in the tissues and the diver will succumb to acute [hypercapnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercapnia "Hypercapnia"). Work of breathing is affected by breathing gas density, which is a function of the gas mixture and the pressure due to depth.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Anthony_and_Mitchell_2016-31)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Mitchell_et_al_2007-32) In atmospheric pressure diving the limitations include the ability of the diver to bend the joints of the suit under pressure, and for the joints to remain watertight while bending.

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Decompression_Dive-Preparation.JPG/250px-Decompression_Dive-Preparation.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Decompression_Dive-Preparation.JPG) [Technical divers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_diving "Technical diving") preparing for a mixed-gas [decompression dive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_practice "Decompression practice"). Note the [backplate and wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backplate_and_wing "Backplate and wing") setup with [side mounted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidemount_diving "Sidemount diving") [stage tanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_cylinder#Applications "Diving cylinder") containing [EAN50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrox "Nitrox") (left side) and pure [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen") (right side). Both equipment and procedures can be adapted to deal with the problems of greater depth. Usually the two are combined, as the procedures must be adapted to suit the equipment, and in some cases the equipment is needed to facilitate the procedures. ### Equipment adaptations for deeper diving \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Deep_diving&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Equipment adaptations for deeper diving")\] The equipment used for deep diving depends on both the depth and the type of diving. [Scuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_set "Scuba set") is limited to equipment that can be carried by the diver or is easily deployed by the [dive team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dive_team "Dive team"), while [surface-supplied diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving "Surface-supplied diving") equipment can be more extensive, and much of it stays above the water where it is operated by the [diving support team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_team "Diving team").\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] * Scuba divers carry larger volumes of [breathing gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas") to compensate for the increased gas consumption and decompression stops. * [Rebreathers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_rebreather "Diving rebreather"), though more complex, manage gas much more efficiently than [open-circuit scuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_set "Scuba set"). * Use of [helium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helium "Helium")\-based breathing gases such as [trimix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimix_/(breathing_gas/) "Trimix (breathing gas)") reduces [nitrogen narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_narcosis "Nitrogen narcosis") and reduces the [toxic effects of oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity "Oxygen toxicity") at depth. * A [diving shot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_shot "Diving shot"), a [decompression trapeze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_trapeze "Decompression trapeze"), or a [decompression buoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_buoy "Decompression buoy") can help divers control their ascent and return to the surface at a position that can be monitored by their surface support team at the end of a dive. * Decompression can be [accelerated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_practice#Accelerated_decompression "Decompression practice") by using specially blended breathing gas mixtures containing lower proportions of inert gas. * [Surface supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_supplied_diving "Surface supplied diving") of breathing gases reduces the risk of running out of gas. * In-water decompression can be minimized by using [dry bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell#Structure_of_a_typical_closed_bell "Diving bell") and [decompression chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_chamber "Diving chamber"). * [Hot-water suits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_suit#Hot_water_suits "Diving suit") can prevent [hypothermia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothermia "Hypothermia") due to the high heat loss when using helium-based breathing gases. * [Diving bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell "Diving bell") and [lockout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_underwater_diving_terminology:_H%E2%80%93O#lockout "Glossary of underwater diving terminology: H–O") [submersibles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submersible "Submersible") expose the diver to the direct underwater environment for less time, and provide a relatively safe shelter that does not require decompression, with a dry environment where the diver can rest, take refreshment, and if necessary, receive first aid in an emergency. * Breathing gas [reclaim system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_underwater_diving_terminology:_P%E2%80%93S#reclaim_system "Glossary of underwater diving terminology: P–S")s reduce the cost of using helium-based breathing gases, by recovering and recycling exhaled surface supplied gas, analogous to rebreathers for scuba diving. * The most radical equipment adaptation for deep diving is to isolate the diver from the direct pressure of the environment, using armoured [atmospheric diving suits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_diving_suits "Atmospheric diving suits") that allow diving to depths beyond those currently possible at ambient pressure. These rigid, articulated exoskeleton suits are sealed against water and withstand external pressure while providing life support to the diver for several hours at an internal pressure of approximately normal surface [atmospheric pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure "Atmospheric pressure"). This avoids the problems of [inert gas narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inert_gas_narcosis "Inert gas narcosis"), [decompression sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_sickness "Decompression sickness"), [barotrauma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barotrauma "Barotrauma"), [oxygen toxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity "Oxygen toxicity"), high [work of breathing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_of_breathing "Work of breathing"), [compression arthralgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compression_arthralgia "Compression arthralgia"), [high-pressure nervous syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-pressure_nervous_syndrome "High-pressure nervous syndrome") and [hypothermia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothermia "Hypothermia"), but at the cost of reduced mobility and dexterity, logistical problems due to the bulk and mass of the suits, and high equipment costs. ### Procedural adaptations for deeper diving \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Deep_diving&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Procedural adaptations for deeper diving")\] Procedural adaptations for deep diving can be classified as those procedures for operating specialized equipment, and those that apply directly to the problems caused by exposure to high ambient pressures. * The most important procedure for dealing with physiological problems of breathing at high ambient pressures associated with deep diving is [decompression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_/(diving/) "Decompression (diving)"). This is necessary to prevent inert gas bubble formation in the body tissues of the diver, which can cause severe injury. [Decompression procedures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_practice "Decompression practice") have been derived for a large range of pressure exposures, using a large range of gas mixtures. These basically entail a slow and controlled reduction in pressure during ascent by using a restricted ascent rate and [decompression stops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_stop "Decompression stop"), so that the inert gases dissolved in the tissues of the diver can be eliminated harmlessly during normal respiration. * [Gas management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dive_planning#Gas_planning "Dive planning") procedures are necessary to ensure that the diver has access to suitable and sufficient breathing gas at all times during the dive, both for the planned dive profile and for any reasonably foreseeable contingency. Scuba gas management is logistically more complex than surface supply, as the diver must either carry all the gas, must follow a route where previously arranged gas supply depots have been set up (stage cylinders). or must rely on a team of support divers who will provide additional gas at pre-arranged signals or points on the planned dive. On very deep scuba dives or on occasions where long decompression times are planned, it is a common practice for support divers to meet the primary team at decompression stops to check if they need assistance, and these support divers will often carry extra gas supplies in case of need. [![Image 4: Closed circuit rebreather](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Plongee-RecycleurInspiration_20040221-153656.jpg/250px-Plongee-RecycleurInspiration_20040221-153656.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plongee-RecycleurInspiration_20040221-153656.jpg) [Closed circuit re­breather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_rebreather#Closed_circuit_mixed_gas_rebreathers "Diving rebreather") ([AP Diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AP_Diving "AP Diving") "In­spi­ra­tion"). * [Rebreather diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebreather_diving "Rebreather diving") can reduce the bulk of the gas supplies for long and deep scuba dives, at the cost of more complex equipment with more potential failure modes, requiring more demanding procedures and higher procedural task loading. * [Surface supplied diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_supplied_diving "Surface supplied diving") distributes the task loading between the divers and the support team, who remain in the relative safety and comfort of the surface control position. Gas supplies are limited only by what is available at the control position, and the diver only needs to carry sufficient bailout capacity to reach the nearest place of safety, which may be a [diving bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell "Diving bell") or lockout submersible. * [Saturation diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving "Saturation diving") is a procedure used to reduce the high-risk decompression a diver is exposed to during a long series of deep underwater exposures. By keeping the diver under high pressure for the whole job, and only decompressing at the end of several days to weeks of underwater work, a single decompression can be done at a slower rate without adding much overall time to the job. During the saturation period, the diver lives in a pressurized environment at the surface, and is transported under pressure to the underwater work site in a closed diving bell. Amongst [technical divers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_diving "Technical diving"), there are divers who participate in ultra-deep diving on scuba below 200 metres (656 ft). This practice requires high levels of training, experience, discipline, fitness and surface support. Only twenty-six people are known to have ever dived to at least 240 metres (790 ft) on self-contained breathing apparatus recreationally.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Gomes2009-22)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Gomes2014-33)[\[nb 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-34)[\[nb 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-35) The "Holy Grail" of deep scuba diving was the 300 metres (980 ft) mark, first achieved by [John Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bennett_/(diver/) "John Bennett (diver)") in 2001, and has only been achieved five times since.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Due to the short bottom times and long decompression, scuba dives to these depths are generally only done for deep cave exploration or as record attempts. The difficulties involved in ultra-deep diving are numerous. Although commercial and military divers\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] often operate at those depths, or even deeper, they are surface supplied. All of the complexities of ultra-deep diving are magnified by the requirement of the diver to carry (or provide for) their own gas underwater. These lead to rapid descents and "bounce dives". This has led to extremely high mortality rates amongst those who practice ultra-deep diving.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Notable ultra-deep diving fatalities include [Sheck Exley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheck_Exley "Sheck Exley"), [John Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bennett_/(diver/) "John Bennett (diver)"), [Dave Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Shaw_/(diver/) "David Shaw (diver)") and [Guy Garman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Garman "Guy Garman"). [Mark Ellyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Ellyatt "Mark Ellyatt"), Don Shirley and [Pascal Bernabé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_Bernab%C3%A9 "Pascal Bernabé") were involved in serious incidents and were fortunate to survive their dives. Despite the extremely high mortality rate, the _[Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records")_ continues to maintain a record for scuba diving[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-deepest_scuba-28) (although the record for deep diving with compressed air has not been updated since 1999, given the high accident rate). Amongst those who do survive significant health issues are reported. [Mark Ellyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Ellyatt "Mark Ellyatt") is reported to have suffered permanent lung damage; [Pascal Bernabé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_Bernab%C3%A9 "Pascal Bernabé") (who was injured on his dive when a light on his mask imploded[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-36)) and [Nuno Gomes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuno_Gomes_/(diver/) "Nuno Gomes (diver)") reported short to medium term hearing loss.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-37)\[_[unreliable source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")_\] Serious issues that confront divers engaging in ultra-deep diving on self-contained breathing apparatus include: [Compression arthralgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compression_arthralgia "Compression arthralgia") Deep aching pain in the knees, shoulders, fingers, back, hips, neck, and ribs caused by exposure to high ambient pressure at a relatively high rate of descent (i.e., in "bounce dives"). [High-pressure nervous syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-pressure_nervous_syndrome "High-pressure nervous syndrome") (HPNS) HPNS, brought on by breathing helium under extreme pressure causes [tremors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremor "Tremor"), [myoclonic jerking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myoclonic_jerk "Myoclonic jerk"), [somnolence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somnolence "Somnolence"), [EEG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EEG "EEG") changes,[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-38) [visual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual "Visual") disturbance, [nausea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausea "Nausea"), [dizziness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizziness "Dizziness"), and decreased [mental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mind "Mind") performance. Symptoms of HPNS are exacerbated by rapid compression, a feature common to ultra-deep "bounce" dives. [Isobaric counterdiffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isobaric_counterdiffusion "Isobaric counterdiffusion") (ICD) ICD is the diffusion of one inert gas into body tissues while another inert gas is diffusing out. It is a complication that can occur during decompression, and that can result in the formation or growth of bubbles without changes in the environmental pressure. [Decompression algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_practice#Decompression_algorithms "Decompression practice") There are no reliable decompression algorithms tested for such depths on the assumption of an immediate surfacing. Almost all decompression methodology for such depths is based upon saturation, and calculates ascent times in days rather than hours. Accordingly, ultra-deep dives are almost always a partly experimental basis.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] In addition, "ordinary" risks like size of gas reserves, hypothermia, dehydration and oxygen toxicity are compounded by extreme depth and exposure and long in-water decompression times. Some technical diving equipment is simply not designed for the greater pressures at these depths, and reports of key equipment (including submersible pressure gauges) imploding are not uncommon.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

A severe risk in ultra-deep air diving is deep water blackout, or depth blackout, a loss of consciousness at depths below 50 metres (160 ft) with no clear primary cause, associated with [nitrogen narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_narcosis "Nitrogen narcosis"), a neurological impairment with anaesthetic effects caused by high partial pressure of nitrogen dissolved in nerve tissue, and possibly acute [oxygen toxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity "Oxygen toxicity").[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Exley_1986-78) The term is not in widespread use at present, as where the actual cause of blackout is known, a more specific term is preferred. The depth at which deep water blackout occurs is extremely variable and unpredictable.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-79) Before the popular availability of [trimix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimix_/(breathing_gas/) "Trimix (breathing gas)"), attempts were made to set world record depths using air. The extreme risk of both narcosis and oxygen toxicity in the divers contributed to a high fatality rate in those attempting records. In his book, _Deep Diving_, [Bret Gilliam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bret_Gilliam "Bret Gilliam") chronicles the various fatal attempts to set records as well as the smaller number of successes.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Gilliam-80) From the comparatively few who survived extremely deep air dives:

In deference to the high accident rate, the [Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records") have ceased to publish records for deep air dives, after Manion's dive.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Gomes2014-33) The risk of death in scuba depth record attempts is much greater than for surface-supplied diving to similar depths, where saturation divers do productive work at depths greater than scuba depth records The reasons are [physiological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_physiology_of_underwater_diving "Human physiology of underwater diving") and logistical. Deep [surface-supplied diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-supplied_diving "Surface-supplied diving") is done using [saturation mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturation_diving "Saturation diving"), where the diver is compressed over a long period and can avoid or minimise [inert gas narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inert_gas_narcosis "Inert gas narcosis"), [high-pressure nervous syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-pressure_nervous_syndrome "High-pressure nervous syndrome") (HPNS), and [compression arthralgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compression_arthralgia "Compression arthralgia"), and is decompressed from suturation in the relative comfort and safety of a diving chamber. The saturation diver is provided with an adequate and secure breathing gas supply, wears a [diving helmet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_helmet "Diving helmet") which protects the airways and is supported by a [bellman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellman_/(diving/) "Bellman (diving)").\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] There is a range of opinions about the value of extreme exposure records, attempted intentionally, and the question may be asked whether the activity has any value beyond merely setting a new record.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-87)[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Fifis_2019-88) ### Gas density and work of breathing \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Deep_diving&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Gas density and work of breathing")\] A high work of breathing means that the diver has correspondingly less reserve capacity to deal with an incident in which high exertion is necessary to rectify a problem, even for a short time. For example, a sudden loss of buoyancy may require the diver to fin upwards until the problem can be more efficiently managed. If this burst of exertion overwhelms the capacity to eliminate the carbon dioxide that it generates, the diver may be unable to avoid being overwhelmed by hypercapnia.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Stewart-89)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Mitchell_et_al_2007-32) Breathing gas can be optimised for low work of breathing by using higher helium fraction and minimum nitrogen, a small amount of which is needed to limit HPNS in the fast descents used by scuba divers to make [gas logistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_gas_planning#Quantity_of_open_circuit_breathing_gas "Scuba gas planning") practicable, and keep the in-water decompression requirements manageable.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Bennett_and_Rostain-90) Use of [rebreathers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_rebreather "Diving rebreather") can help with gas supply logistics, but inherently increases work of breathing as the gas is circulated through the scrubber by the breathing of the diver. Use of hydrogen in the mixture is experimental, and while it does improve work of breathing, and appears to reduce HPNS, it can only be used at considerable depth due to explosion risks, so the gas logistics are further complicated. Even less data is available on decompressing from exposures to mixtures containing hydroge than trimix and heliox exposures.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Stewart-89)[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Harris-91) ### Decompression schedules \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Deep_diving&action=edit§ion=12 "Edit section: Decompression schedules")\] [Decompression schedules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_schedule "Decompression schedule") for [bounce dive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounce_dive "Bounce dive") profiles to record depths are experimental and untested, and the decompression risk is basically unknown, and can only be estimated by extrapolation when using current decompression theory. Profiles and schedules used by record holders who survives the dive may be of some use, as they at least worked once,[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Stewart-89) but no allowance is made for environmental and personal variables, the effects of which are in any case not quantifiable by any currently available decompression algorithm.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-92) The choice of gas mix for extreme depth on scuba is a compromise between density considerations, which call for minimising nitrogen, narcosis issues, which call for minimising nitrogen, and HPNS considerations, which require some nitrogen and limiting the rate of compression. If hydrogen is considered as an alternative, a possible explosion risk is balanced against less narcosis than nitrogen, lower density, possible reduction of HPNS, and an unknown effect on decompression.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-Harris-91)[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-93) ### Inner ear decompression sickness \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Deep_diving&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Inner ear decompression sickness")\] IEDCS is known to occur during ascent after some deep dives, but the causes are uncertain. Inner ear decompression sickness is known to result from isobaric counterdiffusion, but the known triggering conditions do not occur with closed-ircuit rebreathers. Nevertheless the symptoms of intense vertigo and nausea have occurred on both CCR and open circuit dives during ascent, which increase the risk of choking on aspired vomit, and drowning, and are likely to compromise decompression.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_diving#cite_note-94)

A scuba diver must carry enough breathing gas to manage any single reasonably foreseeable incident and the expected consequences of that incident. There is a choice between the mechanical simplicity and reliability but large mass and volume, and the need for multiple gas switches of open circuit equipment, and the complexity and larger number of possible failure modes, and generally higher work of breathing of CCR, with its smaller mass and volume, and integral gas mixture control. ### Psychological issues \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Deep_diving&action=edit§ion=17 "Edit section: Psychological issues")\] * [Risk denial](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Risk_denial&action=edit&redlink=1 "Risk denial (page does not exist)") * [Target fixation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_fixation "Target fixation") * [Dunning–Kruger effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunning%E2%80%93Kruger_effect "Dunning–Kruger effect") * [Sunk cost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunk_cost "Sunk cost")

### Fatalities during depth record attempts \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Deep_diving&action=edit§ion=19 "Edit section: Fatalities during depth record attempts")\] Diving activities are inherently risky, due to the underwater environment, and the diver manages risk by the appropriate use of equipment, using skills developed by learning, training and practice, along with suitable support by the members of a skilled and prepared team. Scuba diving forgoes some of the most relevant safety equipment and procedures to gain mobility and range, and it is inherently riskier than surface supplied diving for a number of reasons, most notably, the limit on gas supply that the diver can carry. Attempts to break depth records push the physiological limits, and this reduces the margin for error to the extent the diver may not be able to recover from an incident that could be managed at shallower depths, and the psychological situation may induce a diver to ignore a developing problem until it is too late. Consequently, depth record attempts have a poor safety record, with a high fatality rate. * [Maurice Fargues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Fargues "Maurice Fargues"), a member of the GRS (_Groupement de Recherches Sous-marines_, Underwater Research Group headed by [Jacques Cousteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Cousteau "Jacques Cousteau")), died in 1947 after losing consciousness at depth in an experiment to see how deep a scuba diver could go. He reached 120 m (394 ft) before failing to return line signals.
